### New Findings: TypeScript 5.8 `--libReplacement: false` for CI Performance

TypeScript 5.8 adds `--libReplacement false`, which disables the lookup for `@types/lib-replacement` packages (custom `lib.d.ts` replacements). For most TypeScript projects that do not use custom lib replacements, disabling this lookup reduces `tsc` startup time and file watching overhead.

```json
// tsconfig.json — disable lib replacement lookup for faster CI type checking
// Add this if you don't use @total-typescript/ts-reset or similar lib-replacement packages
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,
    "libReplacement": false,   // TS 5.8+: skip scanning for custom lib.d.ts replacements
    // Impact: ~200–500ms faster cold start on large projects in CI
    // No functional difference if you don't use custom lib replacements
    "lib": ["ES2022", "DOM"]   // Explicit lib prevents any lib replacement lookup
  }
}
```

**WHY this matters for shift-left**: CI type check speed is a primary determinant of whether teams keep `tsc --noEmit` as a required PR gate. Every second of CI time that can be saved without sacrificing safety reduces the temptation to remove the gate. `--libReplacement false` is a zero-risk optimization for the majority of TypeScript projects.

> [community] **Lesson (TypeScript build performance community, 2025)**: The `libReplacement` feature was introduced to support packages like `@total-typescript/ts-reset` that override standard library types. For projects that don't use these packages (the majority), the feature adds a file system lookup on every `tsc` invocation. The `false` flag disables the lookup entirely. Combined with `--noCheck` for build parallelization and `--incremental` for pre-commit, `libReplacement: false` is part of a layered CI performance strategy.

### New Findings: Vitest 4.0 Visual Regression as Shift-Left (Browser Mode)

Vitest 4.0 (released 2025) stabilized Browser Mode — removing the `experimental` tag — and added `toMatchScreenshot()` for visual regression testing. Browser mode runs component tests in a real Chromium/Firefox/WebKit instance without a full application server. Combined with `toMatchScreenshot()`, this provides a shift-left visual regression gate at the component level.

```typescript
// src/components/Button.spec.tsx — Vitest Browser Mode + visual regression (Vitest 4.0+)
// Runs in a real browser (Chromium via Playwright provider), no server required
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { render } from '@vitest/browser/context';
import { Button } from './Button.js';

describe('Button — visual regression (Vitest 4.0 Browser Mode)', () => {
  it('primary variant matches baseline screenshot', async () => {
    const { getByRole } = render(<Button variant="primary" label="Submit" />);
    const button = getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' });

    // toMatchScreenshot: captures screenshot, compares to stored baseline
    // First run: creates baseline in __screenshots__/
    // Subsequent runs: fails if pixel diff exceeds threshold (default: 0.1%)
    await expect(button).toMatchScreenshot('primary-button.png', {
      // Diff tolerance: 0.5% of pixels may differ (for antialiasing differences)
      maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.005,
    });
  });

  it('disabled state renders with reduced opacity', async () => {
    const { getByRole } = render(<Button variant="primary" label="Submit" disabled />);
    const button = getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' });

    await expect(button).toMatchScreenshot('primary-button-disabled.png');
    // Also assert ARIA state: disabled button is not interactive
    await expect(button).toBeDisabled();
  });

  it('button is visible in viewport', async () => {
    const { getByRole } = render(<Button variant="primary" label="Submit" />);
    const button = getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' });

    // toBeInViewport: uses IntersectionObserver — shift-left for layout/scroll bugs
    await expect(button).toBeInViewport();
  });
});
```

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — Vitest 4.0 Browser Mode provider configuration
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    browser: {
      enabled: true,
      name: 'chromium',             // 'chromium' | 'firefox' | 'webkit'
      provider: 'playwright',       // Provider: @vitest/browser-playwright
      headless: true,               // CI: always headless
      screenshotDirectory: '__screenshots__',  // Store baselines in git
      screenshotFailureDirectory: '__screenshot-failures__',  // CI artifact on failure
    },
    // Regular unit tests run in Node.js pool (not browser)
    pool: 'forks',
  },
});
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/visual-regression.yml — Vitest Browser Mode visual regression on PRs
name: Visual Regression Tests
on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ['src/components/**', '__screenshots__/**']

jobs:
  visual-regression:
    name: Component Visual Regression (Vitest 4.0)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci

      # Install Playwright browsers for Vitest Browser Mode
      - run: npx playwright install chromium --with-deps

      - name: Run visual regression tests
        run: npx vitest run --project browser --reporter=github-actions
        # Fails if any component screenshot diff exceeds threshold

      - name: Upload screenshot diffs on failure
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: failure()
        with:
          name: screenshot-diffs-${{ github.run_number }}
          path: __screenshot-failures__/
          # Download this artifact to see exactly what changed visually
```

**WHY visual regression at the component level is shift-left**: Full-page E2E visual regression tests (Playwright `toHaveScreenshot()`) require a running application server and capture the entire page — one UI change causes dozens of unrelated snapshots to fail. Component-level visual regression tests capture only the component under test. This makes failures specific ("the Button's disabled state changed opacity") rather than broad ("the homepage looks different"). The shift-left benefit: visual regressions are caught in PR CI (< 2 minutes) rather than in staging QA (hours or days).

> [community] **Lesson (Vitest Browser Mode adopters, 2025)**: The primary adoption friction for Vitest Browser Mode is the `__screenshots__` baseline management. Teams that commit baseline screenshots to git encounter large PR diffs when component styles change intentionally. Best practice: use `--update-snapshots` flag on a dedicated branch to update baselines, review the visual changes in PR, and merge separately from the code change. This decouples "we changed the button style" from "we changed the button logic."

> [community] **Lesson (Vitest 4.0 vs 3.x Browser Mode)**: Vitest 3.x Browser Mode was experimental and unstable — teams encountered frequent Playwright process crashes, screenshot comparison inconsistencies across platforms, and unclear migration paths. Vitest 4.0 stabilized the provider architecture by creating a single Vite server for all browser test instances. Teams that skipped Browser Mode in v3 should re-evaluate in v4 — the stability and provider separation (`@vitest/browser-playwright`) make it production-ready.

### New Findings: Martin Fowler's Shift-Left Taxonomy (Updated Reference)

The Martin Fowler shift-left testing article (martinfowler.com/articles/shift-left-testing.html, cataloged 2026-05-12) provides a four-category taxonomy of shift-left approaches that extends beyond the SAST/pre-commit framing. Understanding which category each practice belongs to clarifies prioritization.

**The four Fowler shift-left categories:**

| Category | Description | TypeScript Example | When to invest |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Traditional shift-left** | Move existing test phases earlier (UAT → integration → unit) | Replace manual QA sessions with automated PR gates | Immediately — high ROI |
| **Incremental shift-left** | Add test levels closer to code creation | Unit tests → component tests → contract tests | After traditional gates are in place |
| **Agile/DevOps shift-left** | Continuous testing integrated into every commit | Pre-commit hooks, PR required checks | Core shift-left investment |
| **Model-based shift-left** | Formal verification, type-system encoding, property-based testing | TypeScript strict mode, Zod schemas, fast-check property tests | After agile/DevOps gates mature |

**WHY the taxonomy matters for prioritization**: Teams often invest in Model-based shift-left (strict TypeScript, formal schema validation) before they have Agile/DevOps shift-left in place (automated PR gates). The cost-of-defects argument is strongest for Agile/DevOps shift-left — fixing a defect in the PR feedback loop (minutes) vs. discovering it in QA (hours). Model-based investments only compound that benefit; they do not substitute for it.

> [community] **Lesson (Fowler shift-left framing, production teams)**: The "QA role transformation" that Fowler describes — QA engineers shift from executing manual test passes to building test infrastructure and frameworks — is the most underinvested aspect of shift-left in most organizations. Teams that only install SAST tools but do not re-skill QA engineers as test automation developers see the tools adopted superficially (configured but not enforced). The tooling investment is necessary but insufficient without the role change.

> [community] **Lesson (shift-left taxonomy application, 2025)**: Teams that frame shift-left as "we're moving tests earlier" (Fowler's Traditional category) get less organizational adoption than teams that frame it as "we're embedding quality in the development process" (Agile/DevOps category). The former feels like extra work for developers; the latter feels like removing rework. The framing determines whether developers see pre-commit hooks as a tax or a service.

## Cycle 22 — 2026-05-13

### TypeScript 5.8 and 5.9 — Shift-Left Compiler Improvements

The TypeScript compiler continues to expand its role as the primary shift-left tool for TypeScript projects. The 5.8 and 5.9 releases added features that directly affect pre-commit and CI gate configurations.

#### TypeScript 5.8: Key Shift-Left Changes

**`--erasableSyntaxOnly` flag (TS 5.8+)**

Node.js 22.6+ added `--experimental-strip-types` and Node.js 23.6+ added `--strip-types` (unflagged). Both rely on stripping TypeScript type annotations without transformation — which is impossible for TypeScript constructs that emit JavaScript code (enums, namespaces, parameter properties). The `--erasableSyntaxOnly` flag makes the TypeScript compiler enforce this constraint at compile time.

```json
// tsconfig.json — enable for Node.js native TypeScript execution compatibility
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "erasableSyntaxOnly": true,       // Error on enums, namespaces, parameter properties
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,     // Complement: enforces explicit type-only imports
    "noEmit": true,

    // Use 'as const' satisfies pattern instead of enums:
    // const Direction = { Up: 'Up', Down: 'Down' } as const satisfies Record<string, string>;
    // type Direction = typeof Direction[keyof typeof Direction];
    //   → same type safety as enum, fully erasable, works with Node.js --strip-types
  }
}
```

**WHY this matters for shift-left**: Projects that adopt `erasableSyntaxOnly: true` from day 1 ensure their TypeScript can be executed directly by Node.js 22+ without a build step. The compiler enforces the constraint at authoring time — developers receive an error if they accidentally write an enum or namespace. This is a compile-time guardrail that preserves future runtime optionality at zero runtime cost.

**Granular return branch checking (TS 5.8)**

TypeScript 5.8 now performs independent return-type checks on each branch of a ternary expression inside a `return` statement, rather than computing the union first. This catches a class of defect where `any` silently widens a union.

```typescript
// TypeScript 5.8: catches this defect; TS 5.7 and earlier did not
declare const cache: Map<string, any>;   // common pattern with external caches

function getUrl(key: string): URL {
  return cache.has(key)
    ? cache.get(key)   // TS 5.8 ERROR: cache.get() returns any → not assignable to URL
    : new URL(key);
}
// Fix: cast with type guard or use typed Map<string, URL>
```

**`--libReplacement false` for CI performance**

In projects that do not use `@typescript/lib-*` package replacements, disabling the replacement lookup reduces `tsc --noEmit` cold-start time by eliminating file system probes for non-existent packages.

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "libReplacement": false    // Disable @typescript/lib-* package lookups (default: true)
    // Add when: you don't use lib replacement AND want to shave 5-15% off tsc cold starts
  }
}
```

**`--module node18` (stable in TS 5.8)**

A stable module configuration for Node.js 18 LTS targets. Unlike `nodenext`, it correctly disallows `require()` of ESM modules (which Node 18 does not support natively) and uses import assertions rather than import attributes.

```json
// tsconfig.json for Node.js 18 LTS projects (explicit, not nodenext)
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "node18",      // Stable: never receives new behaviors (safe for long-lived LTS targets)
    "target": "ES2022"       // Node.js 18 supports ES2022 natively
  }
}
```

#### TypeScript 5.9: Opinionated Shift-Left Defaults

TypeScript 5.9 revamped `tsc --init` to generate a significantly more prescriptive `tsconfig.json`. The new defaults are themselves a shift-left recommendation from the TypeScript team.

**New `tsc --init` output (TS 5.9):**

```json
// Generated by: npx tsc --init (TypeScript 5.9+)
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "nodenext",
    "target": "esnext",
    "types": [],                           // No implicit @types/* loading — explicit only
    "moduleDetection": "force",            // NEW: all files treated as modules (no accidental globals)
    "strict": true,
    "jsx": "react-jsx",
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,          // Enforces type-only import syntax
    "isolatedModules": true,
    "noUncheckedSideEffectImports": true   // NEW: prevents unverified side-effect imports
  }
}
```

**Two new shift-left flags included in the default config:**

`"moduleDetection": "force"` — Treats every TypeScript file as an ES module (regardless of `import`/`export` presence). Without this, a file without any `import` or `export` statements is a "script" with global scope — accidentally writing `const x = 1` in two such files creates a global name collision that the TypeScript compiler does not detect as an error by default. `"force"` makes the compiler detect all files as modules, eliminating an entire class of global-state collision defects.

`"noUncheckedSideEffectImports": true` — Warns when a side-effect import (`import './polyfill.js'`) points to a module path that cannot be resolved. Previously, unresolvable side-effect imports were silently ignored (since they "might" work at runtime). This new flag catches typo'd polyfill paths and phantom imports that were never cleaned up during refactors.

```typescript
// Caught by noUncheckedSideEffectImports: true
import './setup/database-seed.js';  // ERROR if database-seed.js doesn't exist
                                     // Previously: silent. Now: compile error at authoring time.

// Caught by moduleDetection: "force"
// File: src/utils/constants.ts — no imports or exports
const MAX_RETRIES = 3;               // Without "force": this is a global, not a module export
                                     // With "force": this is a module-scoped const — correct behavior
```

**`import defer` (TS 5.9 + TC39 Deferred Import Evaluation)**

TypeScript 5.9 adds support for `import defer`, a TC39 Stage 3 proposal that delays module evaluation until exports are first accessed. This is relevant for shift-left because it can reduce test startup time in large suites where many modules are imported but few are exercised.

```typescript
// import defer: module is loaded (parsed) but NOT evaluated until first property access
import defer * as HeavyAnalytics from './analytics/heavy-module.js';

// Module code runs here (first property access):
if (process.env.ANALYTICS_ENABLED) {
  HeavyAnalytics.track('app_start');  // Side effects execute NOW, not at import time
}
// In unit tests that don't set ANALYTICS_ENABLED: the module body never executes
// → faster test startup, no side effects in tests that don't need them
```

**`--module node20` (TS 5.9)**

A new stable module configuration for Node.js 20 LTS. Like `node18`, it never receives new behaviors — safe for long-lived LTS deployment targets where `nodenext` would absorb future Node.js changes.

```json
// Use node20 for Node.js 20 LTS; use nodenext for "latest stable Node.js"
{ "compilerOptions": { "module": "node20", "target": "ES2023" } }
```

**Performance improvements for Zod/tRPC heavy codebases (TS 5.9)**

TypeScript 5.9 adds mapper-level instantiation caching that specifically benefits codebases with deep generic type chains — the exact pattern used by Zod schemas and tRPC router types. In benchmarks on Zod-heavy TypeScript projects, `tsc --noEmit` compile time was reduced by 15–30% compared to TS 5.8.

> [community] **Lesson (TypeScript 5.9 release, 2025)**: The new `tsc --init` defaults are effectively the TypeScript team's official shift-left configuration recommendation. Starting a new TypeScript project with TS 5.9 and accepting the default `tsc --init` output gives you `strict: true`, `moduleDetection: "force"`, `noUncheckedSideEffectImports: true`, and `verbatimModuleSyntax: true` out of the box — a meaningfully stricter starting point than previous versions. Teams should treat these new defaults as "the recommended greenfield baseline" and adopt them project by project when starting new services.

> [community] **Gotcha (TypeScript 5.9 breaking change — ArrayBuffer vs TypedArray)**: TypeScript 5.9 changes the `lib.d.ts` definition so that `ArrayBuffer` is no longer a supertype of `TypedArray` types (e.g., `Uint8Array`). This affects Node.js projects that use `Buffer` because `Buffer extends Uint8Array extends ArrayBufferLike`. Code that previously typed a parameter as `ArrayBuffer` and received a `Buffer` will now produce a type error. **Shift-left impact**: this will surface during `tsc --noEmit` on the upgrade PR. The fix is either: (a) use `.buffer` to extract the underlying `ArrayBuffer`, or (b) widen the parameter type to `ArrayBuffer | SharedArrayBuffer | Buffer`. TypeScript 5.9 migration requires auditing all `ArrayBuffer` parameter types in HTTP, crypto, and binary data handling code.

### Vitest 4.x — Shift-Left Quality Gate Improvements

Vitest 4.x (released 2025) introduced several features that directly improve shift-left testing quality.

#### `aroundEach` and `aroundAll` — Database Transaction Testing

The new `aroundEach` hook replaces the `beforeEach`/`afterEach` transaction rollback pattern with a single generator-style wrapper. This is the idiomatic pattern for database integration tests in Vitest 4.1+.

```typescript
// tests/integration/user.repository.spec.ts — aroundEach for DB transaction isolation
import { describe, it, expect, aroundEach } from 'vitest';
import { db } from '../helpers/database.js';
import { UserRepository } from '../../src/repositories/user.repository.js';

// aroundEach: wraps each test in a DB transaction that is rolled back after the test
// Replaces the fragile beforeEach(begin) + afterEach(rollback) pattern
aroundEach(async (test) => {
  // Setup: begin transaction
  await db.query('BEGIN');

  // Run the test — all DB writes are within this transaction
  await test();

  // Teardown: always rolls back — even if test throws
  await db.query('ROLLBACK');
});

describe('UserRepository', () => {
  const repo = new UserRepository(db);

  it('creates a user and returns it', async () => {
    // This INSERT is wrapped in the aroundEach transaction — rolled back after test
    const user = await repo.create({ email: 'test@example.com', name: 'Test User' });
    expect(user.id).toBeTruthy();
    expect(user.email).toBe('test@example.com');
  });

  it('throws on duplicate email', async () => {
    await repo.create({ email: 'dup@example.com', name: 'User 1' });
    await expect(
      repo.create({ email: 'dup@example.com', name: 'User 2' }),
    ).rejects.toThrow(/duplicate|unique constraint/i);
    // Both inserts are rolled back: next test starts with clean state
  });
});
```

**WHY `aroundEach` is better than `beforeEach`/`afterEach` for database tests**: The previous pattern required two separate hooks that could be mis-ordered or accidentally skipped if the test file was modified. `aroundEach` creates an explicit single context: the transaction is guaranteed to begin before and roll back after, in a way that is readable as a linear flow. Critically, the rollback fires even when the test throws — the equivalent of a `finally` block. This is the shift-left quality gate for integration tests: defects that corrupt shared state are eliminated by construction.

#### `detectAsyncLeaks` — Catching Async Resource Defects at Test Time

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — enable async leak detection in CI
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Enable in CI — converts subtle async timing defects into deterministic failures
    // WHY: unresolved promises from a test that complete after the test ends cause flaky
    // behavior in subsequent tests — they may resolve mid-test with unexpected side effects.
    detectOpenHandles: process.env.CI === 'true' ? true : false,

    // Vitest 4.x: --detect-async-leaks (CLI flag) or detectAsyncLeaks config option
    // Reports tests that leave unresolved timers, intervals, or promise chains open
    // Note: enabling in pre-commit may slow test teardown by 100-200ms per async leak found
    pool: 'forks',   // Required for full async leak detection (not threads)
  }
});
```

```typescript
// Example: async leak that detectAsyncLeaks catches
import { it, expect } from 'vitest';

it('starts a background interval and forgets to clean up', () => {
  // DEFECT: this interval continues running after the test ends
  const interval = setInterval(() => {
    console.log('background tick');
  }, 100);

  expect(1 + 1).toBe(2);
  // Missing: clearInterval(interval)
  // Without detectAsyncLeaks: next test is flaky (background ticks interfere)
  // With detectAsyncLeaks: this test FAILS with "test left open handles" — deterministic
});
```

**WHY `detectAsyncLeaks` is a shift-left tool**: Async leaks are the root cause of a large fraction of flaky tests. Without detection, a developer writes a test with a forgotten `setInterval` or unresolved promise, the test passes, and the next test becomes intermittently flaky for an unrelated reason. `detectAsyncLeaks` converts this implicit nondeterminism into an explicit test failure at the source test — making the defect reportable, assignable, and fixable.

#### `coverage.changed` — Focused Coverage for PRs

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — coverage.changed for PR-scoped coverage analysis
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      // coverage.changed: only report coverage for files changed vs base branch
      // In CI: git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD provides the changed file list
      // WHY: on large codebases, full coverage reports are noisy and slow to generate.
      // PR-scoped coverage focuses the developer's attention on the files they changed.
      changed: process.env.CI ? 'origin/main' : undefined,
      thresholds: {
        // Per-file thresholds: each changed file must meet these thresholds
        perFile: true,
        lines: 80,
        functions: 75,
        branches: 70,
      },
      reporter: ['text', 'lcov'],
    }
  }
});
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/pr-coverage.yml — PR-scoped coverage gate
name: PR Coverage Check
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main, develop]

jobs:
  coverage:
    name: Coverage (changed files only)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0   # Full history required for git diff comparison

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: 'npm' }

      - run: npm ci

      # Run tests with coverage scoped to changed files vs main
      - run: |
          npx vitest run \
            --coverage \
            --coverage.changed=origin/main \
            --reporter=github-actions
        env:
          CI: 'true'
```

**WHY `coverage.changed` improves shift-left feedback quality**: Full-codebase coverage reports on every PR create noise — the developer is reviewing coverage for files they did not touch. `coverage.changed` scopes the gate to files the PR modifies. This makes coverage a relevant, actionable signal: "the function you added is not covered" rather than "some other module has 60% coverage." The per-file threshold enforcement catches gaps in the specific code under review, not in legacy code.

#### Disposable Mocks — Automatic Mock Cleanup

```typescript
// src/services/notification.service.spec.ts — disposable mocks (Vitest 4.x)
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { NotificationService } from './notification.service.js';

describe('NotificationService', () => {
  it('sends an email notification', async () => {
    // Disposable mock: automatically restored when the using block exits
    // Uses TC39 Explicit Resource Management (TypeScript 5.2+ / ES2025)
    await using emailClient = vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ messageId: 'msg_123' });

    const service = new NotificationService({ sendEmail: emailClient });
    await service.notifyUser('user_1', 'Welcome!');

    expect(emailClient).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    // emailClient mock is automatically cleaned up on scope exit
    // No need for: afterEach(() => vi.restoreAllMocks())
  });

  // Alternatively, using doMock() which returns a disposable:
  it('logs a warning when email client fails', async () => {
    using failingEmailClient = vi.fn().mockRejectedValue(new Error('SMTP timeout'));
    const warnSpy = vi.spyOn(console, 'warn').mockImplementation(() => {});

    const service = new NotificationService({ sendEmail: failingEmailClient });
    await service.notifyUser('user_1', 'Welcome!');  // Should not throw

    expect(warnSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith(expect.stringContaining('SMTP timeout'));
    // Both mocks restored automatically
  });
});
```

**WHY disposable mocks are a shift-left pattern**: Forgotten `vi.restoreAllMocks()` calls in `afterEach` are a source of test pollution — one test's mock bleeds into the next. Disposable mocks use JavaScript's `Symbol.asyncDispose` mechanism (TC39 Explicit Resource Management) to bind mock lifecycle to lexical scope. The cleanup is enforced by the language runtime, not developer discipline.

> [community] **Lesson (Vitest 4.1 release team)**: The `aroundEach` hook was added in direct response to a common community pattern: developers implementing database transaction rollback with `beforeEach`/`afterEach` and encountering subtle ordering bugs when tests were added, removed, or re-ordered. The generator-based single hook eliminates the ordering problem entirely. The primary adoption signal: teams migrating from Jest to Vitest who had transaction rollback patterns now have a first-class idiom for it.

> [community] **Gotcha (detectAsyncLeaks + Node.js timers)**: `detectAsyncLeaks` in `pool: 'forks'` mode catches `setInterval`, `setTimeout`, and unresolved promises. However, it does NOT detect TCP sockets left open by database or HTTP clients that do not call `.end()` or `.destroy()`. For database connection leaks (pg.Pool, mysql2 pool), use Testcontainers with a per-test container or explicit pool teardown in `afterAll`. The two mechanisms complement each other: `detectAsyncLeaks` catches timing-based leaks; explicit teardown catches connection-based leaks.

> [community] **Gotcha (coverage.changed + monorepos)**: `coverage.changed='origin/main'` computes changed files using git diff relative to the monorepo root. In an Nx or Turborepo monorepo, files changed in Package A will also trigger coverage analysis in Package B if B imports from A. Use `--project` or per-package Vitest configs to scope coverage analysis to the package under test, not the entire monorepo affected graph.

### Node.js 22 `require()` of ESM — Shift-Left Implications

Node.js 22.12+ (LTS) enables `require()` of synchronous ESM modules without a flag. TypeScript 5.8 supports this via `--module nodenext` (which now correctly models Node.js 22's CJS-can-require-ESM behavior).

**Shift-left impact**: TypeScript projects that publish ESM-only packages no longer need to dual-publish (CJS + ESM). The pre-commit and CI gate changes:

```typescript
// Previously required: dual build (CJS + ESM) to support Node.js consumers
// package.json excerpt:
// "exports": {
//   ".": { "import": "./dist/esm/index.js", "require": "./dist/cjs/index.js" }
// }

// With Node.js 22 + TS 5.8 (--module nodenext):
// Single ESM build — Node.js 22+ CJS consumers can require() it directly
// package.json:
// "type": "module",
// "exports": { ".": "./dist/index.js" }

// CI gate update: remove CJS build job, keep only ESM type check
// tsconfig.json: "module": "nodenext" (already models Node 22 require-ESM support)
```

```yaml
# SIMPLIFIED: single build + type check (ESM only, Node.js 22+)
# .github/workflows/build.yml
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx tsc --noEmit               # Type check ESM output
      - run: npx tsc --project tsconfig.build.json  # Emit ESM dist/
      # No CJS build job needed for Node.js 22+ consumers
```

> [community] **Lesson (Node.js 22 ESM require, 2025)**: Library authors who maintained CJS+ESM dual-publish pipelines report that removing the CJS build reduced their CI pipeline by 30–45 seconds and eliminated an entire class of "works in ESM, breaks in CJS" defects that only surfaced in consumer projects. The shift-left benefit: the CI complexity of maintaining two module formats was itself a source of defects (mismatched exports maps, stale CJS type declarations). Reducing to a single ESM build with Node.js 22 removes that complexity.

> [community] **Gotcha (require(ESM) + top-level await)**: `require()` of ESM only works if the module has no top-level `await` statements. A module with `const db = await initDatabase()` at the top level cannot be `require()`'d — Node.js will throw at runtime. TypeScript 5.8 with `--module nodenext` does NOT statically detect top-level `await` in a module being required — this is a runtime error. Shift-left mitigation: audit all `export`'d modules for top-level `await` before removing the dual-publish setup. Keep top-level async initialization inside explicit `init()` functions rather than at module scope.

### Shift-Left for AI Code Review Tools (2025–2026)

AI code review tools have matured from "suggests style improvements" to "identifies structural defects with security context." The shift-left integration patterns have correspondingly evolved.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ai-review.yml — AI-assisted PR review as shift-left gate
name: AI Code Review
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main, develop]
    types: [opened, synchronize, ready_for_review]

jobs:
  # PATTERN 1: CodeRabbit — AI review that comments on PRs (not a blocking gate)
  coderabbit:
    name: CodeRabbit AI Review
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: coderabbitai/coderabbit-action@v1
        with:
          # CodeRabbit reads PR diff and posts line-level review comments
          # covering: logic errors, security patterns, TypeScript anti-patterns
          api-key: ${{ secrets.CODERABBIT_API_KEY }}
        # WHY non-blocking: AI review complements human review but does not replace it.
        # False positives in AI review that block PRs create reviewer fatigue.
        # Use as informational + human-reviewable, not as hard gate.

  # PATTERN 2: Semgrep Assistant — AI-enhanced finding explanations
  semgrep-ai:
    name: Semgrep + AI Triage
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    container:
      image: semgrep/semgrep
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: |
          semgrep scan \
            --config=p/typescript \
            --config=p/owasp-top-ten \
            --sarif \
            --output=semgrep.sarif
        # Semgrep Assistant (Pro tier): automatically triages findings as
        # "likely true positive", "likely false positive", or "needs context"
        # using the surrounding code as context for the LLM evaluation
      - uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
        if: always()
        with:
          sarif_file: semgrep.sarif
```

```typescript
// scripts/validate-ai-pr-changes.ts — validate AI-generated code passes shift-left gates
// Run as a CI check specifically flagged when commits include AI-generated code markers
import { execSync } from 'node:child_process';

// Common markers in AI-generated code commits (Cursor, Copilot, Claude Code)
const AI_COMMIT_MARKERS = [
  'Co-authored-by: GitHub Copilot',
  'Co-authored-by: Claude',
  'Co-authored-by: Cursor',
  'Generated by:',
];

const recentCommitMessages = execSync('git log -10 --format=%B', { encoding: 'utf8' });
const containsAiMarker = AI_COMMIT_MARKERS.some((marker) =>
  recentCommitMessages.includes(marker),
);

if (containsAiMarker) {
  console.log('AI-generated commits detected — running enhanced shift-left validation');

  // Run mutation testing on changed files for AI PRs
  // AI code is syntactically correct but may have subtle behavioral defects
  execSync('npx stryker run --mutate "$(git diff --name-only origin/main | grep .ts$ | head -5 | tr \'\\n\' \',\')"', {
    stdio: 'inherit',
  });
}
```

> [community] **Lesson (AI code review tools, 2025–2026)**: CodeRabbit, Qodo (formerly CodiumAI), and GitHub Copilot Code Review are converging on similar patterns: AI reads the PR diff in context, identifies potential defects in the changed code, and posts line-level comments. The shift-left value is highest for: (1) catching inconsistent error handling ("other handlers return 400 for validation errors; this one returns 500"), (2) missing authorization checks in new endpoints, and (3) TypeScript `any` escape hatches that were introduced to "make it work." The false-positive rate on style issues remains high (~40%) but on structural patterns is much lower (~15%).

> [community] **Gotcha (AI review + security finding escalation)**: Teams that configure AI code review tools to auto-request changes (blocking PRs) based on AI-identified security patterns report that developers learn to phrase their AI assistant prompts to avoid patterns that trigger the review gate — rather than addressing the underlying issue. Better pattern: AI review generates informational comments; human code owner reviews AI-flagged items; SAST/type gates are the hard blocks. The AI review accelerates human reviewer attention rather than replacing it.

> [community] **Lesson (mutation testing for AI-generated code, 2025)**: Teams that added per-PR Stryker mutation testing scoped to files changed by AI coding assistants found a 3× higher mutant survival rate in AI-generated code compared to human-written code, specifically in: authorization checks (missing boundary conditions), validation logic (missing edge cases in `if` chains), and error handling paths (AI generates happy-path tests for its own generated code). Running mutation testing on changed files in PRs is the highest-leverage complement to SAST for AI-assisted development.

### SBOM and Supply Chain Shift-Left — 2025 Updates

```yaml
# .github/workflows/provenance.yml — SLSA Level 3 provenance attestation
name: SLSA Provenance
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    tags: ['v*']

permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write    # Required for OIDC signing
  attestations: write

jobs:
  build-and-attest:
    name: Build + SLSA Provenance
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: 'npm' }

      - run: npm ci && npm run build

      # Generate CycloneDX SBOM before attesting
      - run: npx @cyclonedx/cyclonedx-npm --output-format JSON --output-file sbom.json

      # SLSA Level 3 provenance: signs the build artifact with OIDC-backed Sigstore
      - uses: actions/attest-build-provenance@v1
        with:
          subject-path: 'dist/**'

      # Also attest the SBOM itself
      - uses: actions/attest-sbom@v1
        with:
          subject-path: 'dist/**'
          sbom-path: 'sbom.json'
```

**Why SLSA provenance is shift-left supply chain security**: SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) provenance creates a cryptographically signed record of: what source code produced this artifact, which CI workflow ran, and which actions were invoked. Consumers of the artifact can verify this provenance chain to confirm the artifact was not tampered with between build and deployment. The `actions/attest-build-provenance` action implements this at SLSA Build Level 3 using GitHub's OIDC token and Sigstore's transparency log.

> [community] **Lesson (SLSA adoption, 2025)**: `actions/attest-build-provenance@v1` was released by GitHub in April 2024 and has seen rapid adoption in open-source TypeScript packages. The setup cost is 3 lines of YAML; the benefit is an auditable, tamper-evident record of every production artifact. Enterprise customers requiring software supply chain compliance (CISA SSDF, NIST 800-218) are increasingly requesting SLSA attestations as part of vendor questionnaires. Add it before you need it — retroactive attestation is impossible.

> [community] **Gotcha (SBOM + TypeScript devDependencies)**: `@cyclonedx/cyclonedx-npm` by default includes `devDependencies` in the SBOM. For regulatory submissions (CISA, procurement), use `--omit=dev` to generate a production-only SBOM. The full SBOM (including devDeps) is useful for internal security scanning via Dependency Track; the production SBOM is the compliance artifact. Generate both and store them separately.

### 1. TypeScript `--isolatedDeclarations` — Declaration Emit as Shift-Left Gate

TypeScript 5.5 introduced `--isolatedDeclarations` (stabilized in 5.6+), a mode that requires each TypeScript file to be typeable purely from its own explicit annotations — without needing to inspect the implementations of other files. This enables parallel, file-level `.d.ts` emit, making large monorepo type-checking dramatically faster. More importantly for shift-left, it is a **writing-time constraint** that prevents a class of inference-driven type errors that only surface during full `tsc --build` runs.

**WHY this matters for shift-left**: In a large monorepo, `tsc --build` can take 30–120 seconds even with incremental mode. `--isolatedDeclarations` shifts the cost of type errors to the individual file author — the developer who forgets to annotate a return type receives an error in the editor immediately, rather than discovering the downstream package fails to type-check after a slow full build.

```json
// packages/shared/tsconfig.json — enable isolatedDeclarations for published packages
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "isolatedDeclarations": true,   // require explicit return types on exported functions
    "declaration": true,
    "declarationMap": true,
    "noEmit": false,
    "composite": true               // enables tsc --build incremental mode
  }
}
```

```typescript
// BEFORE isolatedDeclarations: this compiled silently
// but caused downstream inference chains that slowed tsc --build
export function buildApiUrl(base: string, path: string) {
  return `${base}/${path.replace(/^\//, '')}`;
  // Return type inferred: string — but tsc had to chase the inference from callers
}

// AFTER isolatedDeclarations: explicit annotation required on exported functions
export function buildApiUrl(base: string, path: string): string {
  return `${base}/${path.replace(/^\//, '')}`;
  // Explicit: string — tsc can emit .d.ts without reading callers
  // WHY: each file is an independent declaration unit — parallel build becomes safe
}

// Pattern: use `satisfies` for inline type checking without widening
export const HTTP_METHODS = ['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'DELETE', 'PATCH'] as const satisfies readonly string[];
type HttpMethod = (typeof HTTP_METHODS)[number];
// satisfies verifies the constraint without widening to string[] — isolatedDeclarations compatible
```

> [community] **Lesson (monorepo teams adopting isolatedDeclarations, 2025–2026)**: The primary friction is third-party library code. When calling a library function whose return type is inferred (not annotated), TypeScript cannot determine the return type without reading the library source. Workaround: wrap library calls in project-owned adapter functions with explicit annotations. This forces clean API boundaries anyway — the shift-left constraint improves architecture.

> [community] **Gotcha (`isolatedDeclarations` + barrel files)**: Barrel files (`index.ts` that re-export from submodules) can explode in cost with `isolatedDeclarations`. Each re-export requires the source module to have explicit annotations. A single un-annotated utility function in a deep submodule cascades to an error in the barrel. Fix: use `export type { Foo }` for type-only re-exports and add `isolatedDeclarations: true` to each package incrementally starting with leaf packages (no intra-monorepo imports).

### 2. ESLint 9.x Flat Config Ecosystem Stability — `typescript-eslint` v8 Patterns (2026)

The ESLint v9 flat config migration reached ecosystem stability in late 2025 — the major plugin ecosystem (typescript-eslint, eslint-plugin-vitest, eslint-plugin-playwright, eslint-plugin-n, eslint-plugin-unicorn) all ship v9-compatible releases. Cycle 23 adds practical patterns for the newly stable combination.

**Key addition: `typescript-eslint` v8 type-checked rules in flat config.** Type-checked rules (those requiring `parserOptions.project`) run the TypeScript type checker as part of linting — providing IDE-quality diagnostics at lint time. In v8, enabling these in flat config requires explicit `projectService` configuration.

```typescript
// eslint.config.ts — typescript-eslint v8 type-checked rules (2026 stable pattern)
import eslint from '@eslint/js';
import tseslint from 'typescript-eslint';
import pluginUnicorn from 'eslint-plugin-unicorn';
import pluginN from 'eslint-plugin-n';

export default tseslint.config(
  eslint.configs.recommended,

  // v8 type-checked rules — uses TypeScript's language service for type information
  // Requires `projectService: true` (v8) instead of `project: true` (v7 syntax)
  ...tseslint.configs.recommendedTypeChecked,
  {
    languageOptions: {
      parserOptions: {
        projectService: true,                // v8: new API — replaces project: ['./tsconfig.json']
        tsconfigRootDir: import.meta.dirname, // resolves relative to this eslint.config.ts
      },
    },
  },

  // Node.js-specific rules — replaces legacy eslint-plugin-node
  {
    plugins: { n: pluginN },
    rules: {
      'n/no-process-exit': 'error',          // prefer throw over process.exit in library code
      'n/no-unpublished-require': 'error',   // catches missing devDependency entries
      'n/no-unsupported-features/es-syntax': ['error', { version: '>=22.0.0' }],
    },
  },

  // Unicorn: opinionated utility rules that catch common antipatterns
  {
    plugins: { unicorn: pluginUnicorn },
    rules: {
      'unicorn/no-array-for-each': 'error',  // prefer for...of (debuggable, no callback)
      'unicorn/no-await-expression-member': 'error', // (await promise).property → extract variable
      'unicorn/prefer-at': 'error',          // array[array.length - 1] → array.at(-1)
      'unicorn/prefer-string-raw': 'error',  // double-escaped strings → String.raw``
    },
  },

  // Disable type-checked rules for .js files (no TypeScript info available)
  {
    files: ['**/*.js', '**/*.mjs', '**/*.cjs'],
    ...tseslint.configs.disableTypeChecked,
  }
);
```

> [community] **Lesson (typescript-eslint v8 `projectService` adoption, 2026)**: The `projectService: true` API in typescript-eslint v8 uses TypeScript's `--project-service` mode (a persistent background TypeScript language service) rather than spawning a fresh `tsc` process per ESLint run. In projects with 200+ files, this reduces ESLint's type-checked rule execution from 45–90 seconds to 8–20 seconds. The tradeoff: `projectService` mode caches type information — changes to `tsconfig.json` may not be reflected until the language service restarts.

> [community] **Gotcha (flat config + `eslint-disable` comments)**: ESLint v9's flat config changes how `eslint-disable` scope works when multiple config objects with overlapping `files` globs are stacked. A `/* eslint-disable @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any */` comment at the file top now correctly applies only to the rules active for that file's matched config objects — but teams upgrading from v8 find that some disable comments that previously silenced rules no longer do so if the rule is now configured in a different config object layer. Audit all existing disable comments against the active rule list using `npx eslint --print-config path/to/file.ts`.

### 3. Lefthook — High-Performance Pre-Commit Hooks for TypeScript Monorepos

**Lefthook** (written in Go) is a git hooks manager that runs tasks in parallel across hook stages. It is faster than husky + lint-staged for monorepos because it runs hooks concurrently across files, uses glob-based file filtering natively, and has no Node.js startup overhead.

**Shift-left relevance**: Pre-commit hooks are the first automated gate in the shift-left chain. Every second of hook latency trains developers to skip them (`--no-verify`). Lefthook eliminates the Node.js startup cost that makes husky + lint-staged slow at scale.

```yaml
# lefthook.yml — high-performance pre-commit hook configuration
# Install: npm install --save-dev lefthook
# Activate: npx lefthook install

pre-commit:
  parallel: true          # run all commands concurrently (default: sequential)
  commands:
    typecheck:
      glob: "**/*.ts"     # only run when TypeScript files are staged
      run: npx tsc --noEmit --incremental
      # --incremental reuses .tsbuildinfo from last run — fast for small diffs

    lint:
      glob: "*.{ts,tsx,js,mjs}"
      run: npx eslint --fix {staged_files}
      stage_fixed: true   # re-stage files that were auto-fixed

    biome-check:
      glob: "*.{ts,tsx,css,graphql}"
      run: npx biome check --apply {staged_files}
      stage_fixed: true

    unit-tests:
      glob: "src/**/*.ts"
      # Only run tests related to changed files — skip E2E on pre-commit
      run: npx vitest run --changed --reporter=verbose --no-coverage
      # vitest --changed only runs tests for files that changed or import them

commit-msg:
  commands:
    commitlint:
      run: npx commitlint --edit {1}
      # Enforces Conventional Commits — enables automated changelog generation

pre-push:
  parallel: false         # sequential for push — stricter gate before remote
  commands:
    full-typecheck:
      run: npx tsc --noEmit
    test-with-coverage:
      run: npx vitest run --coverage --reporter=verbose
      # Full coverage run before push — not pre-commit (too slow)
    audit:
      run: npm audit --audit-level=high
      # Block push if high/critical vulnerabilities introduced
```

> [community] **Lesson (Lefthook vs husky+lint-staged, 2025–2026)**: On a 150-file TypeScript project, switching from husky + lint-staged to Lefthook reduced average pre-commit hook time from 12 seconds to 4 seconds. The primary gains were parallel execution of ESLint + tsc (previously sequential) and elimination of the Node.js startup overhead for each lint-staged command. Teams report significantly lower `--no-verify` usage after the switch.

> [community] **Gotcha (Lefthook `stage_fixed: true` + ESLint autofix race)**: When multiple commands with `stage_fixed: true` run in parallel and both fix the same file, the second `git add` call may overwrite the first command's changes. Workaround: assign non-overlapping file globs to auto-fixing commands (ESLint handles `.ts`/`.tsx`/`.js`; Biome handles `.css`/`.graphql`) so they never compete on the same file.

### 4. `dependency-cruiser` — Architectural Enforcement as Shift-Left

`dependency-cruiser` validates import relationships against a set of rules, preventing architecture erosion from accumulating in small PRs over time. It runs in under 5 seconds on most TypeScript projects and can be added to pre-commit or PR gates.

**Shift-left relevance**: Architecture violations (circular dependencies, business-logic imports in the UI layer, test utilities imported in production code) are expensive to fix retroactively. `dependency-cruiser` catches them at the PR level, when the change is still isolated.

```json
// .dependency-cruiser.json — architectural enforcement rules
{
  "$schema": "https://dependency-cruiser.js.org/schema.json",
  "forbidden": [
    {
      "name": "no-circular",
      "severity": "error",
      "comment": "Circular dependencies cause unpredictable module initialization order",
      "from": {},
      "to": { "circular": true }
    },
    {
      "name": "no-test-in-production",
      "severity": "error",
      "comment": "Production code must not import test utilities or fixtures",
      "from": { "pathNot": "\\.test\\.ts$|\\.spec\\.ts$|__tests__" },
      "to": {
        "path": "__fixtures__|__mocks__|test-utils|\\.test\\.ts$|\\.spec\\.ts$"
      }
    },
    {
      "name": "ui-no-domain-direct",
      "severity": "warn",
      "comment": "UI components should import via use-case layer, not domain directly",
      "from": { "path": "^src/ui/" },
      "to": {
        "path": "^src/domain/",
        "pathNot": "^src/domain/.*types\\.ts$"  // allow type-only imports
      }
    },
    {
      "name": "no-barrel-from-deep",
      "severity": "warn",
      "comment": "Deep imports into other packages bypass the package public API",
      "from": { "path": "^src/(?!shared)" },
      "to": { "path": "^src/shared/(?!index\\.ts$)" }
    }
  ],
  "options": {
    "tsPreCompilationDeps": true,   // include type-only imports (import type {...})
    "combinedDependencies": false,
    "reporterOptions": {
      "archi": {
        "collapsePattern": "^src/[^/]+"  // collapse to top-level directories in diagrams
      }
    }
  }
}
```

```typescript
// package.json scripts
// "scripts": {
//   "arch:check": "depcruise src --config .dependency-cruiser.json",
//   "arch:graph": "depcruise src --config .dependency-cruiser.json --output-type dot | dot -T svg > docs/dependency-graph.svg"
// }

// GitHub Actions gate:
// - run: npm run arch:check
//   # Fails the PR on any 'error' severity violation; warns on 'warn' severity
```

> [community] **Lesson (dependency-cruiser in large TypeScript codebases, 2025)**: The most common architectural violations caught by adding `dependency-cruiser` to an existing TypeScript project are: (1) circular dependencies in shared utility modules (often caused by adding convenience re-exports), (2) direct domain object imports in React components that bypass the service layer, and (3) test-only factory functions inadvertently imported in production code. All three categories are difficult to catch in code review because the import paths look syntactically correct.

> [community] **Gotcha (`dependency-cruiser` + TypeScript path aliases)**: Projects using `tsconfig.json` `paths` aliases (e.g., `@/components` → `src/components`) must configure `dependency-cruiser` with `tsConfig: { fileName: './tsconfig.json' }` in the `options` block. Without this, cruiser resolves aliases to `node_modules/@/components` (which doesn't exist) and silently skips all rules matching those paths — producing false negatives.

### 5. GitHub Copilot Test Generation — AI-Assisted Shift-Left in the IDE

GitHub Copilot's `/tests` slash command (generally available in VS Code and JetBrains, 2025+) generates test cases for a selected function or file. For TypeScript projects, it generates Vitest or Jest test cases using the correct import syntax, mock patterns, and `describe`/`it` structure. This shifts the effort of writing initial test scaffolding from developer time to AI time — reducing the activation energy for test-first development.

**Shift-left relevance**: The bottleneck in developer test-writing is not knowledge of how to test — it is the time cost of writing boilerplate. AI test generation removes that friction. Developers review and refine AI-generated tests rather than starting from a blank file — a 5–10 minute task versus a 30–60 minute one.

```typescript
// BEFORE (what Copilot sees — a function to generate tests for):
// File: src/lib/pagination.ts

/**
 * Generates pagination metadata for a paginated API response.
 * @param total - total number of records
 * @param page - current page (1-indexed)
 * @param pageSize - records per page
 * @returns pagination metadata or null if inputs are invalid
 */
export function buildPaginationMeta(
  total: number,
  page: number,
  pageSize: number
): { currentPage: number; totalPages: number; hasNext: boolean; hasPrev: boolean } | null {
  if (total < 0 || page < 1 || pageSize < 1) return null;
  const totalPages = Math.ceil(total / pageSize);
  return {
    currentPage: page,
    totalPages,
    hasNext: page < totalPages,
    hasPrev: page > 1,
  };
}
```

```typescript
// AFTER (what Copilot /tests generates — Vitest, TypeScript):
// File: src/lib/pagination.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { buildPaginationMeta } from './pagination';

describe('buildPaginationMeta', () => {
  it('returns null for negative total', () => {
    expect(buildPaginationMeta(-1, 1, 10)).toBeNull();
  });

  it('returns null for page < 1', () => {
    expect(buildPaginationMeta(100, 0, 10)).toBeNull();
  });

  it('returns null for pageSize < 1', () => {
    expect(buildPaginationMeta(100, 1, 0)).toBeNull();
  });

  it('calculates totalPages correctly', () => {
    const result = buildPaginationMeta(95, 1, 10);
    expect(result?.totalPages).toBe(10); // Math.ceil(95 / 10) = 10
  });

  it('sets hasNext true when not on last page', () => {
    expect(buildPaginationMeta(100, 1, 10)?.hasNext).toBe(true);
  });

  it('sets hasNext false on last page', () => {
    expect(buildPaginationMeta(100, 10, 10)?.hasNext).toBe(false);
  });

  it('sets hasPrev false on first page', () => {
    expect(buildPaginationMeta(100, 1, 10)?.hasPrev).toBe(false);
  });

  it('handles single-page result (total <= pageSize)', () => {
    const result = buildPaginationMeta(5, 1, 10);
    expect(result).toEqual({ currentPage: 1, totalPages: 1, hasNext: false, hasPrev: false });
  });

  it('handles empty result set (total = 0)', () => {
    // NOTE: Copilot may miss edge cases — human review adds this
    const result = buildPaginationMeta(0, 1, 10);
    // totalPages = Math.ceil(0 / 10) = 0; hasNext = 1 < 0 = false
    expect(result).toEqual({ currentPage: 1, totalPages: 0, hasNext: false, hasPrev: false });
  });
});
```

> [community] **Lesson (GitHub Copilot `/tests` production use, 2025–2026)**: Teams using Copilot test generation report that AI-generated tests have good happy-path coverage (typically 70–80% of the obvious cases) but miss: (1) boundary conditions at numeric edges (`0`, `MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, `-1`), (2) concurrent access patterns in async functions, and (3) error propagation when a called dependency throws. The correct workflow is AI-generate → human-review → add missing edge cases. This is faster than writing from scratch and more thorough than skipping tests.

> [community] **Gotcha (AI-generated tests + implementation bias)**: Copilot generates tests by reading the implementation, not the specification. If the implementation has a defect (e.g., `page < totalPages` instead of `page <= totalPages` for the last-page check), the AI-generated test will encode the defect as a passing assertion. Mitigation: use AI-generated tests as a starting scaffold, then review against the function's documented contract — not its implementation.

### 6. TestOps — "Testing as a Feature" Mindset and Shared Ownership

**TestOps** is the practice of treating test infrastructure — test execution pipelines, coverage dashboards, flakiness tracking, test result storage — as a product owned by engineering teams rather than a QA department afterthought. The "testing as a feature" framing reframes the question from "do we have enough tests?" to "does our testing system give us confidence to ship at the speed we want?"

**Core shift-left implication**: TestOps moves quality metrics into the developer dashboard alongside build health and deployment frequency. When flakiness rate, coverage trends, and test execution time are visible in the same place as CI status, developers treat them as first-class engineering concerns.

```typescript
// scripts/testops-report.ts — generate a TestOps health summary from Vitest JSON output
// Run after: npx vitest run --reporter=json --outputFile=test-results.json
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';

interface VitestResult {
  numTotalTests: number;
  numPassedTests: number;
  numFailedTests: number;
  numPendingTests: number;
  testResults: Array<{
    testFilePath: string;
    status: 'passed' | 'failed';
    duration: number;
  }>;
}

const results: VitestResult = JSON.parse(readFileSync('test-results.json', 'utf-8'));

// Calculate TestOps health metrics
const passRate = (results.numPassedTests / results.numTotalTests * 100).toFixed(1);
const slowTests = results.testResults
  .filter(t => t.duration > 5000)    // tests > 5s are slow — potential shift-left candidates
  .sort((a, b) => b.duration - a.duration)
  .slice(0, 5);

const report = {
  cycle: new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10),
  passRate: `${passRate}%`,
  totalTests: results.numTotalTests,
  slowTestCount: slowTests.length,
  slowestTests: slowTests.map(t => ({
    file: t.testFilePath.replace(process.cwd(), ''),
    durationMs: t.duration,
  })),
  health: Number(passRate) >= 99 ? 'GREEN' : Number(passRate) >= 95 ? 'YELLOW' : 'RED',
};

// Write to GitHub Actions step summary
const summary = `
## TestOps Report — ${report.cycle}

**Health**: ${report.health} | **Pass Rate**: ${report.passRate} | **Total Tests**: ${report.totalTests}

### Slow Tests (> 5s) — Shift-Left Optimization Candidates
${report.slowestTests.map(t => `- \`${t.file}\`: ${(t.durationMs / 1000).toFixed(1)}s`).join('\n')}
`.trim();

import { appendFileSync } from 'node:fs';
if (process.env['GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY']) {
  appendFileSync(process.env['GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY'], summary + '\n');
}
console.log(summary);
```

> [community] **Lesson (TestOps adoption, 2025)**: Teams that publish test health summaries to GitHub Actions step summaries (via `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY`) report that developers voluntarily fix slow tests and reduce flakiness — not because it was mandated, but because the metric is now visible on the PR page. Visibility is the cheapest TestOps intervention. The `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` feature costs zero infrastructure — it's a built-in GitHub Actions capability that writes Markdown directly to the PR checks page.

> [community] **Gotcha (TestOps metrics gaming)**: When pass rate or coverage become team KPIs, developers write tests that pass trivially (asserting only that the function returns without throwing). Mitigation: pair pass rate metrics with mutation score metrics. A high pass rate + low mutation score is a clear signal of shallow testing. Mutation scores are harder to game because they require that tests actually verify the output.

### 7. `tsc --build` Incremental Mode and `--watch` in Dev Feedback Loops

The `--incremental` flag (and `--build` mode for project references) stores a `.tsbuildinfo` file that lets subsequent `tsc` runs skip re-checking unchanged files. In large TypeScript projects this is the single highest-leverage change for improving pre-commit hook speed and local feedback loop time.

**Shift-left relevance**: The faster the compile-time feedback loop, the more frequently developers run the type checker during development — before committing, not just after. Incremental mode makes the type checker fast enough to be genuinely interactive.

```json
// tsconfig.json — incremental mode for fastest local type-checking
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "incremental": true,                   // write .tsbuildinfo on each run
    "tsBuildInfoFile": ".tsbuildinfo",     // explicit path for .gitignore

    // strict settings preserved — incremental does not relax type checking
    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true,
    "noImplicitOverride": true,

    "noEmit": true                         // type-check only — emit handled by build tool
  },
  "include": ["src"],
  "exclude": ["node_modules", "dist"]
}
```

```bash
# .gitignore — exclude build artifacts, not tsbuildinfo in CI
# In CI, tsbuildinfo is cached between runs for incremental type-checking

# .gitignore additions:
# .tsbuildinfo          <- add if using a single root tsconfig
# **/.tsbuildinfo       <- add for monorepo (each package has its own)
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/typecheck.yml — cache .tsbuildinfo in CI for incremental runs
name: Type Check
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  typecheck:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci

      # Cache the tsbuildinfo file — restores on subsequent CI runs for the same branch
      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: .tsbuildinfo
          key: tsbuildinfo-${{ hashFiles('src/**/*.ts', 'tsconfig.json') }}
          restore-keys: tsbuildinfo-

      - run: npx tsc --noEmit --incremental
        # First run on a branch: ~30s. Subsequent runs with cache: ~3s.
```

> [community] **Lesson (tsbuildinfo caching in CI, 2025)**: Caching `.tsbuildinfo` in GitHub Actions reduces type-check time from ~25–40 seconds to ~2–5 seconds on pushes to long-lived branches where only a few files changed. The cache key must include both source files and `tsconfig.json` — changing compiler options must invalidate the cache or incorrect incremental results appear.

> [community] **Gotcha (`--incremental` + `strict` mode changes)**: Enabling a new strict flag (e.g., `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`) while using `--incremental` sometimes causes tsc to report fewer errors than expected on the first run, because the `.tsbuildinfo` cache was built without the new flag. Fix: delete `.tsbuildinfo` when changing `compilerOptions` values. Add this as a post-upgrade step in the repo's `tsconfig.json` changelog or PR template.

---

### 8. Type-Safe Environment Variables — Build-Time Validation Pattern

Unvalidated environment variables are a common source of production defects — the application starts but behaves incorrectly because `process.env.DATABASE_URL` is `undefined` at runtime. Validating environment variables at startup (or, better, at build time) shifts this class of defect to the developer's local environment.

```typescript
// src/config/env.ts — type-safe environment variable validation with Zod
// This module runs at process startup and throws synchronously if any required var is missing.
// TypeScript callers get a fully-typed Config object with no undefined values.
import { z } from 'zod';

const envSchema = z.object({
  // Required — startup fails immediately if missing or wrong format
  DATABASE_URL: z.string().url('DATABASE_URL must be a valid URL'),
  JWT_SECRET: z.string().min(32, 'JWT_SECRET must be at least 32 characters'),
  NODE_ENV: z.enum(['development', 'test', 'production']),

  // Optional with defaults
  PORT: z.coerce.number().int().min(1024).max(65535).default(3000),
  LOG_LEVEL: z.enum(['debug', 'info', 'warn', 'error']).default('info'),
  RATE_LIMIT_MAX: z.coerce.number().int().positive().default(100),

  // Feature flags — fail closed (default false) if not explicitly enabled
  FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT: z.coerce.boolean().default(false),
});

// Parse at module load time — throws ZodError with actionable message if invalid
// The error is caught at startup, not during a request handler
export type Config = z.infer<typeof envSchema>;

function parseEnv(): Config {
  const result = envSchema.safeParse(process.env);
  if (!result.success) {
    const errors = result.error.issues
      .map(issue => `  ${issue.path.join('.')}: ${issue.message}`)
      .join('\n');
    throw new Error(`Environment configuration is invalid:\n${errors}\n\nCheck your .env file.`);
  }
  return result.data;
}

export const config: Config = parseEnv();

// Usage: import { config } from './config/env';
// config.DATABASE_URL is string (not string | undefined) — TypeScript enforces this
// config.PORT is number (not string | undefined) — z.coerce.number() handles the conversion
```

```typescript
// src/config/env.test.ts — test that config validation catches real misconfigurations
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';

describe('environment configuration validation', () => {
  const originalEnv = process.env;

  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.resetModules(); // ensure fresh module parse on each test
    process.env = { ...originalEnv };
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    process.env = originalEnv;
  });

  it('throws a descriptive error when DATABASE_URL is missing', async () => {
    delete process.env['DATABASE_URL'];
    await expect(import('./env')).rejects.toThrow('DATABASE_URL');
  });

  it('throws when JWT_SECRET is too short', async () => {
    process.env['JWT_SECRET'] = 'short';
    await expect(import('./env')).rejects.toThrow('at least 32 characters');
  });

  it('coerces PORT string to number', async () => {
    process.env['PORT'] = '4000';
    const { config } = await import('./env');
    expect(config.PORT).toBe(4000);  // number, not string
    expect(typeof config.PORT).toBe('number');
  });
});
```

> [community] **Lesson (env validation at startup, 2025)**: Adding startup environment validation (Zod or similar) is consistently cited as one of the highest-value, lowest-effort shift-left additions in TypeScript backend projects. The change typically surfaces 2–5 real misconfigurations on first deployment — wrong URL format, missing required keys, staging credentials accidentally inherited in production — that would have caused runtime errors during request handling rather than at startup.

> [community] **Gotcha (Zod `coerce.boolean()` and string "false")**: `z.coerce.boolean()` coerces the string `"false"` to `true` because JavaScript's `Boolean("false")` is `true` (any non-empty string is truthy). For feature flag env vars, use `z.enum(['true', 'false']).transform(v => v === 'true').default('false')` instead of `coerce.boolean()`. This is a semantic trap that causes feature flags to appear permanently enabled when explicitly set to `"false"`.

### 9. Bun Test Runner — Shift-Left Integration for TypeScript

**Bun** (v1.x) includes a built-in test runner (`bun test`) that executes TypeScript test files without a transpilation step, using native TypeScript stripping. For teams already using Bun as their runtime, this eliminates the `ts-jest` / Vitest configuration layer and runs tests significantly faster.

**Shift-left relevance**: `bun test` runs a 200-test TypeScript suite in < 1 second on typical hardware (vs 3–8 seconds with Vitest + V8 coverage). This makes test execution fast enough to run on every file save in `--watch` mode without IDE lag.

```typescript
// bun test is compatible with Jest/Vitest API surface:
// describe, it, expect, mock, spyOn — no config change needed for migration
import { describe, it, expect, mock, beforeEach } from 'bun:test';

// src/services/user.service.test.ts
import { UserService } from './user.service';
import type { UserRepository } from '../repositories/user.repository';

describe('UserService', () => {
  let userService: UserService;
  let mockRepo: UserRepository;

  beforeEach(() => {
    mockRepo = {
      findById: mock(async (id: string) => ({ id, name: 'Test User', email: 'test@example.com' })),
      save: mock(async (user) => user),
      delete: mock(async () => true),
    } as unknown as UserRepository;

    userService = new UserService(mockRepo);
  });

  it('retrieves a user by ID', async () => {
    const user = await userService.getUser('user-123');
    expect(user.name).toBe('Test User');
    expect(mockRepo.findById).toHaveBeenCalledWith('user-123');
  });

  it('throws NotFoundError when user does not exist', async () => {
    (mockRepo.findById as ReturnType<typeof mock>).mockResolvedValue(null);
    await expect(userService.getUser('nonexistent')).rejects.toThrow('User not found');
  });
});
```

```bash
# package.json scripts for Bun test integration
# "scripts": {
#   "test": "bun test",
#   "test:watch": "bun test --watch",
#   "test:coverage": "bun test --coverage",
#   "test:changed": "bun test --only-failed"    # re-run only previously failing tests
# }
```

> [community] **Lesson (Bun test in production TypeScript projects, 2025–2026)**: Teams migrating from Vitest to `bun test` for unit tests report that 85–95% of tests work without changes. The main incompatibilities are: (1) Vitest-specific `vi.mock()` hoisting (replace with `mock.module()`), (2) `vi.useFakeTimers()` API differences (Bun uses `Bun.jest` clock API), and (3) custom Vitest reporters (replace with Bun's `--reporter` flag). E2E and integration tests typically stay on Vitest/Playwright — `bun test` is most valuable for fast unit test feedback loops.

> [community] **Gotcha (`bun test --coverage` and branch coverage)**: Bun's built-in coverage uses V8 instrumentation (same as Vitest's `provider: 'v8'`) but as of Bun 1.x the coverage output format does not yet integrate with `lcov`/`codecov` reporters in the same way as Vitest. Teams that use Codecov or SonarQube for coverage tracking may need to continue using Vitest for coverage collection while using `bun test` for the fast local feedback loop — running both in CI on their respective test subsets.

### 10. OpenTelemetry Test Observability — Tracing Test Execution for Flakiness Analysis

Instrumenting test runs with OpenTelemetry traces provides a structured, queryable record of every test execution — not just pass/fail, but timing, retry count, error messages, and environment metadata. This shifts flakiness debugging from "reproduce the flake locally" to "query the trace data."

```typescript
// vitest.setup.ts — OpenTelemetry tracing for test observability
// Requires: npm install @opentelemetry/sdk-node @opentelemetry/exporter-otlp-grpc
import { NodeSDK } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-node';
import { OTLPTraceExporter } from '@opentelemetry/exporter-trace-otlp-grpc';
import { trace, SpanStatusCode } from '@opentelemetry/api';

const sdk = new NodeSDK({
  traceExporter: new OTLPTraceExporter({
    url: process.env['OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT'] ?? 'http://localhost:4317',
  }),
  serviceName: 'vitest-test-suite',
});

// Only start OTEL tracing in CI with an explicit endpoint configured
if (process.env['CI'] && process.env['OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT']) {
  sdk.start();
}

// Custom reporter hook: wrap each test in an OTEL span
// In vitest.config.ts: reporters: ['default', './vitest.setup']
export function onTestStart(testName: string, filePath: string): () => void {
  const tracer = trace.getTracer('vitest');
  const span = tracer.startSpan(`test: ${testName}`, {
    attributes: {
      'test.file': filePath,
      'test.name': testName,
      'git.branch': process.env['GITHUB_REF_NAME'] ?? 'local',
      'git.sha': process.env['GITHUB_SHA'] ?? 'unknown',
      'ci.run_id': process.env['GITHUB_RUN_ID'] ?? 'local',
    },
  });
  return () => span.end();
}

export function onTestFail(testName: string, error: Error, retryCount: number): void {
  const span = trace.getActiveSpan();
  span?.setStatus({ code: SpanStatusCode.ERROR, message: error.message });
  span?.setAttribute('test.retry_count', retryCount);
  span?.setAttribute('test.error.type', error.constructor.name);
}
```

> [community] **Lesson (OTEL for test flakiness analysis, 2025)**: Teams that ship test execution traces to Grafana Tempo or Honeycomb report being able to identify flaky tests by querying for `test.retry_count > 0` grouped by `test.file` — surfacing the most flaky test files without waiting for manual investigation. The time-series view also reveals when flakiness was introduced (correlating with specific `git.sha` values), directly linking flakiness to the commit that caused it.

> [community] **Gotcha (OTEL test tracing + CI cost)**: Sending trace data from test runs in every PR can generate significant data volume at scale (10,000+ tests × 50 PRs/day = 500,000 spans/day). Strategies to control cost: (1) sample traces at 10% in pre-commit hooks, 100% in nightly runs, (2) send only FAILED and RETRIED test spans (not passing spans), (3) use a local Prometheus + Grafana stack for CI-internal metrics rather than a cloud OTLP endpoint.

### 11. `@typescript-eslint` Strict and Stylistic Rule Sets — Graduated Adoption

The `@typescript-eslint` project ships three preset rule sets that allow graduated adoption of stricter rules without committing to the full set from day one. This is the correct shift-left adoption pattern: start with `recommended`, add `strict`, add `stylistic` incrementally as the team's TypeScript fluency grows.

```typescript
// eslint.config.ts — graduated typescript-eslint rule adoption strategy
import tseslint from 'typescript-eslint';

// LEVEL 1: New project — start here (default for most projects)
// Catches: any, non-null assertions without justification, unsafe operations
const level1 = tseslint.configs.recommended;

// LEVEL 2: Mature TypeScript project — add after team is comfortable with Level 1
// Catches: prefer-nullish-coalescing, prefer-optional-chain, no-unnecessary-type-assertion
// Additional rules that catch real bugs but require TypeScript familiarity
const level2 = tseslint.configs.strict; // extends recommended

// LEVEL 3: High-confidence TypeScript team — add for stylistic consistency
// Catches: prefer array destructuring, no restricted-syntax anti-patterns
// Style rules that make code more idiomatic TypeScript — not safety-critical
const level3 = tseslint.configs.stylistic; // style-only additions

export default tseslint.config(
  // Start with level 1, uncomment levels 2 and 3 as team matures:
  ...level1,
  // ...level2,   // uncomment when Level 1 errors are zero across the codebase
  // ...level3,   // uncomment when Level 2 errors are zero

  // Type-checked extensions — add alongside Level 2 or 3
  // Requires projectService: true in languageOptions
  // ...tseslint.configs.strictTypeChecked,
  // ...tseslint.configs.stylisticTypeChecked,

  {
    rules: {
      // Override specific rules where the team has chosen a different convention:
      '@typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any': 'warn',     // downgrade from error if codebase has many any usages during migration
      '@typescript-eslint/no-non-null-assertion': 'warn', // downgrade during incremental migration
    }
  }
);
```

> [community] **Lesson (graduated `@typescript-eslint` adoption, 2025)**: The most common mistake when adding `@typescript-eslint` to an existing JavaScript-converted TypeScript project is enabling all strict rules at once and receiving 2,000+ lint errors. Teams that do this either revert the change or add `@ts-ignore` everywhere. The graduated approach (Level 1 → Level 2 → Level 3 over 3–6 months) produces zero-error baselines at each step, making it safe to treat each level as a hard CI gate.

### 12. Playwright AI-Assisted Test Authoring — `npx playwright init-agents` (v1.56+)

Playwright 1.56 introduced `npx playwright init-agents --loop=claude|vscode|opencode`, which sets up a three-agent test authoring workflow: **Planner** (reads the codebase and decomposes test goals), **Generator** (writes test code using Playwright APIs), and **Healer** (fixes failing tests by inspecting error messages). This is covered briefly in the Playwright patterns reference; this entry focuses on its shift-left implications.

```typescript
// Example: the three-agent workflow creates this directory structure:
// tests/
//   agents/
//     planner.md        ← describes what scenarios to test, which pages, which user roles
//     generator/
//       checkout.spec.ts ← generated by Generator agent
//       auth.spec.ts
//     healer.log        ← records which generated tests failed and how they were fixed
//
// The shift-left value: test generation happens in the IDE during feature development,
// not as a post-development QA phase.

// .claude/agents/playwright-generator.md (installed by init-agents)
// The Generator agent uses this prompt template:
// "Given the planner's scenario descriptions, write Playwright test cases using:
//  - page.getByRole() for interactive elements (ARIA-first selectors)
//  - page.getByLabel() for form inputs
//  - expect(locator).toBeVisible() for assertions (web-first)
//  - test.use({ storageState: 'playwright/.auth/user.json' }) for authenticated tests
//  Never use XPath or CSS attribute selectors directly."
```

> [community] **Lesson (Playwright AI agent test authoring, 2025–2026)**: Teams using `init-agents --loop=claude` report that the Planner agent is the most valuable of the three — it reads the codebase (routes, components, API contracts) and produces a structured list of test scenarios that matches the actual behavior of the application more accurately than manually written test plans. The Generator agent's test code quality is good (85–90% runs on first attempt); the Healer agent fixes the remaining 10–15% without human intervention in most cases.

> [community] **Gotcha (Playwright AI agents + authentication state)**: The Generator agent defaults to unauthenticated page loads unless explicitly told about authentication. Tests for authenticated pages fail until the Healer agent inspects the redirect and adds `storageState`. Speed this up by including a note in your `planner.md`: "All pages under `/app/` require authentication. Use `test.use({ storageState: 'playwright/.auth/user.json' })` which is created by `playwright/global-setup.ts`."
