### Pattern 183 — Vitest Browser Mode `userEvent` from `@vitest/browser/context` for Real Interaction Testing [official]

When running Vitest in browser mode (Playwright or WebdriverIO provider), the `userEvent` import should come from `@vitest/browser/context`, not from `@testing-library/user-event`. The browser-mode `userEvent` dispatches real browser events through the provider's automation API — actual pointer events, keyboard scancodes, and clipboard operations against the real DOM — rather than simulated synthetic events. This catches interaction defects that jsdom simulation misses: CSS `pointer-events: none` blocking clicks, `contenteditable` paste behaviour, and `input` elements with `inputmode` restrictions.

```typescript
// src/components/RichTextEditor.test.tsx
import { render } from 'vitest-browser-react';
import { userEvent, page } from '@vitest/browser/context';
import { RichTextEditor } from './RichTextEditor';

describe('RichTextEditor', () => {
  it('formats selected text as bold via keyboard shortcut', async () => {
    render(<RichTextEditor initialContent="hello world" />);

    // Use browser-mode userEvent — real keyboard events through Playwright
    const editor = page.getByRole('textbox', { name: /editor/i });

    // Select all text
    await userEvent.click(editor);
    await userEvent.keyboard('{Control>}a{/Control}');

    // Apply bold formatting via keyboard shortcut
    await userEvent.keyboard('{Control>}b{/Control}');

    // Assert DOM reflects the formatting — checks real browser behaviour
    await expect.element(editor.getByRole('strong')).toBeInTheDocument();
  });

  it('blocks paste of script tags via clipboard sanitiser', async () => {
    render(<RichTextEditor initialContent="" />);
    const editor = page.getByRole('textbox', { name: /editor/i });

    // Paste malicious content via real clipboard API
    await userEvent.click(editor);
    await userEvent.paste('<script>alert(1)</script>normal text');

    // Sanitiser should strip the script tag
    const content = await editor.textContent();
    expect(content).not.toContain('<script>');
    expect(content).toContain('normal text');
  });

  it('respects pointer-events: none on disabled state', async () => {
    render(<RichTextEditor initialContent="read only" disabled />);
    const editor = page.getByRole('textbox', { name: /editor/i });

    // Real browser click — should be blocked by CSS pointer-events: none
    await userEvent.click(editor);
    // Verify no selection occurred (cursor stays at initial position)
    await expect.element(editor).not.toHaveFocus();
  });
});

// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    browser: {
      enabled: true,
      provider: 'playwright',
      headless: true,
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Browser mode tests run 5–20x slower than jsdom unit tests because each test file spins up a real browser context (even in headless mode). Reserve browser-mode `userEvent` for interaction-sensitive components where the jsdom simulation is known to be inaccurate: drag-and-drop, clipboard operations, `contenteditable`, `<canvas>` interactions, CSS animation triggers, and form controls with non-standard `inputmode`. Do not migrate all unit tests to browser mode — the speed penalty makes it unsuitable as a default. Run browser-mode tests as a dedicated `test:browser` CI step that executes after unit tests pass.

---

### Pattern 184 — Vitest `coverage.include` + `thresholds.100` for Critical Domain Modules [official]

Rather than applying a single aggregate threshold to the entire codebase (which allows low-coverage utility files to drag down the average), Vitest supports per-path coverage thresholds via `thresholds` overrides. Pairing this with `coverage.include` scoping and a `thresholds.100` requirement on core domain modules creates a two-tier coverage contract: 100% coverage on business-critical code (payment processing, auth, data access layer), flexible thresholds elsewhere. This is stricter than per-file thresholds because it applies to the logical module group rather than individual files.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      // Include all source files in measurement (even untested ones)
      include: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
      exclude: [
        'src/**/*.d.ts',
        'src/**/*.stories.tsx',
        'src/**/index.ts',    // barrel files — re-exports only
        'src/generated/**',   // codegen output
      ],
      reporter: ['text', 'lcov', 'json-summary'],
      // Per-path threshold overrides — 100% on critical modules
      thresholds: {
        // Global minimums — non-critical code
        lines: 80,
        branches: 75,
        functions: 80,
        statements: 80,
        // Strict 100% on payment domain
        'src/domain/payments/**': {
          lines: 100,
          branches: 100,
          functions: 100,
          statements: 100,
        },
        // Strict 100% on auth module
        'src/auth/**': {
          lines: 100,
          branches: 100,
          functions: 100,
          statements: 100,
        },
        // 90% on data access layer — allow escape hatches for raw SQL
        'src/db/**': {
          lines: 90,
          branches: 85,
          functions: 90,
          statements: 90,
        },
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Requiring 100% branch coverage on payment and auth modules forces tests for every `if` branch, including defensive error handling paths that are nearly impossible to trigger in a unit test without extensive mocking (e.g., a `catch` block that handles a network timeout in a payment gateway call). Teams often paper over these branches with `/* v8 ignore next */` comments, which defeats the purpose. Before applying 100% branch coverage, audit the target module for branches that can only be covered with integration tests — move those branches into dedicated integration test files and exclude them from the unit-level threshold using `/* v8 ignore */` with a comment linking to the integration test that covers them.

---

### Pattern 185 — Vitest `fileParallelism: false` with `maxConcurrency` for Database-Bound Integration Suites [official]

By default Vitest runs test files in parallel across multiple workers — ideal for unit tests but problematic for integration suites that share a single database instance. Parallel test files race to insert and query the same rows, producing non-deterministic foreign key violations and flaky assertions. `fileParallelism: false` forces sequential file execution (one file at a time) while `maxConcurrency` controls how many tests within a single file can run concurrently. The combination gives precise control over the concurrency surface without abandoning parallelism entirely.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — separate config for integration tests
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Run test files sequentially — prevents DB-level race conditions
    fileParallelism: false,
    // Within a file, allow up to 3 concurrent tests (uses test.concurrent)
    maxConcurrency: 3,
    // Use pool forks for true process isolation per test file
    pool: 'forks',
    include: ['src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
    setupFiles: ['./test/db-setup.ts'],
    testTimeout: 30_000,
  },
});

// test/db-setup.ts — per-file DB state management
import { db } from '../src/db/client';

beforeAll(async () => {
  // Each file gets a named schema to prevent row collisions
  const schema = `test_${process.env.VITEST_WORKER_ID ?? '0'}`;
  await db.execute(`CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS ${schema}`);
  await db.execute(`SET search_path TO ${schema}`);
  await db.execute('CALL run_migrations()');
});

afterAll(async () => {
  const schema = `test_${process.env.VITEST_WORKER_ID ?? '0'}`;
  await db.execute(`DROP SCHEMA ${schema} CASCADE`);
});

// Example: tests within a file can be concurrent (different rows)
describe('order repository', () => {
  it.concurrent('creates order for user A', async () => {
    const order = await orderRepo.create({ userId: 'user-A', total: 100 });
    expect(order.id).toBeDefined();
  });

  it.concurrent('creates order for user B', async () => {
    const order = await orderRepo.create({ userId: 'user-B', total: 200 });
    expect(order.id).toBeDefined();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Sequential file execution (`fileParallelism: false`) eliminates cross-file DB race conditions but increases total suite duration proportionally to the number of test files. For 20 integration test files averaging 5 seconds each, sequential execution takes at least 100 seconds — compared to ~25 seconds with 4 parallel workers. Mitigate this with sharding (`--shard=1/4`) to distribute sequential-within-shard execution across 4 CI runners, achieving parallelism at the shard level while maintaining isolation at the file level. Pair with schema-per-worker isolation as shown above to allow `maxConcurrency > 1` within each file safely.

---

### Pattern 186 — MSW v2 `http.passthrough()` for Selective Real-Network Integration Tests [community]

MSW v2 introduced `http.passthrough()` as a first-class handler return value that lets specific requests bypass the service worker and reach the real network. This enables selective real-network integration tests: mock the application's own API endpoints while allowing third-party requests (analytics, feature flags, payment SDKs) to pass through to their real servers during local development. In CI, the pattern inverts: all third-party requests are mocked with deterministic fixtures, while internal API requests use `http.passthrough()` to hit a real test environment.

```typescript
// test/msw/handlers.ts
import { http, HttpResponse, passthrough } from 'msw';

export const handlers = [
  // Internal API — always mock for determinism
  http.get('/api/users/:id', ({ params }) => {
    return HttpResponse.json({ id: params.id, name: 'Test User', role: 'admin' });
  }),

  // LaunchDarkly feature flags — pass through in development, mock in CI
  http.get('https://sdk.launchdarkly.com/sdk/latest-all', () => {
    if (process.env.CI) {
      // Return deterministic flags in CI to prevent flakiness
      return HttpResponse.json({
        'new-checkout-flow': { value: true, variation: 0 },
        'dark-mode': { value: false, variation: 1 },
      });
    }
    // Real LaunchDarkly call during local dev — tests real flag values
    return passthrough();
  }),

  // Stripe.js — always passthrough (browser SDK, intercept not meaningful)
  http.post('https://api.stripe.com/v1/payment_methods', () => {
    return passthrough();
  }),

  // Catch-all: log unhandled requests in development, warn in CI
  http.all('*', ({ request }) => {
    if (process.env.CI) {
      console.warn(`[MSW] Unhandled request: ${request.method} ${request.url}`);
    }
    return passthrough();
  }),
];

// test/setup.ts
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';
import { handlers } from './msw/handlers';
export const server = setupServer(...handlers);

beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'warn' }));
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());
afterAll(() => server.close());
```

**Tradeoff.** `passthrough()` in development tests introduces non-determinism: tests that reach real third-party APIs can fail due to network conditions, API rate limits, or upstream service changes — none of which are related to the code under test. Reserve `passthrough()` for local developer workflows where real-network feedback is valuable (verifying feature flag behaviour against a real account, testing Stripe webhook signatures). In CI, replace all `passthrough()` calls with deterministic mocked responses using an environment variable guard (`process.env.CI`). Document which handlers use `passthrough()` and why, so future maintainers understand the intentional bypass rather than treating it as an oversight.

---

### Pattern 187 — TypeScript `satisfies` Operator for Test Fixture Type-Safety Without Widening [community]

The TypeScript `satisfies` operator (introduced in TS 4.9) validates that a value matches a type without widening the inferred type to the declared type. In test fixtures, this distinction matters: declaring `const fixture: UserProfile = { ... }` widens the inferred type to `UserProfile`, losing the literal types of individual fields. Subsequent test assertions against literal field values (`.toBe('admin')`) then lose autocomplete and exactness. Using `satisfies` instead preserves the narrow literal type while still validating the fixture against the declared interface — type errors surface at the fixture declaration site rather than propagating silently into test assertions.

```typescript
// src/types/user.ts
interface UserProfile {
  id: string;
  role: 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer';
  permissions: string[];
  metadata: Record<string, unknown>;
}

// test/fixtures/users.ts
import type { UserProfile } from '../../src/types/user';

// BAD: declares as UserProfile — role is widened to string union
// const adminUser: UserProfile = { id: 'u-1', role: 'admin', ... };

// GOOD: satisfies validates against UserProfile but preserves literal types
export const adminUser = {
  id: 'u-1',
  role: 'admin',           // inferred as literal 'admin', not 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer'
  permissions: ['users:read', 'users:write'],
  metadata: { tier: 'enterprise' },
} satisfies UserProfile;

// TypeScript error if fixture is invalid — catches fixture rot at declaration
// export const invalidUser = {
//   id: 'u-2',
//   role: 'superuser',    // TS Error: 'superuser' not assignable to 'admin'|'editor'|'viewer'
//   permissions: [],
//   metadata: {},
// } satisfies UserProfile;

// In tests: narrow types preserved — autocomplete works, no 'as' casts needed
import { adminUser } from '../fixtures/users';
import { authorizeAction } from '../../src/auth/authorize';

describe('authorizeAction', () => {
  it('grants write access to admin role', () => {
    // adminUser.role is inferred as literal 'admin' — no widening
    const result = authorizeAction(adminUser, 'users:write');
    expect(result.granted).toBe(true);
    expect(result.reason).toBe('role:admin');
  });

  it('fixture type is structurally valid — satisfies catches interface drift', () => {
    // If UserProfile adds a required field, the satisfies operator
    // produces a TS error at the fixture declaration site — not in test assertions
    expect(adminUser.metadata.tier).toBe('enterprise');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `satisfies` is a compile-time-only operator — it produces no runtime code. The type narrowing benefit disappears when the fixture is passed to a function that accepts the wider type (`UserProfile`), since TypeScript widens the argument back to the parameter type at the call site. Use `satisfies` for fixture objects that are directly accessed in test assertions (`.role`, `.permissions[0]`). For fixtures that are immediately passed to the function under test as arguments, the narrowing benefit is minimal — use a type annotation instead. Adopt `satisfies` consistently with an ESLint rule (`@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-assertions`) set to discourage `as` casts in favour of `satisfies` to enforce it across the test suite.

---

### Pattern 188 — Vitest `vi.waitFor` with Custom Polling Interval for Async Side-Effect Verification [official]

`vi.waitFor` polls a callback until it stops throwing or until a timeout is reached. Unlike `expect.poll`, `vi.waitFor` works with any throwable assertion — including assertions about side effects (emitted events, database writes, external API calls captured by MSW). Customising the `interval` prevents tight-polling CPU spikes in suites that test high-latency async operations (background job processors, event-driven architectures, webhook delivery). The `timeout` parameter sets the maximum wait before failing the test.

```typescript
// src/jobs/email-processor.test.ts
import { vi } from 'vitest';
import { server } from '../test/setup';
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { processEmailQueue } from '../../src/jobs/email-processor';

describe('email processor', () => {
  it('delivers queued emails within 5 seconds of processing', async () => {
    const deliveredEmails: string[] = [];

    // Capture outbound email delivery calls via MSW
    server.use(
      http.post('https://api.sendgrid.com/v3/mail/send', async ({ request }) => {
        const body = await request.json() as {
          personalizations: Array<{ to: Array<{ email: string }> }>;
        };
        deliveredEmails.push(body.personalizations[0].to[0].email);
        return new HttpResponse(null, { status: 202 });
      }),
    );

    // Seed 3 emails into the queue and start processor
    await seedEmailQueue(['user1@test.com', 'user2@test.com', 'user3@test.com']);
    processEmailQueue(); // fire-and-forget — processes in background

    // Wait for all 3 emails to be delivered, polling every 200ms
    await vi.waitFor(
      () => {
        // Throws if condition not met — vi.waitFor retries until timeout
        if (deliveredEmails.length < 3) {
          throw new Error(`Only ${deliveredEmails.length}/3 emails delivered`);
        }
      },
      {
        timeout: 5_000,   // fail after 5 seconds
        interval: 200,    // check every 200ms — avoids tight polling
      },
    );

    expect(deliveredEmails).toEqual(
      expect.arrayContaining(['user1@test.com', 'user2@test.com', 'user3@test.com']),
    );
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `vi.waitFor` with a long `timeout` and short `interval` masks slow async operations by hiding the true latency from the test result. A test that "passes in 4.8 seconds" every time is signalling a performance regression — but the green status obscures it. Pair `vi.waitFor` with a performance assertion: after `waitFor` resolves, check the elapsed time with `performance.now()` and fail if the operation took longer than an acceptable threshold. This converts `vi.waitFor` from a flakiness suppressor into an actual SLA gate. Keep `interval` at 100–500ms for most async operations — intervals below 50ms spin the CPU unnecessarily in workers that could be running other tests.

---

### Pattern 189 — TypeScript `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` as Shift-Left Null Safety for Array and Object Access [official]

`"noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true` in `tsconfig.json` adds `| undefined` to the inferred type of every array index access (`arr[0]`) and string-keyed object access (`obj['key']`). This forces developers to handle the case where an index is out of bounds or a key is absent — catching a whole class of runtime `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` defects at compile time. For test files, it ensures that fixtures accessed by index are either null-checked or the test explicitly asserts the array has enough elements.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true
  }
}

// src/domain/cart.ts — production code becomes null-safe by default
function getFirstItem(cart: CartItem[]): CartItem {
  // Without noUncheckedIndexedAccess: cart[0] is CartItem (may be undefined at runtime)
  // With noUncheckedIndexedAccess: cart[0] is CartItem | undefined — must handle
  const item = cart[0];
  if (!item) throw new CartEmptyError();
  return item; // now CartItem — TypeScript verified the null check
}

// Function with record access — same principle
function getUserPermission(
  permissions: Record<string, string[]>,
  userId: string,
): string[] {
  // permissions[userId] is string[] | undefined with noUncheckedIndexedAccess
  return permissions[userId] ?? [];
}

// test/domain/cart.test.ts — test code also benefits
import { createCart } from '../../src/domain/cart';

describe('cart domain', () => {
  it('returns the first item when cart is populated', () => {
    const cart = createCart([{ sku: 'A1', qty: 2 }, { sku: 'B3', qty: 1 }]);
    const items = cart.getItems();

    // noUncheckedIndexedAccess: items[0] is CartItem | undefined
    // Must assert existence before accessing properties
    const firstItem = items[0];
    expect(firstItem).toBeDefined();
    // Use explicit guard after toBeDefined — TypeScript needs narrowing:
    if (!firstItem) throw new Error('Expected cart to have items');
    expect(firstItem.sku).toBe('A1');
    expect(firstItem.qty).toBe(2);
  });

  it('prefers destructuring over index access to satisfy the type checker cleanly', () => {
    const cart = createCart([{ sku: 'Z9', qty: 5 }]);
    const [firstItem] = cart.getItems();
    // Destructuring assignment: firstItem is CartItem | undefined
    expect(firstItem).toBeDefined();
    if (!firstItem) throw new Error('Expected cart to have items');
    expect(firstItem.sku).toBe('Z9');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Enabling `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` on an existing codebase typically produces hundreds of TypeScript errors — every array index access that was previously assumed non-null now requires a guard. The migration path: enable it in a dedicated `tsconfig.strict.json` that extends the base config, run `tsc --project tsconfig.strict.json --noEmit` in CI as a warning-only step, and track the error count declining over sprints. Do not require `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` to be zero-errors before merging PRs initially — set a ratchet (errors must not increase beyond the baseline) and allocate cleanup time incrementally. For test files specifically, use destructuring assignment with explicit length assertions (`const [first, second] = items; expect(items).toHaveLength(2)`) instead of raw index access — this satisfies the type checker without verbose null guards.

---

### Pattern 190 — `eslint-plugin-vitest` Rule Suite for Shift-Left Test Quality Gates [official]

`eslint-plugin-vitest` provides a dedicated ESLint rule set targeting Vitest-specific anti-patterns: duplicate test names, skipped tests left in production code, assertions outside test bodies, and `expect` calls with no matchers. Running these rules as CI-blocking errors (not warnings) elevates test quality gates to the same level as production code linting — defective tests are caught before they can hide defects in the code under test.

```typescript
// eslint.config.mjs (flat config)
import vitest from 'eslint-plugin-vitest';
import tseslint from 'typescript-eslint';

export default tseslint.config(
  {
    files: ['**/*.test.{ts,tsx}', '**/*.spec.{ts,tsx}'],
    plugins: { vitest },
    rules: {
      // Error: no focused tests in CI (catch .only left in code)
      'vitest/no-focused-tests': 'error',
      // Warning: no skipped tests committed (technical debt signal)
      'vitest/no-skipped-tests': 'warn',
      // Error: expect() calls must have a matcher chained
      'vitest/valid-expect': 'error',
      // Error: each test must have at least one expect assertion
      'vitest/expect-expect': ['error', {
        assertFunctionNames: ['expect', 'assertOrderConfirmed', 'assertUserHasRole'],
      }],
      // Error: no duplicate test names in a describe block
      'vitest/no-identical-title': 'error',
      // Warning: no commented-out test code (dead test debt)
      'vitest/no-commented-out-tests': 'warn',
      // Error: concurrent snapshot tests need local context
      'vitest/require-local-test-context-for-concurrent-snapshots': 'error',
      // Warning: prefer .toBeNull() over .toBe(null)
      'vitest/prefer-to-be-null': 'warn',
      // Warning: prefer .toBeUndefined() over .toBe(undefined)
      'vitest/prefer-to-be-undefined': 'warn',
    },
  },
);

// Pre-commit hook — run ESLint on staged test files only (fast)
// lint-staged.config.mjs
// export default {
//   '**/*.test.{ts,tsx}': ['eslint --fix --max-warnings=0'],
//   '**/*.spec.{ts,tsx}': ['eslint --fix --max-warnings=0'],
// };
```

**Tradeoff.** `vitest/expect-expect` fires on tests that use custom assertion helpers that wrap `expect` internally — the rule cannot trace through function calls to find the nested `expect`. Teams that extract domain-specific assertion helpers (e.g., `assertOrderConfirmed(order)`) must configure the rule with `assertFunctionNames: ['expect', 'assertOrderConfirmed', 'assertUserHasRole']` to prevent false positives. Without this configuration, teams disable `expect-expect` entirely, losing protection against vacuous tests that accidentally pass. Document every custom assertion helper in the ESLint config comment alongside the rule so future maintainers understand why the exceptions exist.

---

### Pattern 191 — Vitest `test.extend` for Reusable Test Fixtures with Typed Cleanup Contracts [official]

`test.extend` (Vitest 1.3+) adds fixture support directly to the `test` function — similar to Playwright's fixture model. Each fixture declares its value and a cleanup function in a generator, with Vitest guaranteeing cleanup execution even when the test throws. Unlike `beforeEach`/`afterEach` setup, fixtures are lazy (only instantiated when requested by name in the test function signature), composable (fixtures can depend on other fixtures), and typed (the fixture type flows into the test function signature automatically).

```typescript
// test/fixtures/index.ts
import { test as baseTest } from 'vitest';
import { db } from '../../src/db/client';
import { createTestUser, deleteTestUser } from '../helpers/user-factory';
import type { User } from '../../src/types/user';
import type { Database } from '../../src/db/types';

interface TestFixtures {
  db: Database;
  adminUser: User;
  editorUser: User;
}

export const test = baseTest.extend<TestFixtures>({
  // db fixture — provides a transaction-scoped DB connection
  db: async ({}, use) => {
    const trx = await db.transaction();
    await use(trx);
    // Always rolls back — test data never persists
    await trx.rollback();
  },

  // adminUser depends on the db fixture — Vitest resolves dependency graph
  adminUser: async ({ db }, use) => {
    const user = await createTestUser(db, { role: 'admin', email: 'admin@test.com' });
    await use(user);
    // Cleanup runs even if test throws — guaranteed by the generator protocol
    await deleteTestUser(db, user.id);
  },

  // editorUser — separate user fixture, same transaction scope
  editorUser: async ({ db }, use) => {
    const user = await createTestUser(db, { role: 'editor', email: 'editor@test.com' });
    await use(user);
    await deleteTestUser(db, user.id);
  },
});

// test/auth/permissions.test.ts — clean fixture consumption
import { test } from '../fixtures';
import { expect } from 'vitest';
import { checkPermission } from '../../src/auth/permissions';

// TypeScript infers adminUser and db from fixture types — no casting needed
test('admin can read user list', async ({ adminUser, db }) => {
  const result = await checkPermission(db, adminUser.id, 'users:list');
  expect(result).toBe(true);
});

test('editor cannot delete users', async ({ editorUser, db }) => {
  const result = await checkPermission(db, editorUser.id, 'users:delete');
  expect(result).toBe(false);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `test.extend` is optimal for fixtures with complex setup/teardown that must be shared across many test files — the fixture model eliminates copy-pasted `beforeEach` blocks. However, fixtures are not visible in the test file body until consumed through the function parameter, making them invisible to developers unfamiliar with the pattern who expect `beforeEach` style setup at the top of the file. Add a comment above each `test.extend` call listing the available fixture names and their types, and include the fixture module path in your team's testing conventions documentation. Fixtures with dependencies (e.g., `adminUser` depending on `db`) execute in dependency order — if `db` setup fails, `adminUser` setup is never attempted, which is correct behaviour but can produce confusing error messages when the root cause is the database connection rather than the user factory.

---

### Pattern 192 — TypeScript `readonly` Arrays and `Readonly<T>` in Test Assertions to Prevent Accidental Mutation [community]

Test fixtures and assertion helpers that accept mutable arrays can accidentally mutate the input as a side effect of test setup — sorting a `results` array for `toEqual` comparison mutates the original, invalidating assertions that depend on insertion order. Typing fixture return values as `ReadonlyArray<T>` and assertion inputs as `Readonly<T>` makes mutation a compile-time error, catching a subtle class of test defect where the act of asserting changes the state being asserted.

```typescript
// src/repositories/order-repository.ts
interface Order {
  id: string;
  createdAt: Date;
  total: number;
}

// Return type uses ReadonlyArray — communicates that callers should not mutate
async function listOrders(userId: string): Promise<ReadonlyArray<Order>> {
  return db.query<Order>(
    'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id=$1 ORDER BY created_at',
    [userId],
  );
}

// test/repositories/order-repository.test.ts
import { listOrders } from '../../src/repositories/order-repository';

describe('listOrders', () => {
  it('returns orders in chronological order', async () => {
    await seedOrders([
      { userId: 'u-1', total: 50, createdAt: new Date('2026-01-01') },
      { userId: 'u-1', total: 75, createdAt: new Date('2026-01-02') },
    ]);

    const orders: ReadonlyArray<Order> = await listOrders('u-1');

    // TypeScript error: cannot mutate a ReadonlyArray
    // orders.sort((a, b) => b.total - a.total); // TS Error: sort does not exist

    // Correct: create a sorted copy if needed for assertion
    const sortedByTotal = [...orders].sort((a, b) => b.total - a.total);
    expect(sortedByTotal[0]?.total).toBe(75);

    // Original order assertion is safe — ReadonlyArray was not mutated
    expect(orders[0]?.total).toBe(50);
    expect(orders[1]?.total).toBe(75);
  });

  it('returns empty array for user with no orders', async () => {
    const orders: ReadonlyArray<Order> = await listOrders('u-no-orders');
    expect(orders).toHaveLength(0);
    expect(orders).toEqual([]);
  });
});

// Utility: deep-freeze fixture objects in tests to catch runtime mutations
// (complements TypeScript compile-time checks for values created with 'as any')
function freeze<T>(obj: T): Readonly<T> {
  return Object.freeze(obj);
}
// const frozenOrder = freeze({ id: 'o-1', total: 100, createdAt: new Date() });
```

**Tradeoff.** `ReadonlyArray<T>` prevents mutation but not all accidental side effects — methods like `.find()`, `.filter()`, and `.some()` are allowed on `ReadonlyArray` and can still execute side-effectful callbacks. A callback in `.find()` that increments a counter or logs to a spy will execute as a side effect of the assertion. `Object.freeze()` at runtime complements the compile-time `readonly` guarantee for objects: a frozen object throws `TypeError` on any property assignment in strict mode, catching runtime mutations that bypass TypeScript's type system via `as any` casts. Add `Object.freeze()` to fixture factory functions in test helper files as a defence-in-depth measure for critical shared fixtures.

---

### Pattern 193 — Vitest `onTestFailed` Hook for Automatic Diagnostic Capture on Failure [official]

`onTestFailed` is a per-test hook (Vitest 1.4+) that runs only when the enclosing test fails. Unlike `afterEach`, it does not execute on passing tests, making it zero-overhead for green suites. It is the correct location for diagnostic capture: database state dumps, screenshot captures (browser mode), log tail collection, and HTTP request history from MSW — diagnostics that are expensive to generate but only needed when a test fails. Placing diagnostics in `afterEach` wastes resources on every passing test.

```typescript
// test/integration/checkout.test.ts
import { onTestFailed } from 'vitest';
import { server } from '../setup';
import { db } from '../../src/db/client';
import { page } from '@vitest/browser/context';
import * as fs from 'node:fs/promises';
import * as path from 'node:path';

describe('checkout flow', () => {
  it('completes payment for a valid cart', async () => {
    const capturedRequests: Array<{ method: string; url: string; status: number }> = [];

    // Register diagnostic capture — only runs if this specific test fails
    onTestFailed(async (result) => {
      const diagnosticDir = path.join(
        'test-failures',
        `${result.task.id}-${result.task.name.replace(/\s+/g, '-')}`,
      );
      await fs.mkdir(diagnosticDir, { recursive: true });

      // 1. Screenshot of browser state at failure
      const screenshot = await page.screenshot();
      await fs.writeFile(path.join(diagnosticDir, 'screenshot.png'), screenshot);

      // 2. Database state dump
      const rows = await db.query(
        'SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10',
      );
      await fs.writeFile(
        path.join(diagnosticDir, 'db-state.json'),
        JSON.stringify(rows.rows, null, 2),
      );

      // 3. MSW request history
      await fs.writeFile(
        path.join(diagnosticDir, 'requests.json'),
        JSON.stringify(capturedRequests, null, 2),
      );

      console.error(`[onTestFailed] Diagnostics saved to: ${diagnosticDir}`);
    });

    // Track MSW requests for this test
    server.events.on('request:end', ({ request, response }) => {
      capturedRequests.push({
        method: request.method,
        url: request.url,
        status: response?.status ?? 0,
      });
    });

    // The actual test
    await navigateToCheckout();
    await fillPaymentDetails({ card: '4242 4242 4242 4242', expiry: '12/28', cvv: '123' });
    await submitPayment();
    await expect.element(page.getByText('Order confirmed')).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `onTestFailed` is registered inside the test body — the diagnostic setup code executes on every test run, even when the test passes (the _callback_ is skipped, but the registration and event listener attachment still occur). For tests with expensive event listener setup (attaching to `server.events`), this registration overhead is unavoidable. In suites with thousands of tests, aggregate registration overhead is measurable. Mitigate by moving the MSW request tracker into a `beforeEach` helper that is always active, and restrict `onTestFailed` to the screenshot and database dump operations — the two most expensive diagnostics that benefit most from the conditional execution guarantee.

---

### Pattern 194 — V8 vs Istanbul Coverage Provider Selection Based on Runtime and Speed Requirements [official]

Vitest supports two coverage providers — V8 (native runtime instrumentation) and Istanbul (source instrumentation). The choice between them is not stylistic: it depends on runtime environment, acceptable build overhead, and coverage accuracy requirements. V8 coverage is faster and zero-overhead at instrumentation time, but requires a V8-based runtime (Node.js, Chrome). Istanbul works on any JavaScript runtime and supports more granular ignore directives, but adds instrumentation overhead to every instrumented source file, slowing cold-start and potentially masking performance regressions in benchmarks.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — choosing the right provider
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

// OPTION A: V8 provider (default) — for Node.js projects, CI speed priority
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      // V8 ignore directive in source: /* v8 ignore next -- @preserve */
      // Use @preserve to prevent minifiers from stripping the comment
      include: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
      exclude: [
        'src/generated/**',
        'src/**/*.stories.tsx',
        'src/**/index.ts',
      ],
      reporter: ['text', 'lcov'],
      thresholds: { lines: 85, branches: 80, functions: 85 },
    },
  },
});

// OPTION B: Istanbul provider — for Bun/Deno or when PR review accuracy matters
// export default defineConfig({
//   test: {
//     coverage: {
//       provider: 'istanbul',
//       // Istanbul ignore directive: /* istanbul ignore next -- @preserve */
//       // Supports per-function and per-branch granularity
//       include: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
//       exclude: ['src/generated/**'],
//       reporter: ['text', 'html', 'lcov', 'json-summary'],
//       thresholds: { lines: 85, branches: 80 },
//     },
//   },
// });

// Example source annotation — both providers
function parseConfig(raw: unknown): Config {
  if (typeof raw !== 'object' || raw === null) {
    /* v8 ignore next -- @preserve */ // defensive; covered by integration test
    throw new ConfigParseError('Input must be an object');
  }
  return raw as Config;
}
```

**Tradeoff.** V8 coverage reports are based on bytecode ranges — a single TypeScript expression may map to multiple V8 coverage segments, causing unexpected "uncovered" highlights on code that visually appears covered. This is most pronounced in complex ternary expressions, template literals, and optional chaining chains. Istanbul instruments at the AST level and produces more predictable per-statement, per-branch, and per-function coverage mapping. For teams that use coverage reports as a code review tool (reviewing `lcov` output in PR comments), Istanbul's more intuitive mapping is worth the instrumentation overhead. For teams that only use coverage as a CI gate (pass/fail threshold), V8's speed advantage typically dominates.

---

### Pattern 195 — Vitest `typecheck` Mode with `.typetest.ts` Filter for Type-Only Regression Tests [official]

Vitest's `typecheck` mode runs `tsc` over test files that use `expectTypeOf` and `assertType`, surfacing type assertion failures as test failures alongside runtime test results. Separating type-only tests into dedicated `*.typetest.ts` files and filtering `typecheck.include` to match only those files prevents the typecheck runner from processing every test file (which would double the `tsc` invocation time). The result: a dedicated type regression suite that runs in CI as a fast parallel step alongside the runtime test suite.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    typecheck: {
      // Only type-check files with .typetest.ts extension — not all test files
      include: ['**/*.typetest.ts'],
      // Use project's tsconfig for type-checking
      tsconfig: './tsconfig.json',
      // Fail on TypeScript errors in typetest files (not just assertType failures)
      ignoreSourceErrors: false,
    },
  },
});

// src/types/result.typetest.ts — pure type tests, no runtime code
import { expectTypeOf } from 'vitest';
import type { Result, Ok, Err } from '../result';

// Verify that Ok<T> and Err<E> are structurally correct
declare const ok: Ok<number>;
declare const err: Err<string>;

expectTypeOf(ok).toMatchTypeOf<Ok<number>>();
expectTypeOf(err).toMatchTypeOf<Err<string>>();

// Verify Result<T, E> discriminated union narrows correctly in if-blocks
function processResult(r: Result<number, string>): string {
  if (r.ok) {
    expectTypeOf(r).toMatchTypeOf<Ok<number>>();
    expectTypeOf(r.value).toBeNumber();
    return `success: ${r.value}`;
  } else {
    expectTypeOf(r).toMatchTypeOf<Err<string>>();
    expectTypeOf(r.error).toBeString();
    return `error: ${r.error}`;
  }
}

// Regression gate: verify union structure has not drifted
// This test fails at type-check time if the union structure changes
type _NarrowingCheck = Ok<number> extends Err<string> ? 'ERROR: union overlap' : 'OK';
expectTypeOf<_NarrowingCheck>().toEqualTypeOf<'OK'>();
```

**Tradeoff.** Type-only test files increase the `tsc` invocation surface. If `typecheck.include` accidentally matches all `*.ts` test files (e.g., `'**/*.test.ts'` instead of `'**/*.typetest.ts'`), the typecheck step processes every test file and its imports — dramatically increasing typecheck time on large test suites. Validate the `include` pattern with `vitest typecheck --reporter=verbose` and confirm only intended files are processed. Type tests are also fragile in a different way from runtime tests: a TypeScript minor version upgrade can change type inference behaviour, causing previously-passing `expectTypeOf` assertions to fail with no change in source code. Pin the TypeScript version in `package.json` as an exact version (not `^`) in projects that use type tests to prevent silent breakage from automatic upgrades.

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 50

> [community] **Gotcha (Vitest `test.extend` fixture cleanup skipped when `use()` is never called inside the fixture generator, 2026)**: Teams writing conditional fixtures (where the fixture body short-circuits before calling `await use(value)` if a precondition fails) discover that neither the fixture value is passed to the test nor is any cleanup after `use()` executed — Vitest logs a warning rather than throwing a test failure when a generator exits without calling `use()`. **WHY**: `test.extend` fixtures are generator functions that must call `await use(fixtureValue)` exactly once. If a fixture throws before calling `use()`, the test is marked as failed with the fixture setup error. If the generator exits without calling `use()` (e.g., due to a conditional `return` before `use()`), the fixture contract is violated — Vitest cannot guarantee cleanup of resources allocated before the `return`. The fix: never use conditional returns before `use()` in fixture generators. If a fixture depends on a precondition, throw an explicit error with a descriptive message — this produces a clear test failure that identifies the fixture as the source of the problem, rather than a silent contract violation.

> [community] **Gotcha (Vitest `coverage.thresholds` per-path overrides silently pass when the glob matches zero coverage report entries, 2026)**: Teams configuring `'src/domain/payments/**': { lines: 100 }` in the threshold overrides section find that the 100% threshold never blocks CI — even when payment domain files have 40% line coverage. **WHY**: The per-path threshold key is a glob matched against the relative paths stored in the coverage report. If the coverage report stores paths in a different format (absolute paths, or paths relative to a different base directory) than the threshold glob expects, the glob never matches any entry and the threshold is never evaluated — Vitest does not warn about unmatched threshold globs. The fix: run `vitest run --coverage --reporter=json` and inspect the `filePath` keys in `coverage/coverage-summary.json` to determine the exact path format used, then write threshold globs to match that exact format precisely.

> [community] **Gotcha (Vitest `onTestFailed` registered inside `test.concurrent` produces race-condition writes when multiple concurrent tests fail simultaneously using `result.task.name` as the output path key, 2026)**: Teams using `onTestFailed` inside `test.concurrent` blocks to save diagnostics keyed by test name find that concurrent failures produce interleaved file writes when two concurrent tests happen to share the same name across separate `describe` blocks. **WHY**: `test.concurrent` runs multiple tests simultaneously within a single worker. When two concurrent tests fail at nearly the same time, both `onTestFailed` callbacks are invoked and their async file writes interleave — `fs.mkdir` from the second callback finds the directory already created by the first, and `fs.writeFile` calls on the same filename overwrite each other. The fix: include `result.task.id` (a unique per-test-run identifier) alongside `result.task.name` in the diagnostic directory path: `path.join('test-failures', `${result.task.id}-${result.task.name}`)`. Task IDs are unique across concurrent test executions even when names are identical.

> [community] **Gotcha (Vitest `isolate: false` causes module-level `vi.mock` factories to be evaluated only once, making the first file's factory shadow subsequent files' different factories for the same module path, 2026)**: Teams enabling `isolate: false` for performance find that two test files that both call `vi.mock('../src/auth/client')` with different factory implementations exhibit the behaviour of whichever file's factory ran first — the second file's `vi.mock` call is silently ignored. **WHY**: With `isolate: false`, Vitest does not clear the module registry between test files. `vi.mock` registers a module factory at evaluation time; with a shared module cache, re-registering a factory for a path that is already mocked has no effect — the cached mock module is returned for all subsequent imports. The fix: either re-enable `isolate: true` for test files that use conflicting mocks of the same module path, or refactor both files to use `vi.mocked(module).mockImplementation(...)` inside `beforeEach` instead of module-level `vi.mock` factories — this reconfigures the single shared mock instance per test rather than replacing the module factory.

> [community] **Gotcha (Vitest `typecheck` mode with `ignoreSourceErrors: false` blocks the entire typecheck step when a single shared utility import contains a type error, even in files with no `expectTypeOf` calls, 2026)**: Teams enabling `vitest typecheck` with `ignoreSourceErrors: false` find that a type error in any file matched by `typecheck.include` blocks the entire typecheck step — including files that were only included for their `expectTypeOf` assertions and have no type errors themselves. **WHY**: `ignoreSourceErrors: false` tells Vitest to fail on TypeScript compiler errors anywhere in the type-checked file's import graph, not just in `assertType`/`expectTypeOf` call sites. A single broken shared utility becomes a blocker for the entire typecheck suite because Vitest's typecheck step traverses the full import graph. The fix: use `typecheck.include: ['**/*.typetest.ts']` to restrict the scope to dedicated type-test files only, separate from the regular `*.test.ts` runtime suite. Run type-checking of production source files as a separate `tsc --noEmit` CI step so source type errors and test type assertion failures are reported as distinct steps with distinct error messages.

## Cycle 51 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 195 — `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` with Array Guard Helpers

TypeScript's `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` flag adds `| undefined` to every array index and record lookup, forcing explicit null checks before use. While this eliminates entire classes of `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` at compile time, it creates friction in assertion-heavy test code where you know an array element must exist. The idiomatic fix is a typed `at()` helper that narrows to a non-optional type, keeping test readability while maintaining type safety.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json — enable the compile-time guard
// "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true

// test/helpers/array.ts
/**
 * Assert that an array element exists at the given index.
 * Throws a descriptive error at test time instead of silently returning undefined.
 */
export function mustGet<T>(arr: readonly T[], index: number, label?: string): T {
  const item = arr[index];
  if (item === undefined) {
    throw new Error(
      `mustGet: no element at index ${index}${label ? ` (${label})` : ''}` +
      ` — array has ${arr.length} element(s)`
    );
  }
  return item;
}

// src/cart/cart.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { mustGet } from '../helpers/array';
import { buildCart } from './cart';

describe('buildCart', () => {
  it('places the most expensive item first', () => {
    const cart = buildCart([
      { sku: 'A', price: 5 },
      { sku: 'B', price: 20 },
      { sku: 'C', price: 12 },
    ]);
    // Without mustGet: cart.items[0]?.sku === 'B' (no compile error, silently undefined if empty)
    // With mustGet: throws with context if items is empty — fails fast with a readable message
    expect(mustGet(cart.items, 0, 'first item').sku).toBe('B');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `mustGet` adds a thin abstraction layer. Teams must ensure all test helper files are included in the project's `tsconfig.json` `include` path so `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` applies consistently. If helpers live in a `test/` directory excluded from the main tsconfig, create a `tsconfig.test.json` that extends the base with `"noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true` explicitly. [official]

### Pattern 196 — Discriminated Union Exhaustiveness as a Type-Level Test

TypeScript's `never` type combined with the `never` assignability rule creates a compile-time exhaustiveness check: if a switch or if-else chain misses a union member, the default branch receives a non-`never` type and the assignment `const _: never = value` becomes a type error. This pattern turns every discriminated union into a shift-left regression gate — adding a new variant to the union immediately breaks the build until all handlers are updated.

```typescript
// src/events/domain-event.ts
export type DomainEvent =
  | { type: 'OrderPlaced';   orderId: string;  total: number }
  | { type: 'OrderShipped';  orderId: string;  carrier: string }
  | { type: 'OrderCancelled'; orderId: string; reason: string };

// src/events/event-handler.ts
function assertNever(value: never, label: string): never {
  throw new Error(`Unhandled ${label} variant: ${JSON.stringify(value)}`);
}

export function handleEvent(event: DomainEvent): string {
  switch (event.type) {
    case 'OrderPlaced':
      return `Order ${event.orderId} placed for $${event.total}`;
    case 'OrderShipped':
      return `Order ${event.orderId} shipped via ${event.carrier}`;
    case 'OrderCancelled':
      return `Order ${event.orderId} cancelled: ${event.reason}`;
    default:
      // If a new DomainEvent variant is added without updating this switch,
      // the compiler reports: "Argument of type '{ type: "NewVariant" }' is
      // not assignable to parameter of type 'never'."
      return assertNever(event, 'DomainEvent');
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Exhaustiveness checks in application code are a shift-left win. However, they only protect code paths that actually use the discriminated union in a switch/if. Library code that uses `if (event.type === 'OrderPlaced')` and falls through silently bypasses the check. Require `@typescript-eslint/switch-exhaustiveness-check` as an ESLint rule for all union-dispatching switch statements — this catches the missing case without requiring the `assertNever` runtime call. [official]

### Pattern 197 — Pact Consumer-Driven Contract Tests in CI

Consumer-driven contract testing (CDCT) with Pact moves API compatibility verification from integration environments to the local development loop. The consumer writes tests that describe the interactions it expects from a provider; Pact generates a JSON contract file. The provider then verifies the contract file independently. Both steps run in CI before deployment, eliminating a whole class of "works in isolation, breaks in staging" integration failures.

```typescript
// tests/contracts/order-consumer.pact.test.ts
import { PactV3, MatchersV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import { OrderApiClient } from '../../src/clients/order-api';
import path from 'path';

const { like, string, integer } = MatchersV3;

const provider = new PactV3({
  consumer: 'checkout-service',
  provider: 'order-service',
  dir: path.resolve(process.cwd(), 'pacts'),
});

describe('OrderApiClient — Pact consumer contract', () => {
  it('fetches an order by ID', async () => {
    await provider.addInteraction({
      states: [{ description: 'order 42 exists' }],
      uponReceiving: 'a GET request for order 42',
      withRequest: { method: 'GET', path: '/orders/42' },
      willRespondWith: {
        status: 200,
        body: {
          id: integer(42),
          status: string('shipped'),
          total: like(199.99),
        },
      },
    });
    await provider.executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
      const client = new OrderApiClient(mockServer.url);
      const order = await client.getOrder(42);
      expect(order.id).toBe(42);
      expect(order.status).toBe('shipped');
    });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Pact excels at synchronous HTTP contracts but has limited support for async messaging (Kafka, SQS) — Pact's `MessageConsumerPact` covers this but requires the provider to implement a message publisher test helper, adding setup cost. Evaluate Pact only when services are genuinely decoupled: if the consumer and provider are always co-deployed in a monorepo, contract tests duplicate integration test coverage at higher maintenance cost. [official]

---

### Pattern 198 — TypeScript Template Literal Types for Route Parameter Safety

Template literal types enforce URL route parameter shapes at compile time. By encoding the route pattern as a TypeScript type, you get compile-time feedback when callers pass malformed route segments — before any request is made at runtime. This pattern is particularly effective for typed route builders shared between frontend and backend code in a TypeScript monorepo.

```typescript
// packages/shared/src/routes.ts

// Encode route segment constraints as template literal types
type UserId   = `usr_${string}`;
type OrderId  = `ord_${string}`;
type ApiPath  = `/api/v2/users/${UserId}/orders/${OrderId}`;

/**
 * Type-safe route builder: the compiler rejects calls that pass
 * raw strings instead of prefixed IDs.
 */
export function buildOrderPath(userId: UserId, orderId: OrderId): ApiPath {
  return `/api/v2/users/${userId}/orders/${orderId}`;
}

// apps/checkout/src/api.ts
import { buildOrderPath } from '@shared/routes';

// Correct — passes typed IDs
const path = buildOrderPath('usr_abc123', 'ord_xyz789');

// Compile error: Argument of type '"abc123"' is not assignable to
// parameter of type '`usr_${string}`'
// const bad = buildOrderPath('abc123', 'ord_xyz789');

// Test — verifies the structural contract
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
describe('buildOrderPath', () => {
  it('constructs a valid API path from typed IDs', () => {
    expect(buildOrderPath('usr_abc', 'ord_xyz')).toBe('/api/v2/users/usr_abc/orders/ord_xyz');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Template literal type constraints are structural, not semantic: `'usr_'` followed by any string satisfies `UserId`. A caller who passes `'usr_'` (empty suffix) compiles successfully but likely violates domain invariants. Pair template literal types with a branded type or a runtime validation function (e.g., Zod's `z.string().startsWith('usr_').min(6)`) for domain-critical IDs. The compile-time check stops typos; the runtime check stops malformed IDs. [official]

---

### Pattern 199 — Vitest `vi.spyOn` with `mockRestore` in `afterEach` for Safe Module Spy Cleanup

`vi.spyOn` replaces a module's exported function with a spy that records calls and can be configured to return custom values. Without explicit restoration, spies persist across test files when `isolate: false` is in effect — or persist within a file across tests when spy setup is placed in a `describe` block without `afterEach`. The pattern of calling `vi.restoreAllMocks()` in `afterEach` (not `afterAll`) ensures each test begins with pristine module behaviour.

```typescript
// src/notifications/email.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, afterEach, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import * as mailer from '../lib/mailer';
import { sendWelcomeEmail } from './email';

describe('sendWelcomeEmail', () => {
  // Spy is set up fresh per test — not at describe scope
  let sendSpy: ReturnType<typeof vi.spyOn>;

  beforeEach(() => {
    // Create spy before each test so each test owns its call history
    sendSpy = vi.spyOn(mailer, 'send').mockResolvedValue({ messageId: 'mock-id' });
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    // Restore the original implementation — critical when isolate: false is used
    vi.restoreAllMocks();
  });

  it('sends to the correct recipient', async () => {
    await sendWelcomeEmail('user@example.com', 'Alice');
    expect(sendSpy).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(sendSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({ to: 'user@example.com', subject: expect.stringContaining('Welcome') })
    );
  });

  it('does not throw when mailer returns an error', async () => {
    sendSpy.mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('SMTP timeout'));
    // sendWelcomeEmail should swallow the error and log it, not rethrow
    await expect(sendWelcomeEmail('user@example.com', 'Alice')).resolves.not.toThrow();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `vi.restoreAllMocks()` restores the original implementation but also clears any `mockReturnValue` configured outside of `beforeEach`. If you have a test that relies on a long-lived mock configured in `beforeAll`, calling `restoreAllMocks` in `afterEach` will clear it. Prefer `vi.clearAllMocks()` (clears call history and queued return values, but does not restore the original implementation) when the spy's entire lifespan is within a single `describe` block. [official]

---

### Pattern 200 — `eslint-plugin-import` `import/no-cycle` to Catch Circular Dependencies Before Runtime

Circular module dependencies in TypeScript cause subtle initialization-order bugs: a module's exported value may be `undefined` at import time if two modules form a cycle that the bundler resolves in an unexpected order. `eslint-plugin-import`'s `import/no-cycle` rule statically detects import cycles and fails the lint step before any test or build runs. This is pure shift-left: a problem that would manifest as a mysterious `undefined` at runtime is surfaced as a lint error the moment the cycle is created.

```typescript
// .eslintrc.cjs — add to existing config
module.exports = {
  plugins: ['import'],
  rules: {
    // Report any import cycle regardless of depth
    'import/no-cycle': ['error', { maxDepth: Infinity, ignoreExternal: true }],
    // Also block importing from a module's index if the module can self-reference
    'import/no-self-import': 'error',
  },
  settings: {
    'import/resolver': {
      typescript: { alwaysTryTypes: true },
    },
  },
};

// Example: this import WOULD create a cycle and is caught at lint time
// src/orders/order.service.ts
import { CartService } from '../cart/cart.service'; // lint error if cart imports from orders

// src/cart/cart.service.ts — the cycle closer
// import { OrderService } from '../orders/order.service'; // ← triggers import/no-cycle
```

**Tradeoff.** `import/no-cycle` with `maxDepth: Infinity` performs a full dependency graph traversal and can be slow in large monorepos (30–120 seconds for 10,000+ modules). Mitigate by running `no-cycle` only on `lint-staged` changed files in pre-commit, and as a full-graph scan in nightly CI only. Alternatively, use `madge --circular --ts-config tsconfig.json src/` as a faster cycle-detection step that does not require ESLint's full plugin infrastructure. [community]

---

### Pattern 201 — TypeScript `satisfies` for Test Fixture Type Narrowing Without Widening

The `satisfies` operator (TypeScript 4.9+) validates that an expression matches a type but preserves the expression's narrowest literal type for downstream use. In test fixtures, this means you get the safety of interface conformance checking at the fixture declaration site while retaining precise literal types in assertion calls — without the type-widening side effect of explicit type annotation.

```typescript
// test/fixtures/users.ts
import type { User } from '../../src/domain/user';

// Using 'as User' or ': User' would widen role to string — losing literal 'admin'
// 'satisfies User' validates the shape AND keeps role as literal type 'admin'
export const adminUser = {
  id:    'usr_001',
  name:  'Alice Admin',
  email: 'alice@example.com',
  role:  'admin',        // type: 'admin' (not string)
  active: true,
} satisfies User;

// src/permissions/permissions.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { adminUser } from '../fixtures/users';
import { canDeleteUsers } from '../../src/permissions';

describe('canDeleteUsers', () => {
  it('returns true for admin role', () => {
    // adminUser.role is typed as literal 'admin' — not widened to string
    // so type-narrowing logic in canDeleteUsers is verified at compile time
    const result = canDeleteUsers(adminUser);
    expect(result).toBe(true);
  });

  it('detects interface drift at fixture declaration (not at assertion)', () => {
    // If User gains a required field 'department', the error appears HERE
    // at the fixture, not in every test that uses adminUser
    const _ = adminUser; // compile error if User interface changed
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `satisfies` only validates at the point of the expression — it does not enforce the type in assignments to other variables or function parameters later. If you pass `adminUser` to a function expecting `User`, TypeScript still checks assignability normally. The primary benefit is fixture declaration: the error appears at the fixture file rather than scattered across the 30 test files that use it. Use `satisfies` consistently for all shared test fixtures; prefer explicit annotation only for fixtures that are intentionally wider than the interface (e.g., partial mocks). [official]

---

### Pattern 202 — Contract-First API Typing with `zod` + `z.infer` as the Single Source of Truth

Defining API request/response schemas with Zod once and deriving TypeScript types from them (`z.infer<typeof schema>`) ensures runtime validation and compile-time types stay in sync. This eliminates the dual-maintenance problem where a TypeScript interface and a runtime validator diverge over time. When the schema changes, the type changes automatically — and any test or implementation that relies on the old shape fails at compile time.

```typescript
// src/api/schemas/order.schema.ts
import { z } from 'zod';

export const OrderStatusSchema = z.enum(['pending', 'shipped', 'delivered', 'cancelled']);
export const OrderSchema = z.object({
  id:        z.string().regex(/^ord_[a-z0-9]{8,}$/),
  status:    OrderStatusSchema,
  total:     z.number().positive(),
  items:     z.array(z.object({ sku: z.string(), qty: z.number().int().positive() })),
  createdAt: z.string().datetime(),
});

// Derive TypeScript type — guaranteed to match the runtime schema
export type Order = z.infer<typeof OrderSchema>;
export type OrderStatus = z.infer<typeof OrderStatusSchema>;

// src/api/order-handler.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { OrderSchema } from '../schemas/order.schema';

describe('OrderSchema', () => {
  it('rejects orders with negative totals', () => {
    const result = OrderSchema.safeParse({ id: 'ord_abc12345', status: 'pending',
      total: -5, items: [], createdAt: new Date().toISOString() });
    expect(result.success).toBe(false);
    expect(result.error?.issues[0].path).toContain('total');
  });

  it('rejects orders with malformed IDs', () => {
    const result = OrderSchema.safeParse({ id: '12345', status: 'shipped',
      total: 99, items: [], createdAt: new Date().toISOString() });
    expect(result.success).toBe(false);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Zod schemas add runtime overhead on every parse call. For hot paths (e.g., parsing every incoming HTTP request body in a high-throughput API), profile the Zod validation cost with your actual schema complexity. For schemas with deeply nested arrays and refinements, consider `@sinclair/typebox` or `ajv` (with JSON Schema generated from TypeScript types) as alternatives that compile to native JSON Schema and validate 10–50× faster than Zod for large payloads. Use Zod in tests and boundary validation; evaluate performance-oriented alternatives for streaming or sub-millisecond-budget paths. [community]

### Pattern 203 — `@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises` with `void` Operator Convention

Unhandled promise rejections are one of the most common sources of silent test failures and production incidents in Node.js TypeScript applications. The `@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises` rule flags any `Promise`-returning call that is neither awaited nor explicitly handled with `.catch()`. Pairing this rule with the `checkThenables: true` and `ignoreVoid: true` options and a team convention of using `void expr` for intentionally fire-and-forget calls makes every unhandled promise an explicit, visible decision.

```typescript
// .eslintrc.cjs
module.exports = {
  rules: {
    '@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises': [
      'error',
      {
        ignoreVoid: true,         // allow `void somePromise()` for intentional fire-and-forget
        checkThenables: true,     // also catch PromiseLike (e.g. Bluebird, rxjs toPromise)
      },
    ],
    // Block .then() chains without a .catch() handler
    '@typescript-eslint/prefer-promise-reject-errors': 'error',
  },
};

// src/jobs/cleanup.ts
async function runCleanup(): Promise<void> {
  await deleteExpiredSessions();
  await compactAuditLog();
}

// BAD — lint error: Promise returned from runCleanup is not handled
// runCleanup();

// GOOD — explicitly fire-and-forget with void operator
void runCleanup();

// GOOD — awaited in an async context
async function scheduleCleanup() {
  await runCleanup();
}

// Test: verify cleanup does not reject
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
it('runCleanup resolves without throwing', async () => {
  vi.mock('../db/sessions', () => ({ deleteExpiredSessions: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(0) }));
  vi.mock('../db/audit', () => ({ compactAuditLog: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined) }));
  await expect(runCleanup()).resolves.toBeUndefined();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `ignoreVoid: true` means that `void expr` silences the rule. This is correct for truly fire-and-forget operations (sending analytics events, non-critical logging). However, it can be misused to silence a floating-promise lint error without genuinely considering whether the rejection should be handled. Establish a team convention: `void` is only for operations whose rejection is explicitly acceptable and logged by a global unhandled-rejection handler. All other promises must be awaited or explicitly caught. [official]

---

### Pattern 204 — Incremental TypeScript Type Checking with `tsc --incremental` and Build Info Caching

`tsc --incremental` serialises the compiler's type information to a `.tsbuildinfo` file after each run, enabling subsequent `tsc` invocations to skip re-processing unchanged files. In pre-commit hooks and CI, this transforms `tsc --noEmit` from a 30–60 second cold scan to a 3–8 second incremental scan on typical projects — removing the primary motivation for developers to skip or bypass the type-check gate.

```json
// tsconfig.json — enable incremental compilation
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "incremental": true,
    "tsBuildInfoFile": ".tsbuildinfo",
    "noEmit": true,
    "strict": true
  }
}
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — cache the .tsbuildinfo across CI runs
jobs:
  type-check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: .tsbuildinfo
          key: tsbuildinfo-${{ hashFiles('tsconfig.json', 'src/**/*.ts') }}
          restore-keys: tsbuildinfo-
      - run: npx tsc --noEmit --incremental
```

```typescript
// package.json scripts — use incremental in dev, full check in release
// "type-check":         "tsc --noEmit --incremental"   // fast; dev + pre-commit
// "type-check:full":    "tsc --noEmit"                  // clean; release CI
// "type-check:clean":   "rm -f .tsbuildinfo && tsc --noEmit --incremental"
```

**Tradeoff.** `.tsbuildinfo` grows over time and can become stale if `tsconfig.json` changes significantly (e.g., enabling a new strict flag). A stale build info file can cause `tsc --incremental` to report no errors when errors actually exist. Always run `type-check:full` (without `--incremental`) in the release/merge CI job and use `--incremental` only in pre-commit and PR draft jobs. Add `.tsbuildinfo` to `.gitignore` to prevent developer-local build info files from polluting CI cache state. [official]

---

### Pattern 205 — Vitest `vi.stubEnv` for Environment-Variable-Dependent Unit Tests

Tests that read `process.env` variables directly are environment-sensitive: they pass on a developer machine with a `.env` file but fail in CI where the variable is absent. `vi.stubEnv` replaces a specific environment variable for the duration of a test and automatically restores the original value, making environment-dependent tests hermetic without manual save-and-restore patterns.

```typescript
// src/config/feature-flags.ts
export function isPaymentsV2Enabled(): boolean {
  return process.env.PAYMENTS_V2_ENABLED === 'true';
}

// src/config/feature-flags.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { isPaymentsV2Enabled } from './feature-flags';

describe('isPaymentsV2Enabled', () => {
  it('returns true when PAYMENTS_V2_ENABLED is "true"', () => {
    // vi.stubEnv replaces only the specified variable, leaves all others intact
    vi.stubEnv('PAYMENTS_V2_ENABLED', 'true');
    expect(isPaymentsV2Enabled()).toBe(true);
    // Automatic restore happens via vi.unstubAllEnvs() in afterEach (configured globally)
  });

  it('returns false when PAYMENTS_V2_ENABLED is absent', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('PAYMENTS_V2_ENABLED', '');
    expect(isPaymentsV2Enabled()).toBe(false);
  });

  it('returns false when PAYMENTS_V2_ENABLED is "1" (not strict "true")', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('PAYMENTS_V2_ENABLED', '1');
    expect(isPaymentsV2Enabled()).toBe(false);
  });
});
```

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — enable global restore so vi.stubEnv auto-cleans after each test
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    unstubEnvs: true, // Automatically calls vi.unstubAllEnvs() after each test
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `vi.stubEnv` mutates `process.env` for the duration of the test. In `test.concurrent` blocks, concurrent tests that stub the same variable will interfere with each other because `process.env` is shared mutable state within a worker. Never use `vi.stubEnv` inside `test.concurrent` — use a dependency-injection pattern instead (pass the env value as a function argument or inject a config object) so each concurrent test operates on independent state. [official]

### Pattern 206 — TypeScript Mapped Types for Exhaustive Mock Factories

A common test anti-pattern is a `createMockUser` factory that returns a plain object literal: when the `User` interface gains a new required field, existing mock factories silently produce incomplete mocks that satisfy no interface check because the object literal is typed as the return type manually. Using a mapped type that requires all interface keys to be explicitly provided forces the mock factory to be updated whenever the interface changes — the compile error appears at the factory, not scattered across test files.

```typescript
// test/factories/user.factory.ts
import type { User } from '../../src/domain/user';

// This type requires every key of User to be present in the builder argument.
// If User gains a new required field, this type causes a compile error HERE.
type RequiredMock<T> = { [K in keyof Required<T>]: T[K] };

export function createMockUser(overrides: Partial<User> = {}): User {
  const base: RequiredMock<User> = {
    id:        'usr_test001',
    name:      'Test User',
    email:     'test@example.com',
    role:      'viewer',
    active:    true,
    createdAt: '2024-01-01T00:00:00.000Z',
    // If User gains 'department: string', the compiler errors HERE immediately
  };
  return { ...base, ...overrides };
}

// src/permissions/admin.test.ts
import { createMockUser } from '../factories/user.factory';
import { isAdmin } from '../../src/permissions';

describe('isAdmin', () => {
  it('returns false for a viewer', () => {
    expect(isAdmin(createMockUser({ role: 'viewer' }))).toBe(false);
  });
  it('returns true for an admin', () => {
    expect(isAdmin(createMockUser({ role: 'admin' }))).toBe(true);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `RequiredMock<T>` uses `Required<T>` which makes optional interface fields required in the base object. This is intentional for mock factories — you want every field to have an explicit default so factory outputs are fully deterministic. However, for interfaces with many optional fields (e.g., a rich domain object with 20 optional display properties), maintaining a `RequiredMock` base becomes burdensome. In those cases, use `Partial<T>` for the base and add an explicit `as T` cast with a comment documenting which fields are intentionally omitted. [official]

---

### Pattern 207 — Pre-commit Hook with `lint-staged` and Parallel Type Checking via `tsc --noEmit`

Running `tsc --noEmit` on the entire project in a pre-commit hook is the correct type-checking strategy, but only on changed files it misses cross-file type errors that the full project graph would catch. The pragmatic balance is: run `lint-staged` for ESLint + formatting on staged files only (fast, < 5 seconds), and run `tsc --noEmit --incremental` on the full project (using the `.tsbuildinfo` cache) in parallel. This gives sub-10-second feedback with full type coverage.

```json
// package.json — lint-staged configuration
{
  "lint-staged": {
    "*.{ts,tsx}": [
      "eslint --fix --max-warnings=0",
      "prettier --write"
    ],
    "*.{js,json,md}": "prettier --write"
  }
}
```

```bash
# .husky/pre-commit — run lint-staged and tsc in parallel
#!/usr/bin/env sh
. "$(dirname -- "$0")/_/husky.sh"

# Run both in parallel; exit 1 if either fails
npx lint-staged &
LINT_PID=$!

npx tsc --noEmit --incremental &
TSC_PID=$!

wait $LINT_PID
LINT_STATUS=$?

wait $TSC_PID
TSC_STATUS=$?

[ $LINT_STATUS -ne 0 ] && echo "lint-staged failed" && exit 1
[ $TSC_STATUS -ne 0 ]  && echo "tsc --noEmit failed" && exit 1
exit 0
```

**Tradeoff.** Parallelizing lint-staged and tsc in a bash pre-commit hook can exceed the available CPU on underpowered CI runners (2-core machines), causing both jobs to compete and take longer than running them sequentially. Profile with `time git commit --allow-empty -m "test"` on the target machine. On developer laptops (8+ cores), parallel execution typically saves 4–8 seconds. On 2-core CI runners, sequential execution with incremental tsc is often faster overall. [community]

---

### Pattern 208 — Vitest `expect.assertions(n)` as a Guard for Async Exception Tests

When testing that an async function throws, forgetting to `await` the assertion or placing `expect` inside a `.catch()` that never runs causes the test to pass vacuously — no assertion was ever evaluated, but the test reports success. `expect.assertions(n)` declares the exact number of assertions that must run; if the test exits with fewer, Vitest fails it explicitly. This pattern is mandatory for async exception paths.

```typescript
// src/payments/charge.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { chargeCard } from './charge';
import { vi } from 'vitest';

vi.mock('../lib/stripe', () => ({
  stripe: {
    charges: {
      create: vi.fn(),
    },
  },
}));

import { stripe } from '../lib/stripe';

describe('chargeCard — error paths', () => {
  it('throws PaymentDeclinedError when Stripe returns card_declined', async () => {
    // Declare exactly 2 assertions must run — guards against vacuous pass
    expect.assertions(2);

    vi.mocked(stripe.charges.create).mockRejectedValueOnce(
      Object.assign(new Error('Your card was declined.'), { code: 'card_declined' })
    );

    try {
      await chargeCard({ amount: 5000, currency: 'usd', source: 'tok_visa_debit_declined' });
      // If chargeCard does NOT throw, expect.assertions(2) will fail the test —
      // protecting against the case where the mock is misconfigured
    } catch (err) {
      expect(err).toBeInstanceOf(Error);
      expect((err as { code?: string }).code).toBe('card_declined');
    }
  });

  it('throws for zero amount (guard: rejectsWith pattern)', async () => {
    // Alternative pattern: rejects.toThrow is cleaner for simple cases
    await expect(
      chargeCard({ amount: 0, currency: 'usd', source: 'tok_visa' })
    ).rejects.toThrow('Amount must be positive');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `expect.assertions(n)` requires you to count assertions manually — if you add a new `expect` call to the test body, you must update the count or the test fails. The `rejects.toThrow()` pattern (second test above) avoids this counting overhead and is preferred for the common case of verifying a single rejection. Reserve `expect.assertions(n)` for tests where the assertion count itself is the safety property — i.e., where a vacuous pass would be a genuine false negative risk. [official]

---

### Pattern 209 — TypeScript `noImplicitReturns` + `strictNullChecks` for Complete Path Coverage at Compile Time

`noImplicitReturns` combined with `strictNullChecks` forces every function code path to explicitly return a value of the declared return type. Together they eliminate a class of logic defects where a function silently returns `undefined` from a branch that should return a typed value — an error that typically manifests as a subtle null-dereference downstream rather than at the function call site. This is compile-time branch coverage for the return-value contract.

```typescript
// tsconfig.json — ensure both flags are active
// "strict": true covers strictNullChecks; add noImplicitReturns explicitly
// "noImplicitReturns": true
// "noFallthroughCasesInSwitch": true  ← companion flag

// src/pricing/discount.ts
type CustomerTier = 'standard' | 'silver' | 'gold' | 'platinum';

// WITHOUT noImplicitReturns: missing the 'standard' branch compiles silently,
// discountRate(order) returns undefined, downstream multiplication produces NaN
function discountRate(tier: CustomerTier): number {
  if (tier === 'gold')     return 0.15;
  if (tier === 'silver')   return 0.10;
  if (tier === 'platinum') return 0.25;
  // 'standard' falls through — tsc with noImplicitReturns reports:
  // "Not all code paths return a value."
  return 0; // Fix: explicit return for the default case
}

// Combined with noUncheckedIndexedAccess, noFallthroughCasesInSwitch:
function applyTierDiscounts(tiers: CustomerTier[]): number[] {
  return tiers.map((tier) => {
    switch (tier) {
      case 'standard':  return 0;
      case 'silver':    return 0.10;
      case 'gold':      return 0.15;
      case 'platinum':  return 0.25;
      // noFallthroughCasesInSwitch: compiler errors if any case is missing a return
    }
  });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `noImplicitReturns` can produce friction in functions that intentionally have void branches — e.g., event handlers that `return` early for guard conditions. The fix is to declare the return type as `void` or `undefined` explicitly. Adding `noImplicitReturns` to a large existing codebase may surface dozens of latent defects simultaneously. Enable it first in `tsconfig.strict-new.json` scoped to new code only, then expand incrementally using `include` path patterns to enforce it on stabilised modules. [official]
