## Cycle 64 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 375** — `useUnknownInCatchVariables` types caught errors as `unknown` instead of `any`
```typescript
// ❌ Without useUnknownInCatchVariables: catch variable is implicitly `any`
// tsconfig: { "useUnknownInCatchVariables": false }
try {
  await fetchUserData(userId);
} catch (err) {
  // err is `any` — all of these compile without error
  console.log(err.response.data.message);  // silent runtime crash risk
  throw err.notARealProperty;             // silent runtime crash risk
}

// ✅ With useUnknownInCatchVariables: true (default under strict:true)
try {
  await fetchUserData(userId);
} catch (err: unknown) {
  if (err instanceof Error) {
    console.log(err.message);              // safe — narrowed to Error
  } else if (typeof err === "string") {
    console.log(err);                      // safe — narrowed to string
  } else {
    console.log("Unknown error", err);    // safe — no property access
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: `useUnknownInCatchVariables` forces explicit narrowing at every catch site, which is correct behaviour for error handling where the throw type is genuinely unknown — but it adds boilerplate to every catch block in codebases that throw only `Error` instances, and teams frequently bypass it by casting `err as Error` at the top of the catch body, which restores the `any`-equivalent unsafety the rule was introduced to prevent without triggering any further diagnostic.

---

**Pattern 376** — `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature` forces bracket notation on dynamically-keyed objects
```typescript
interface Config {
  [key: string]: string;
  name: string;          // known property — dot access allowed
}

// ❌ Without noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature:
// Both compile — but dotAccess gives false IDE autocomplete confidence
const cfg: Config = { name: "app", version: "1.0" };
const version = cfg.version;   // compiles — but version may not exist

// ✅ With noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature: true
// Dot access only allowed on declared properties:
const name = cfg.name;           // OK — declared in interface
const version2 = cfg["version"]; // OK — bracket notation signals dynamic lookup

// Attempts to dot-access undeclared keys are compiler errors:
// const bad = cfg.version;  // Error: Property 'version' comes from index signature
//                           // Use bracket notation: cfg["version"]
```
Tradeoff: `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature` makes the distinction between statically-known and dynamically-keyed access visible at every call site, surfacing structural intent at the cost of verbosity — but it generates friction in codebases that mix declared and index-signature properties on the same interface (a common pattern in configuration objects and environment variable wrappers), because developers must track which properties are declared and which are index-accessed, and the compiler provides no codemods or automated refactoring support for migrating existing dot accesses to bracket notation at scale.

---

**Pattern 377** — `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-argument` prevents `any`-typed values from entering typed function parameters
```typescript
// Suppose a third-party response is typed as `any`:
async function getApiResponse(): Promise<any> {
  const res = await fetch("/api/data");
  return res.json();  // returns any
}

// ❌ Without no-unsafe-argument: any flows silently into typed params
function processUser(user: { id: number; name: string }): string {
  return `User: ${user.name} (${user.id})`;
}

const raw = await getApiResponse();
processUser(raw);   // compiles — raw is any, so it satisfies any parameter type
// at runtime: user.name may be undefined, user.id may be a string, etc.

// ✅ With no-unsafe-argument enforced: narrows at the boundary
import { z } from "zod";
const UserSchema = z.object({ id: z.number(), name: z.string() });
type User = z.infer<typeof UserSchema>;

const raw2 = await getApiResponse();
const user: User = UserSchema.parse(raw2);  // throws at boundary if invalid
processUser(user);  // safe — user is now statically typed as User
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-argument` is one of the most effective rules for preventing `any` propagation at function-call boundaries — it surfaces every site where untyped data from external sources (API responses, `JSON.parse`, dynamic imports) enters typed domain logic — but it produces the highest volume of errors in projects that interact with untyped or loosely-typed third-party libraries, because every library function that returns `any` creates a downstream cascade of `no-unsafe-argument` violations, forcing teams to either add validation schemas for every external type or suppress the rule at integration layers.

---

**Pattern 378** — `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-return` prevents `any`-typed values from leaking out of typed functions
```typescript
// ❌ Without no-unsafe-return: any can silently satisfy any return type
function parseConfig(raw: unknown): AppConfig {
  const parsed = JSON.parse(raw as string);  // parsed is `any`
  return parsed;  // compiles — any is assignable to AppConfig
  // but the returned value is structurally unvalidated at runtime
}

// ✅ With no-unsafe-return enforced: must validate before returning
import { z } from "zod";

const AppConfigSchema = z.object({
  apiUrl: z.string().url(),
  timeout: z.number().positive(),
  features: z.record(z.boolean()),
});
type AppConfig = z.infer<typeof AppConfigSchema>;

function parseConfig(raw: unknown): AppConfig {
  const parsed = JSON.parse(raw as string);
  return AppConfigSchema.parse(parsed);  // throws ZodError if invalid
  // return type is now statically verified — no any leak
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-return` closes the `any`-return loophole that allows unvalidated data to silently satisfy typed return signatures, which is particularly valuable in data transformation pipelines where the return type is the contract consumed by downstream services — but it generates a high false-positive rate in generic utility functions where the return type is intentionally derived from a type parameter (`function identity<T>(x: T): T { return x; }`), because TypeScript's inference sometimes widens type parameters to `any` in complex generic chains, causing the rule to fire on code that is structurally correct.

---

**Pattern 379** — `@typescript-eslint/restrict-template-expressions` prevents non-string values in template literals
```typescript
// ❌ Without restrict-template-expressions: any value coerces silently
function buildLogMessage(level: "info" | "error", payload: unknown): string {
  return `[${level}] ${payload}`;  // payload coerces via .toString()
  // if payload is { toJSON: ... }, result is "[object Object]"
  // if payload is undefined, result is "[info] undefined"
}

// ✅ With restrict-template-expressions: { allowNumber: true, allowBoolean: true }
function buildLogMessage(
  level: "info" | "error",
  payload: string | number | boolean
): string {
  return `[${level}] ${payload}`;  // all types produce meaningful strings
}

// For structured payloads, serialise explicitly:
function buildStructuredLog(level: "info" | "error", payload: unknown): string {
  const serialised = JSON.stringify(payload) ?? "null";
  return `[${level}] ${serialised}`;  // explicit serialisation — no coercion surprise
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/restrict-template-expressions` prevents the silent `[object Object]` and `undefined` coercion bugs that arise when untyped or structured values are interpolated in template literals — a frequent source of garbled log messages and malformed URLs — but it is overly strict in generic utility functions that intentionally template-format any serializable value, and configuring `allowAny: true` to exempt those cases re-opens the loophole the rule was introduced to close, requiring teams to carefully scope rule exceptions to prevent universal suppression.

---

**Pattern 380** — `@typescript-eslint/require-await` removes async keywords from functions with no `await` expressions
```typescript
// ❌ async without await: unnecessary wrapping, misleading signature
class UserRepository {
  async findById(id: string): Promise<User | null> {
    const cached = this.cache.get(id);   // synchronous cache lookup
    if (cached) return cached;
    return null;  // no await — the async wrapper adds Promise overhead
    // callers still need to await this, but the function is not truly async
  }

  // ✅ Synchronous function with explicit null return:
  findByIdSync(id: string): User | null {
    return this.cache.get(id) ?? null;
  }

  // ✅ When the interface contract requires Promise, mark the intent explicitly:
  async findByIdWithFallback(id: string): Promise<User | null> {
    const cached = this.cache.get(id);
    if (cached) return cached;
    return await this.db.query<User>(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1`, [id]);
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/require-await` prevents the misleading `async` annotation on functions that perform no asynchronous operations — functions that are async-in-name-only wrap their return value in an unnecessary `Promise` resolution cycle and signal to callers that they involve I/O or concurrency when they do not — but the rule fires on abstract base-class methods and interface-conformant stubs that declare `async` to satisfy a `Promise`-returning interface contract without yet implementing the async body, which is a valid pattern during incremental implementation that the rule conflates with accidental async annotations.

---

**Pattern 381** — `@typescript-eslint/no-unnecessary-type-parameters` eliminates phantom generics that add type complexity without constraint
```typescript
// ❌ Phantom generic: T appears only in return position, adding no constraint
// callers can write wrapValue<string>(42) — no compile-time safety
function wrapValue<T>(value: unknown): T {
  return value as T;  // T is unconstrained, essentially a cast with extra steps
}

// ✅ Either return an honest type or constrain the generic meaningfully:
function wrapValue(value: unknown): unknown {
  return value;  // honest return type — caller must narrow
}

// Genuine generic: T constrains input AND output — type parameter earns its place
function getFirst<T>(arr: readonly T[]): T | undefined {
  return arr[0];  // T appears in both param and return — constraint is load-bearing
}

// Genuine generic with constraint: T bounds shape, Readonly adds value
function wrapFrozen<T extends Record<string, unknown>>(value: T): Readonly<T> {
  return Object.freeze({ ...value });
}

// Phantom via return-only generic — should be removed:
function castTo<T>(value: unknown): T {
  return value as T;  // T only in return — no type safety, just a named cast
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-unnecessary-type-parameters` eliminates generics that provide the syntactic appearance of type safety without any actual type constraint — a pattern that is common in wrapper functions, factory utilities, and adapter layers where developers reach for generics by convention rather than by necessity — but it fires on legitimate single-use generics in higher-order functions where the type parameter correlates input and output types even if it appears in only one structural position from the rule's static analysis perspective, requiring teams to add inline eslint-disable comments on valid generic utilities to suppress false positives.

---

**Pattern 382** — `strictFunctionTypes` catches unsafe callback substitution in higher-order function patterns
```typescript
// ❌ Without strictFunctionTypes: contravariant parameter assignment accepted
type EventHandler<T> = (event: T) => void;

interface MouseEvent { x: number; y: number; button: "left" | "right" }
interface PointerEvent extends MouseEvent { pressure: number }

function registerHandler(handler: EventHandler<MouseEvent>): void {
  // framework calls handler with MouseEvent instances
  handler({ x: 10, y: 20, button: "left" });
}

// Without strictFunctionTypes, this compiles — but crashes at runtime:
const pointerHandler: EventHandler<PointerEvent> = (e) => {
  console.log(e.pressure * 2);  // accesses .pressure — undefined on plain MouseEvent
};
registerHandler(pointerHandler);  // unsound: pointer handler called with mouse event

// ✅ With strictFunctionTypes: true — the assignment is a compile error
// TypeScript correctly rejects PointerEvent handler where MouseEvent handler is required
// because PointerEvent is more specific — a MouseEvent caller cannot guarantee .pressure
// Fix: handler must accept the broader type at the parameter position:
const mouseHandler: EventHandler<MouseEvent> = (e) => {
  console.log(e.x, e.y);  // accesses only MouseEvent properties — safe
};
registerHandler(mouseHandler);  // correct: handler accepts what the caller provides
```
Tradeoff: `strictFunctionTypes` enforces the correct contravariant subtyping rule for function parameters — a fundamental type-system soundness property — and prevents the class of runtime crashes that arise when a narrower-typed callback is substituted where a wider-typed one is expected — but it interacts poorly with method declarations on interfaces and classes (which TypeScript still checks bivariantly for historical compatibility with pre-`strict` class hierarchies), creating an inconsistency where `interface.method(param: T)` is bivariant but `interface.method: (param: T) => void` is contravariant, producing confusing results when teams mix method-declaration and property-declaration styles on the same interface.

---

**Pattern 383** — Conditional types with `infer` extract nested type shapes without runtime overhead
```typescript
// Extract the element type of an array or readonly array:
type ElementOf<T> = T extends ReadonlyArray<infer E> ? E : never;

// Extract parameter types from a function signature:
type FirstParam<T extends (...args: any[]) => any> =
  T extends (first: infer P, ...rest: any[]) => any ? P : never;

// Extract the return type deeply — unwrap nested Promises:
type DeepAwaited<T> = T extends Promise<infer U> ? DeepAwaited<U> : T;

// Practical use: extract DTO type from a service method signature for test fixtures
// This keeps fixture types automatically in sync with the service contract:
type CreateUserDto = FirstParam<typeof UserService.prototype.createUser>;

// Test fixture builder typed directly from the service signature:
function buildCreateUserDto(
  overrides: Partial<CreateUserDto> = {}
): CreateUserDto {
  return {
    email: "test@example.com",
    name: "Test User",
    role: "viewer",
    ...overrides,
  };
}
// If UserService.createUser's parameter type changes, CreateUserDto updates
// automatically — the fixture type error surfaces at compile time, not in test output.
```
Tradeoff: Conditional types with `infer` enable type-level deconstruction that keeps downstream types automatically in sync with their source signatures — a powerful shift-left technique that eliminates the drift between service contracts and test fixture types — but deeply recursive conditional types with `infer` cause quadratic or exponential type-checking overhead in large generic pipelines, and the TypeScript compiler enforces a recursion depth limit that produces an opaque "Type instantiation is excessively deep" error when the inferred type chain exceeds approximately 100 recursive expansions, truncating the type result silently.

---

**Pattern 384** — Mapped types with key remapping enforce property naming conventions at the type level
```typescript
// Enforce that all event handler props follow the `on<Event>` naming convention:
type EventMap = {
  click: MouseEvent;
  focus: FocusEvent;
  blur: FocusEvent;
  keydown: KeyboardEvent;
};

// Mapped type with key remapping via `as` and Capitalize intrinsic:
type EventHandlerProps = {
  [K in keyof EventMap as `on${Capitalize<string & K>}`]?: (
    event: EventMap[K]
  ) => void;
};
// Produces: { onClick?: (e: MouseEvent) => void; onFocus?: (e: FocusEvent) => void; ... }

// Component accepts only correctly-named handlers — enforced at compile time:
function registerEventHandlers(handlers: EventHandlerProps): void {
  for (const [key, handler] of Object.entries(handlers)) {
    const eventName = key.slice(2).toLowerCase();  // onClick → click
    if (handler) document.addEventListener(eventName, handler as EventListener);
  }
}

// ❌ Compile error — wrong naming convention:
// registerEventHandlers({ clickHandler: () => {} });  // not on<Event> shape
// ✅ Compile success:
registerEventHandlers({ onClick: (e) => console.log(e.clientX) });
```
Tradeoff: Mapped types with key remapping (`as` clauses) move naming-convention enforcement from documentation and code-review comments into the type system, making violations into compile errors rather than review feedback — but they obscure the resulting property names from IDE autocomplete in some editors because the `Capitalize` / `Lowercase` intrinsic string manipulation types are opaque to the language server until fully resolved, and they make the mapped type itself harder to read for developers unfamiliar with template literal type semantics, raising the barrier to contribution in codebases with mixed TypeScript experience levels.

---

**Pattern 385** — `satisfies` operator validates object literals against a type without widening the inferred type
```typescript
// ❌ Type annotation widens inferred types, losing literal precision:
const routeConfig: Record<string, { method: string; path: string }> = {
  getUser: { method: "GET", path: "/users/:id" },
  createUser: { method: "POST", path: "/users" },
};
// routeConfig.getUser.method is inferred as `string` — not "GET"
// autocomplete and exhaustiveness checks lose the literal type information

// ✅ `satisfies` validates the shape without widening:
const routeConfig2 = {
  getUser: { method: "GET", path: "/users/:id" },
  createUser: { method: "POST", path: "/users" },
} satisfies Record<string, { method: string; path: string }>;
// routeConfig2.getUser.method is still inferred as "GET" (literal type preserved)
// but the shape is validated against the Record constraint at compile time

type Method = typeof routeConfig2.getUser.method;  // "GET" — not widened to string
// Enables exhaustive switch on method values downstream without type assertions
```
Tradeoff: The `satisfies` operator (introduced in TypeScript 4.9) fills the gap between type annotation (which widens inferred types, losing literal precision) and no annotation (which preserves precision but provides no structural validation) — it is particularly valuable for configuration objects, route tables, and enum-like constant maps where both validation and literal-type preservation are needed — but `satisfies` only validates at the declaration site, not at mutation sites on mutable objects, so a team that uses `satisfies` on an object literal but then spreads or assigns into the object downstream loses the structural guarantee without any compiler warning.

---

**Pattern 386** — `@typescript-eslint/no-redundant-type-constituents` removes `any` and `never` pollution from union/intersection types
```typescript
// ❌ Redundant constituents: any absorbs all other members in a union
type SafeId = string | any;   // collapses to `any` — string provides no constraint
type NeverPath = string & never;  // collapses to `never` — string is unreachable

// These arise from generic code that produces any/never under certain instantiations:
type ApiResult<T> = T extends void ? never : T | ApiError;
// If T is inferred as any in a loose context, the union absorbs both branches

// ✅ Cleaned up — explicit types without redundant constituents:
type SafeId2 = string;    // explicit — no any contamination
type ApiResult2<T> = T extends void ? ApiError : T | ApiError;

// Utility to detect any pollution in your own types at compile time:
type IsAny<T> = 0 extends (1 & T) ? true : false;
type CheckSafeId = IsAny<SafeId>;   // true  — SafeId is any-contaminated
type CheckSafeId2 = IsAny<SafeId2>; // false — SafeId2 is clean

// Use IsAny<T> in conditional type guards to prevent any propagation:
type StrictReturn<T> = IsAny<T> extends true ? never : T;
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-redundant-type-constituents` surfaces the silent type-collapse that occurs when `any` or `never` appears as a union or intersection constituent — which is almost always a latent bug from a misconfigured generic or an overly-permissive import — but it fires on intentional uses of `any` as a "type escape" union constituent in legacy code that is being incrementally typed, where `string | any` is a deliberate in-progress marker indicating "this will be narrowed later," and suppressing the rule on these sites requires inline comments that interrupt the migration tracking workflow.

---

**Pattern 387** — `@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-imports` separates type imports from value imports for tree-shaking correctness
```typescript
// ❌ Mixed value and type imports — bundler may not eliminate type-only imports
import { User, createUser, UserRole } from "./user";
// If User and UserRole are pure types, bundlers that lack type-import analysis
// may include the ./user module in the bundle even if only types were needed

// ✅ Separate type imports with consistent-type-imports rule:
import type { User, UserRole } from "./user";
import { createUser } from "./user";
// `import type` is erased entirely by TypeScript — zero runtime bundle contribution
// bundler can safely tree-shake the type-only import path

// In test files, consistent-type-imports also prevents accidental mock leakage:
import type { UserService } from "./user-service";  // type-only — no module execution
import { mockUserService } from "./__mocks__/user-service";  // value import for mock

// Prevents: import UserService accidentally executing the real service module
// before the mock is installed, causing constructor side effects in test setup
function setupTest(service: UserService): void {
  // UserService type used only for parameter annotation — no runtime reference
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-imports` ensures that type-only imports are explicitly marked with `import type`, which allows TypeScript to elide them completely during compilation and enables bundlers to perform accurate tree-shaking on type-boundary modules — but the rule requires all pre-existing imports to be audited and split when enabled on an established codebase, and in projects that use barrel exports (`index.ts` files that re-export both types and values), the split between `import type` and `import` from the same barrel file can be confusing because the barrel itself always executes regardless of whether only its type exports are consumed.

---

**Pattern 388** — `@typescript-eslint/no-import-type-side-effects` prevents type imports from triggering module side effects
```typescript
// ❌ Regular import for type-only usage causes module side effects:
import { MyEventEmitter } from "./event-emitter";
// Even if MyEventEmitter is used only as a type annotation,
// this import executes event-emitter.ts at module load time,
// which may register global listeners, polyfills, or singletons

type EventEmitterAlias = MyEventEmitter;  // used only as a type — but module ran

// ✅ import type prevents side-effect execution:
import type { MyEventEmitter } from "./event-emitter";
type EventEmitterAlias = MyEventEmitter;
// event-emitter.ts is NOT executed — no side effects triggered

// ✅ The inline type modifier alone does NOT prevent module execution:
// import { type MyEventEmitter, createEmitter } from "./event-emitter";
// The createEmitter value import causes the whole module to execute regardless.
// no-import-type-side-effects warns about this pattern.

// Correct pattern when mixing type and value imports from the same module:
import type { MyEventEmitter } from "./event-emitter";  // type only — no execution
import { createEmitter } from "./event-emitter";         // value — module executes once
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-import-type-side-effects` prevents the subtle footgun where inline `type` modifiers on individual named imports (`import { type Foo, bar }`) give the false impression that the module side effects are suppressed when they are not — the module still executes because the value import `bar` requires it — but this distinction matters only in codebases where module-level side effects are meaningful (singleton initialization, global polyfills, framework bootstrap), and in most application code where modules are pure functions and classes, the rule adds annotation overhead without a corresponding runtime safety benefit.

---

**Pattern 389** — `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-enum-comparison` prevents direct comparison of enum members with non-enum values
```typescript
// ❌ Comparing enum to raw string — breaks if enum value is refactored
enum OrderStatus {
  Pending = "PENDING",
  Fulfilled = "FULFILLED",
  Cancelled = "CANCELLED",
}

function handleStatus(status: OrderStatus): void {
  if (status === "PENDING") {           // raw string: silent drift if value changes
    fulfillOrder();
  }
}

// ✅ Compare only enum member to enum member:
function handleStatus2(status: OrderStatus): void {
  if (status === OrderStatus.Pending) { // enum member reference — rename-safe
    fulfillOrder();
  }
}

// ❌ Numeric enum comparison with magic number is even more dangerous:
enum Priority { Low = 1, Medium = 2, High = 3 }
function escalate(p: Priority): void {
  if (p === 2) { triggerAlert(); }  // magic number: breaks on enum reordering
}

// ✅ Use enum member reference:
function escalate2(p: Priority): void {
  if (p === Priority.Medium) { triggerAlert(); }
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-enum-comparison` enforces that enum members are only compared against other members of the same enum — preventing the drift between raw literal values and enum member values that occurs when enum values are refactored — but it requires all comparison sites to be updated to use the enum member reference rather than the underlying string or number, and it produces friction in serialization and deserialization code at API boundaries where the incoming value is a `string` or `number` that must be validated and cast to the enum before it can be compared, adding a mandatory validation step that some teams treat as unnecessary ceremony for internal state machines.

---

### Community Gotchas

**G64-1** — `satisfies` does not narrow mutable properties after the declaration site
Teams adopting the `satisfies` operator to validate configuration objects while preserving literal type inference discover that the structural validation `satisfies` provides applies only at the declaration site — the inferred type of the object after `satisfies` is the literal inference, not the constraint type, which means that if a property is subsequently reassigned, TypeScript validates the assignment against the inferred literal type (too narrow) rather than the constraint type (as intended). A `routeConfig satisfies Record<string, RouteDefinition>` where `routeConfig.getUser.method` is inferred as `"GET"` will reject `routeConfig.getUser.method = "POST"` because `"POST"` is not assignable to `"GET"` — even though `"POST"` satisfies the constraint `string` — producing a counterintuitive error that makes the configuration object harder to update programmatically.
Why this matters: The `satisfies` operator was designed for immutable configuration objects and constant maps, but teams use it on objects that are later mutated in test setup, configuration merging, and dynamic routing registration. The interplay between `satisfies`-preserved literal inference and subsequent assignment produces errors that are difficult to diagnose because the type shown in IDE hover is the constraint type (`string`), not the inferred literal type (`"GET"`) that is actually blocking the assignment, creating a gap between the type displayed and the type enforced.
Fix: Use `as const satisfies Record<string, RouteDefinition>` for genuinely immutable configuration objects — this makes the immutability explicit and aligns the developer's intent with the compiler's enforcement. For mutable configuration objects that use `satisfies` for structural validation, add an explicit type annotation instead (`const config: Record<string, RouteDefinition> = { ... }`) which widens the inferred types to the constraint, enabling subsequent mutation at the cost of literal-type precision.

---

**G64-2** — `@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-imports` conflicts with auto-import IDE tooling that generates value imports for types
Teams enabling `consistent-type-imports` find that their IDE's auto-import feature (VS Code, WebStorm, and similar) generates regular value imports (`import { User } from "./user"`) rather than type-only imports (`import type { User } from "./user"`) when the developer selects a type from the completion menu. The linting rule then flags every auto-imported type as a violation, creating a friction loop where the developer must manually convert each auto-imported type import to a type import, negating the productivity benefit of auto-import. The issue is compounded in editors that partially support `import type` auto-import — they generate `import type` for some symbols but not others depending on whether the editor correctly determines at auto-import time that the symbol is type-only.
Why this matters: The consistent-type-imports rule is valuable for bundle size and tree-shaking correctness, but its value is contingent on developer adoption at the point of import creation. When the primary import-creation mechanism (IDE auto-import) consistently generates the wrong import form, developers develop a habit of ignoring the ESLint warning rather than correcting the import, which means the rule achieves visibility into the problem but no actual compliance. The fix requires tooling changes at the editor level, not just the linting level, and different developers on the same team may have different editor configurations.
Fix: Enable TypeScript's own `verbatimModuleSyntax` compiler option (introduced in TypeScript 5.0) — this makes the TypeScript compiler itself enforce `import type` for type-only imports during compilation, not just during linting, and modern IDE versions (VS Code 1.79+, WebStorm 2023.2+) respect `verbatimModuleSyntax` when generating auto-imports, resolving the IDE-linting gap at the tool level. Add `"verbatimModuleSyntax": true` to `tsconfig.json` and retire the `consistent-type-imports` ESLint rule to avoid redundant enforcement from two separate tools.

---

**G64-3** — `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` widens array element types to `T | undefined` and breaks bounded-loop index access patterns
Teams enabling `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` find that the common array access pattern — `for (let i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) { const item = arr[i]; }` — now types `item` as `T | undefined`, requiring a non-null assertion or a narrowing check before using `item`, despite the loop bounds making it structurally impossible for `arr[i]` to be `undefined`. The `for...of` pattern is unaffected because it does not use index access syntax, but `for...of` is not always available (some legacy targets or imperative algorithms require index-based iteration), and the `for...of` equivalence is not obvious to developers who reach for `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` to catch out-of-bounds access bugs — they encounter the flag widening provably in-bounds accesses and generating noise that obscures the genuine out-of-bounds bugs the flag was intended to surface.
Why this matters: TypeScript has no flow analysis for loop bounds — it does not track that `i < arr.length` constrains `i` to the valid index range — so `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` applies the `| undefined` widening unconditionally to all index access expressions, regardless of surrounding guards. This means the flag produces the largest volume of spurious errors precisely in the code patterns (bounded index loops) that are least likely to contain out-of-bounds bugs, while the genuine risk patterns (unbounded dynamic index access on sparse arrays and record types) are comparatively rare and harder to find in the noise.
Fix: Migrate index-based loops to `for...of` wherever possible — this is the idiomatic TypeScript iteration pattern and eliminates the `| undefined` widening entirely. For algorithms that genuinely require index access, use a helper that performs the bounds check once and returns a non-nullable type: `function at<T>(arr: T[], i: number): T { const v = arr[i]; if (v === undefined) throw new RangeError(\`Index ${i} out of bounds\`); return v; }` — this localizes the `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` narrowing to one place and keeps call sites clean.

---

**G64-4** — `verbatimModuleSyntax` breaks re-export barrel patterns that mix type and value exports in a single statement
Teams enabling TypeScript 5.0's `verbatimModuleSyntax` (which supersedes `isolatedModules`) find that barrel files (`index.ts`) that re-export both types and values from the same module must now split their re-exports into type-only and value re-export forms. The pattern `export { User, createUser } from "./user"` — where `User` is a type and `createUser` is a value — is now a compiler error: TypeScript requires either `export type { User }` (type-only) or `export { createUser }` (value), but not a mixed-form re-export in a single statement. This breaks every barrel file in a codebase that follows the common pattern of grouping all re-exports from a module into one export statement.
Why this matters: The barrel file pattern is ubiquitous in TypeScript monorepos and component libraries — a single `index.ts` per package re-exports the package's public API surface in one place. `verbatimModuleSyntax` requires every re-export statement in every barrel file to be audited and split, which is a large mechanical migration in established codebases. Automated codemods do not reliably handle all cases, and the split introduces visual noise in barrel files (two export statements per module instead of one) that some teams find degrades the readability of the package's public API surface.
Fix: Use the `export type { User }` form for all type-only re-exports and `export { createUser }` for value re-exports, accepting the split as a clarity benefit — the explicit `type` keyword on re-exports is now a signal to readers that a symbol is erased at runtime, which improves comprehension at the cost of verbosity. Automate the migration with a script that diffs `.d.ts` output against the source barrel to identify which exports are type-only. For large barrel files, co-locate type and value re-exports in adjacent lines grouped by source module to maintain visual association.

---

**G64-5** — `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-enum-comparison` fires on exhaustive switch statements that compare union members containing enums against string literals
Teams enabling `no-unsafe-enum-comparison` discover that it fires inside `switch` statements on union-typed discriminants when the union contains an enum member and the case labels are string or number literals. The pattern `switch (status) { case "PENDING": ... }` where `status: OrderStatus | "UNKNOWN"` is flagged because the comparison of the `OrderStatus` enum member values against string literals in the case arms is classified as an unsafe enum comparison — even though the string literal `"PENDING"` exactly matches the enum member value `OrderStatus.Pending = "PENDING"`. The rule cannot distinguish between a comparison against a literal that happens to equal an enum member and a comparison against the enum member reference itself.
Why this matters: String-valued enums in TypeScript exist precisely to enable readable comparisons with their underlying string values at API boundaries where the serialized form (a JSON string) must be matched against the enum. The `no-unsafe-enum-comparison` rule's goal is to prevent drift between enum values and the literals compared against them — a valid concern — but the fix it proposes (comparing `status === OrderStatus.Pending` rather than `status === "PENDING"`) is not always possible in a `switch` statement without restructuring to an if-else chain, and `switch (status)` with `case OrderStatus.Pending:` is only valid when `status` is typed as `OrderStatus`, not as `OrderStatus | "UNKNOWN"`.
Fix: Restructure union types that mix enum members with raw string or number literals to use a discriminated union instead — `type Status = { kind: "enum"; value: OrderStatus } | { kind: "unknown"; raw: string }` — this separates the enum domain from the raw-string domain and eliminates the comparison ambiguity entirely. At API boundaries where the incoming value is a raw string that may or may not match an enum member, perform a validation step first (`isOrderStatus(raw): raw is OrderStatus`) and operate on the validated enum type downstream, keeping `no-unsafe-enum-comparison` satisfied and the type narrowing explicit.

## Cycle 67 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 405** — Enforce `noUncheckedSideEffectImports` to block bare import side-effect modules without explicit opt-in
```typescript
// tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "noUncheckedSideEffectImports": true  // TypeScript 5.6+
  }
}

// ❌ Side-effect import with no type resolution — silently absent before 5.6:
import "./polyfills/promise";   // no exported symbol — TypeScript 5.5 never checked if this resolved

// ✅ After enabling noUncheckedSideEffectImports, TypeScript errors if the module does not exist:
// Error: Cannot find module './polyfills/promise' or its corresponding type declarations.

// ✅ Opt-in pattern for known dynamic polyfill directories:
//    Use a type declaration stub so TypeScript resolves the side-effect module:
// polyfills/promise.d.ts
export {};  // empty export makes it a module; TypeScript resolves the bare import

// ✅ Production guard: combine with a lint rule to require a comment on all side-effect imports:
// eslint-disable-next-line import/no-unassigned-import -- intentional polyfill
import "./polyfills/promise";
```
Tradeoff: `noUncheckedSideEffectImports` catches deleted or misspelled polyfill modules that previously silently produced no-op imports at build time — a class of bug that caused production environments to ship without intended polyfills — but it requires every legitimate side-effect import to be accompanied by a stub `.d.ts` or a declaration in `types` fields, adding a maintenance burden for large polyfill inventories in multi-target builds where polyfill paths are environment-conditional.

---

**Pattern 406** — Use `@typescript-eslint/no-deprecated` to surface deprecated API call sites at lint time before they become runtime failures
```typescript
// utils/legacy.ts
/** @deprecated Use `fetchUserV2` instead — scheduled for removal in v4.0 */
export function fetchUser(id: string): Promise<User> {
  return legacyApiClient.get(`/users/${id}`);
}

export function fetchUserV2(id: string, options?: FetchOptions): Promise<User> {
  return apiClient.get(`/users/${id}`, options);
}

// consumer.ts — ❌ flagged by @typescript-eslint/no-deprecated:
import { fetchUser } from "./utils/legacy";
const user = await fetchUser("u-123"); // ESLint error: 'fetchUser' is deprecated

// ✅ Correct usage after migration:
import { fetchUserV2 } from "./utils/legacy";
const user = await fetchUserV2("u-123", { retries: 3 });

// .eslintrc — enable with error severity to block deprecated API usage at pre-commit:
// "@typescript-eslint/no-deprecated": "error"
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-deprecated` requires type-checked linting (`parserOptions.project`) which adds 30–90 seconds to lint runs in large monorepos — making it impractical as a fast pre-commit check without scoping it to changed files only — and it fires on every call site of deprecated symbols, creating a large burst of errors when a heavily-used utility is first deprecated, requiring a coordinated migration window rather than incremental adoption.

---

**Pattern 407** — Use `isolatedDeclarations` to enforce that exported functions and variables are explicitly annotated so declaration files can be generated without full type resolution
```typescript
// tsconfig.json — TypeScript 5.5+
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "isolatedDeclarations": true
  }
}

// ❌ Exported function whose return type cannot be inferred in isolation:
export function parseConfig(raw: unknown) {  // Error: return type must be explicit with isolatedDeclarations
  return raw as AppConfig;
}

// ✅ Explicit return type satisfies isolatedDeclarations:
export function parseConfig(raw: unknown): AppConfig {
  return raw as AppConfig;
}

// ❌ Exported const with inferred complex type:
export const defaultConfig = { retries: 3, timeout: 5000 };
// Error: exported variable must have explicit type annotation

// ✅ Annotated const:
export const defaultConfig: AppConfig = { retries: 3, timeout: 5000 };
```
Tradeoff: `isolatedDeclarations` enables parallel declaration file generation (used by tools like `dts-bundle-generator` and Rollup's DTS plugin) which cuts type-check time in monorepos by 40–70% — but it mandates explicit return-type annotations on every exported function, which adds annotation overhead on small utilities where the inferred type is obvious, and it interacts poorly with higher-order functions whose return types are complex generics that are more readable when inferred than when written out.

---

**Pattern 408** — Use `@typescript-eslint/prefer-find` to replace `.filter(...)[0]` with `.find(...)` for single-element retrieval
```typescript
// ❌ Filter-then-index pattern — always allocates a full intermediate array:
function getAdminUser(users: User[]): User | undefined {
  return users.filter(u => u.role === "admin")[0];
}

// ❌ Slightly better but still allocates:
function getAdminUser2(users: User[]): User | undefined {
  const admins = users.filter(u => u.role === "admin");
  return admins.length > 0 ? admins[0] : undefined;
}

// ✅ prefer-find enforces this equivalent, allocation-free form:
function getAdminUser3(users: User[]): User | undefined {
  return users.find(u => u.role === "admin");
}

// ✅ Also applies to readonly arrays — prefer-find handles ReadonlyArray<T>:
function getAdminFromReadonly(users: ReadonlyArray<User>): User | undefined {
  return users.find(u => u.role === "admin");  // no intermediate array
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/prefer-find` eliminates a common micro-allocation pattern (`.filter()[0]`) that adds O(n) allocation overhead in hot paths such as per-request middleware chains and render loops — but the autofix replaces `[0]` with `.find()` without accounting for cases where the caller later inspects the length of the filtered array, turning a single-pass operation into a pattern that requires a separate `.filter()` call if the count is also needed, so teams must audit autofixed sites for that dual-use pattern.

---

**Pattern 409** — Use `@typescript-eslint/no-unnecessary-boolean-literal-compare` to eliminate redundant `=== true` and `=== false` comparisons on boolean-typed variables
```typescript
// ❌ Redundant boolean literal comparisons — flagged by the rule:
function shouldShowBanner(config: AppConfig): boolean {
  if (config.showBanner === true) {   // redundant: config.showBanner is already boolean
    return true;
  }
  if (config.isLoggedIn === false) {  // redundant: use !config.isLoggedIn
    return false;
  }
  return config.showBanner;
}

// ✅ Direct boolean usage — equivalent, shorter, no comparison noise:
function shouldShowBanner2(config: AppConfig): boolean {
  if (config.showBanner) {
    return true;
  }
  if (!config.isLoggedIn) {
    return false;
  }
  return config.showBanner;
}

// ✅ The rule also catches strict-equality comparisons against boolean literals in ternaries:
const label = config.isAdmin === true ? "Admin" : "User";   // ❌
const label2 = config.isAdmin ? "Admin" : "User";           // ✅
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-unnecessary-boolean-literal-compare` removes semantic noise in boolean expressions and its autofix is safe on strict-boolean-typed fields — but enabling it across a codebase that previously used `=== true` as an explicit readability convention (common in teams transitioning from JavaScript where truthy checks on non-boolean types were bug-prone) creates a style regression for those developers, and it must not be applied to optional boolean fields (`flag?: boolean`) where `flag === true` and `!!flag` have genuinely different semantics.

---

**Pattern 410** — Use `@typescript-eslint/prefer-nullish-coalescing` to replace `||` fallback patterns that incorrectly short-circuit on `0`, `""`, and `false`
```typescript
// ❌ Logical OR fallback silently replaces falsy non-null values:
function getPageSize(config: { pageSize?: number }): number {
  return config.pageSize || 10;  // Bug: returns 10 when pageSize is 0 (valid value)
}

// ❌ String fallback with OR:
function getTitle(override?: string): string {
  return override || "Untitled";  // Bug: returns "Untitled" when override is "" (intentional empty)
}

// ✅ Nullish coalescing operator — only falls back on null/undefined:
function getPageSize2(config: { pageSize?: number }): number {
  return config.pageSize ?? 10;  // 0 is preserved; only null/undefined falls through
}

// ✅ String fallback — empty string preserved:
function getTitle2(override?: string): string {
  return override ?? "Untitled";  // "" is preserved; only null/undefined falls through
}

// Rule configuration — strictNullChecks must be enabled for the rule to be effective:
// "@typescript-eslint/prefer-nullish-coalescing": ["error", { "ignorePrimitives": { "boolean": false } }]
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/prefer-nullish-coalescing` prevents a widespread class of falsy-fallback bugs where `0`, `""`, and `false` are silently replaced — catching real production bugs in numeric configuration and form field defaults — but the autofix from `||` to `??` is a semantic change that can introduce new bugs when the original `||` behavior was intentional (e.g., collapsing both `null` and `""` to a default), requiring manual review at each autofix site to confirm intent.

**Pattern 411** — Use `@typescript-eslint/no-mixed-enums` to prevent enums from mixing numeric-auto and string-initialized members
```typescript
// ❌ Mixed enum — numeric auto-increment and string members in one declaration:
enum EventType {
  Click = "CLICK",    // string member
  Hover,              // Error: numeric auto-increment follows string member — value is 1, not "HOVER"
  Focus = "FOCUS",    // string member
  Blur,               // numeric: 2
}

// This produces:
// EventType.Click === "CLICK"  (string)
// EventType.Hover === 1        (number — unintended)
// EventType.Focus === "FOCUS"  (string)
// EventType.Blur  === 2        (number — unintended)

// ✅ Pure string enum — all members explicitly initialized:
enum EventType2 {
  Click = "CLICK",
  Hover = "HOVER",
  Focus = "FOCUS",
  Blur = "BLUR",
}

// ✅ Pure numeric enum — all auto-incremented from 0:
enum HttpStatus {
  Ok = 200,
  Created = 201,
  BadRequest = 400,
  Unauthorized = 401,
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-mixed-enums` prevents the silent numeric fallback that occurs when a string-initialized enum member is followed by an un-initialized member — a bug that is invisible in TypeScript's type system because the mixed enum is structurally valid — but the rule forces every member of a string enum to have an explicit string initializer, which is verbose for large enums (20+ members) where auto-naming conventions would make the values predictable, leading some teams to use `const` object maps with `as const` instead of string enums to avoid the verbosity.

**Pattern 412** — Use `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-unary-minus` to prevent applying the unary minus operator to non-number types
```typescript
// ❌ Unary minus on potentially non-numeric types — flagged by the rule:
function negate(value: unknown): number {
  return -value;  // Error: value is unknown; unary minus may produce NaN silently
}

// ❌ Unary minus on any-typed variable from external data:
function invertOffset(offset: any): number {
  return -offset;  // No TypeScript error without the rule, but -"px" === NaN
}

// ✅ Validate the type before applying unary minus:
function negate2(value: unknown): number {
  if (typeof value !== "number") {
    throw new TypeError(`Expected number, got ${typeof value}`);
  }
  return -value;  // TypeScript now knows value is number
}

// ✅ Typed parameter — rule satisfied, no runtime risk:
function invertOffset2(offset: number): number {
  return -offset;
}

// ESLint config:
// "@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-unary-minus": "error"
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-unary-minus` catches a class of silent `NaN` propagation bugs that occur when negating values from loosely-typed API responses or configuration objects — NaN is notoriously difficult to trace once it enters a numeric pipeline — but it requires type-checked linting and fires frequently on legacy codebases with `any`-typed interop layers where negation was safe by convention, generating noise that trains developers to suppress the rule rather than fix the underlying `any` escape hatch.

**Pattern 413** — Use `@typescript-eslint/prefer-string-starts-ends-with` to replace `.indexOf()` and `.slice()` boundary checks with `startsWith`/`endsWith`
```typescript
// ❌ Boundary check using indexOf — intent not obvious, easy to get the index wrong:
function hasProtocol(url: string): boolean {
  return url.indexOf("https://") === 0;  // magic 0 — checks start
}

// ❌ Slice-based suffix check — fragile, off-by-one prone:
function isJsonFile(filename: string): boolean {
  return filename.slice(-5) === ".json";  // magic -5 — couples to extension length
}

// ❌ charAt boundary check:
function startsWithSlash(path: string): boolean {
  return path.charAt(0) === "/";
}

// ✅ prefer-string-starts-ends-with enforces the readable equivalents:
function hasProtocol2(url: string): boolean {
  return url.startsWith("https://");
}

function isJsonFile2(filename: string): boolean {
  return filename.endsWith(".json");
}

function startsWithSlash2(path: string): boolean {
  return path.startsWith("/");
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/prefer-string-starts-ends-with` eliminates magic-number boundary checks that are brittle when the prefix or suffix length changes — `endsWith(".json")` does not break when `.json` is renamed to `.jsonc`, whereas `slice(-5)` silently fails — but the autofix is not always applicable when the original `indexOf` check is part of a larger expression that inspects the index value for purposes beyond a boolean boundary test, requiring manual rewriting for multi-purpose index checks.

**Pattern 414** — Use `@typescript-eslint/no-useless-empty-export` to remove empty `export {}` statements from files that already have top-level exports
```typescript
// ❌ Redundant empty export in a file that already has named exports:
// utils/date.ts
export function formatDate(date: Date): string {
  return date.toISOString().slice(0, 10);
}

export function parseDate(str: string): Date {
  return new Date(str);
}

export {};  // ❌ no-useless-empty-export: this file is already a module

// The empty export was added by a developer who misunderstood the isolation requirement
// or who copy-pasted a d.ts pattern into a .ts implementation file.

// ✅ Remove the empty export — the named exports already make this file a module:
// utils/date.ts
export function formatDate(date: Date): string {
  return date.toISOString().slice(0, 10);
}

export function parseDate(str: string): Date {
  return new Date(str);
}
// No export {} needed
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-useless-empty-export` removes a form of comment-like noise (`export {}`) that some developers use as an explicit signal that a file is intentionally a module rather than a script — removing it eliminates that documentation value — but `export {}` in a file that already has named exports provides zero semantic effect and accumulates silently in codebases where developers copy-paste `export {}` from `.d.ts` patterns into implementation files, polluting the module surface with a no-op statement.

**Pattern 415** — Use `@typescript-eslint/no-array-delete` to prevent `delete arr[i]` which creates sparse arrays with `undefined` holes that bypass array length
```typescript
// ❌ delete on array index — creates a hole, does NOT reduce length:
const items: string[] = ["a", "b", "c", "d"];
delete items[1];
// items is now ["a", empty, "c", "d"] — items.length is still 4
// items[1] === undefined but 1 in items === false (sparse!)
// JSON.stringify(items) === '["a",null,"c","d"]'

// ❌ Iterating a sparse array produces undefined for the hole:
for (const item of items) {
  console.log(item.toUpperCase());  // TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined at index 1
}

// ✅ Use splice to remove an element and compact the array:
const items2: string[] = ["a", "b", "c", "d"];
items2.splice(1, 1);  // items2 is now ["a", "c", "d"] — length is 3

// ✅ Filter for declarative removal:
const items3 = ["a", "b", "c", "d"].filter((_, i) => i !== 1);
// items3 is ["a", "c", "d"]
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-array-delete` prevents sparse-array creation bugs that manifest as `undefined` iteration values rather than the expected type — a class of bug that TypeScript's type system cannot detect because `delete arr[i]` is structurally valid and `arr[i]` continues to type-check as `string` rather than `string | undefined` — but the rule fires on intentional sparse-array construction patterns used in typed buffer management and indexed data structures where holes are semantically meaningful, requiring `// eslint-disable-next-line` annotations at those deliberate use sites.

**Pattern 416** — Use `@typescript-eslint/no-useless-constructor` to remove constructors that only call `super()` with forwarded arguments and add no initialization logic
```typescript
// ❌ Useless constructor that only delegates to super:
class AdminUser extends User {
  constructor(id: string, name: string, role: string) {
    super(id, name, role);  // no additional initialization — this constructor adds nothing
  }
}

// ❌ Useless empty constructor on a base class:
class EventEmitter {
  private listeners: Map<string, Function[]> = new Map();

  constructor() {
    // empty — TypeScript initializes the field automatically
  }
}

// ✅ Remove the useless constructor — TypeScript handles field initialization and super() delegation:
class AdminUser2 extends User {
  // No constructor needed — User's constructor is inherited automatically
}

// ✅ Only add a constructor when there is actual initialization logic:
class AdminUser3 extends User {
  private readonly permissions: Set<string>;
  constructor(id: string, name: string, role: string, permissions: string[]) {
    super(id, name, role);
    this.permissions = new Set(permissions);  // actual initialization — constructor is justified
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-useless-constructor` reduces ceremony in class hierarchies and removes constructors that mislead readers into believing initialization logic is present — but it fires on constructors that contain only access-modifier parameter declarations (`constructor(private name: string)`) which are not useless despite delegating all logic to TypeScript field initialization, and teams must verify that the rule's autofix correctly handles abstract class constructors where an explicit `constructor` declaration is sometimes used as a documentation anchor for the class's initialization contract.

**Pattern 417** — Use `@typescript-eslint/parameter-properties` to enforce consistent use (or prohibition) of TypeScript constructor parameter properties
```typescript
// ❌ Inconsistent mix: some fields use parameter properties, others use explicit assignment:
class UserService {
  private readonly logger: Logger;  // explicit field declaration

  constructor(
    private readonly db: Database,      // parameter property
    private readonly cache: Cache,      // parameter property
    logger: Logger,                     // NOT a parameter property — assigned below
  ) {
    this.logger = logger;  // manual assignment
  }
}

// ✅ Consistent: all constructor-injected dependencies use parameter properties:
class UserService2 {
  constructor(
    private readonly db: Database,
    private readonly cache: Cache,
    private readonly logger: Logger,  // consistent — all are parameter properties
  ) {}
}

// ✅ Alternative: ban parameter properties entirely (some teams prefer explicit fields for testability):
// "@typescript-eslint/parameter-properties": ["error", { "prefer": "class-property" }]
class UserService3 {
  private readonly db: Database;
  private readonly cache: Cache;
  private readonly logger: Logger;
  constructor(db: Database, cache: Cache, logger: Logger) {
    this.db = db; this.cache = cache; this.logger = logger;
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/parameter-properties` with `prefer: "parameter-property"` reduces constructor boilerplate by 60–80% in dependency-injection-heavy classes — but parameter properties make the class's public surface harder to read in IDE hover because the fields do not appear in the class body listing, and they interact poorly with some decorator-based DI frameworks (NestJS, Angular) that inspect class field metadata at runtime and expect fields to be declared in the class body rather than in the constructor signature.

**Pattern 418** — Use `@typescript-eslint/no-confusing-void-expression` to prevent `void` expressions from appearing in positions where a non-void value is expected
```typescript
// ❌ void expression in return position of a non-void function:
function processItem(item: Item): string {
  return console.log(item);  // console.log returns void — this always returns undefined
  // TypeScript would catch this only with strictNullChecks + noImplicitReturns
}

// ❌ Arrow function implicitly returns a void expression — looks like it returns a value:
const items = ["a", "b", "c"];
const results = items.map(item => console.log(item));
// results is void[] — likely a bug: the developer intended a side-effect forEach

// ❌ Ternary with void branch:
const msg = condition ? getValue() : console.log("fallback");
// msg is string | void — probably unintended

// ✅ Use void keyword explicitly to signal intentional void usage in expression position:
const items2 = ["a", "b", "c"];
items2.forEach(item => console.log(item));  // use forEach for side effects

// ✅ Or wrap in a block-body arrow to prevent implicit return:
items2.map(item => { console.log(item); return item; });
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-confusing-void-expression` catches a class of `void`-as-value bugs that are invisible to TypeScript's type system when `void` appears in union positions — `(string | void)` is valid and TypeScript does not warn on the void branch — but the rule fires on intentional patterns like `return void someCallback()` that developers use to explicitly discard a return value and signal to readers that the function returns `undefined`, which is a widely used idiom in event handlers, requiring `allowVoidOperator: true` to permit the explicit-discard pattern.

---

**Pattern 419** — Use `@typescript-eslint/no-for-in-array` to prevent `for...in` iteration over arrays, which iterates string keys rather than element values
```typescript
// ❌ for...in on array — iterates "0", "1", "2" (string keys), not values:
const names: string[] = ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol"];
for (const i in names) {
  console.log(names[i].toUpperCase());  // works by accident: names["0"] === names[0]
}
// But: for...in also iterates any enumerable properties added to Array.prototype,
// and i is always a string — typeof i === "string" — not a number index.

// ❌ for...in on array with prototype pollution:
Array.prototype.customMethod = function() {};
for (const i in names) {
  // i will be "0", "1", "2", and "customMethod" — iterates prototype!
}

// ✅ for...of — iterates values, not keys:
for (const name of names) {
  console.log(name.toUpperCase());
}

// ✅ forEach — equivalent with index available:
names.forEach((name, index) => {
  console.log(`${index}: ${name.toUpperCase()}`);
});

// ✅ for...in is only appropriate for plain objects:
const record: Record<string, number> = { a: 1, b: 2 };
for (const key in record) {
  if (Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(record, key)) {
    console.log(key, record[key]);
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-for-in-array` prevents a category of prototype-pollution vulnerability where `Array.prototype` methods added by third-party libraries are iterated as if they were array elements — a security and correctness issue that is invisible until a polyfill or library adds an enumerable `Array.prototype` property — but the rule fires on code that deliberately uses `for...in` on arrays to iterate numeric string keys for sparse-array processing algorithms, which are a legitimate albeit rare pattern in typed buffer management code.

### Community Gotchas

**G67-1** — `noUncheckedSideEffectImports` produces errors for ambient module declarations in `@types` packages that use `export {}` stubs
Teams enabling `noUncheckedSideEffectImports` in TypeScript 5.6 discover that the compiler now validates side-effect imports against the module resolution graph, but several popular `@types/*` packages provide type coverage for side-effect-only modules using `export {}` stubs in their `.d.ts` files. When the ambient module declaration resolves successfully but the corresponding JavaScript module file does not exist in `node_modules` (because the package ships types without the runtime), TypeScript 5.6 may emit a resolution error depending on the `moduleResolution` strategy in use — `node16` and `bundler` strategies validate both the type and runtime paths, while `node` strategy only validates type paths — producing environment-specific errors that pass in CI with `moduleResolution: "node"` but fail in build tools configured with `moduleResolution: "bundler"`.
Why this matters: The gap between `node` and `bundler` module resolution strategies means that `noUncheckedSideEffectImports` behaves inconsistently across development environments, build tools, and CI configurations in the same monorepo. Developers who have `moduleResolution: "node"` in their editor's `tsconfig.json` (via `tsconfig.editor.json`) but `moduleResolution: "bundler"` in their build `tsconfig.json` will not see the error locally until the build step runs, defeating the shift-left goal of the flag. The issue is particularly acute for CSS module imports and worker entry-point imports that are side-effect-only and handled by bundlers but have no runtime resolution path that TypeScript can verify.
Fix: Standardize on `moduleResolution: "bundler"` in all `tsconfig.json` files in the monorepo — editor, build, and test configurations alike — so `noUncheckedSideEffectImports` produces consistent results everywhere. For `@types/*` packages whose stubs do not resolve under `bundler` resolution, file issues upstream or add local stub `.d.ts` files in a `types/` directory referenced via `typeRoots` to provide the missing resolution path.

---

**G67-2** — `@typescript-eslint/no-deprecated` generates false positives for JSDoc `@deprecated` tags on interface members when the implementing class overrides the method without re-tagging it
Teams enabling `@typescript-eslint/no-deprecated` at error severity encounter false positives at call sites of interface methods that were tagged `@deprecated` on the interface but overridden without the `@deprecated` tag in implementing classes. Because the rule evaluates deprecation from the declared type of the variable (the interface) rather than the runtime value (the class instance), call sites that hold an interface-typed reference emit a deprecation error even when the concrete method in use is the non-deprecated override. The pattern is common in adapter layers and facade interfaces where a base interface method is deprecated in favor of a newer signature, and specific implementations provide the new signature without the deprecation tag.
Why this matters: Interface-level `@deprecated` annotations are the idiomatic TypeScript mechanism for deprecating a contract method across all implementations simultaneously — consumers of the interface should migrate to the new method, while implementations that provide the new signature are not themselves deprecated. The rule's behavior of propagating the interface-level deprecation to all call sites regardless of the implementation in use makes it impossible to use `@deprecated` as a migration signal on interface contracts without either removing the tag (losing the consumer warning) or adding `@deprecated` to the new implementation (creating a misleading deprecation on a current method).
Fix: Use `@deprecated` on the interface method alongside `@see {newMethod}` to guide migration, and suppress the ESLint error at the one-line boundary where the adaptor class holds an interface-typed reference with `// eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/no-deprecated` and a comment explaining the override. Alternatively, narrow the variable's type from the interface to the concrete class at the injection site to avoid the interface-level deprecation propagating to the call site — this trades type abstraction for deprecation clarity and is appropriate when the concrete type is known at the injection point.

---

**G67-3** — `isolatedDeclarations` rejects type parameters with inferred constraints in exported generic utility functions
Teams migrating to `isolatedDeclarations` discover that exported generic utility functions whose type parameters have constraints inferred from other type parameters are rejected unless the constraint is written explicitly. The pattern `export function pick<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, keys: K[]): Pick<T, K>` is accepted because `K extends keyof T` is explicitly stated, but variations that use conditional type expressions as constraints — such as `export function onlyStringKeys<T extends Record<string, unknown>, K extends Extract<keyof T, string>>` — are rejected because the constraint `Extract<keyof T, string>` depends on `T`, which TypeScript cannot resolve in isolation without access to `T`'s full type information during the parallel declaration-file pass.
Why this matters: The `isolatedDeclarations` constraint is designed to enable parallel, incremental declaration-file generation in large monorepos — it speeds up builds dramatically — but its restriction on dependent constraints is not always clear from the error message (`Inferred type of exported function could not be expressed in an isolated declarations context`), and the fix is not obvious: developers must either simplify the constraint (losing precision) or add an explicit type annotation that rewrites the constraint without inter-parameter dependency. In utility type libraries where complex generic constraints are the primary value, `isolatedDeclarations` may require significant redesign of the public API surface.
Fix: Rewrite dependent-constraint generics to use a two-step approach: declare the dependent constraint as a type alias at the top of the file, then reference it in the function signature. For `Extract<keyof T, string>`, define `type StringKeys<T> = Extract<keyof T, string>` and use `K extends StringKeys<T>` in the function signature — this makes the constraint structurally explicit in the declaration file without requiring full type resolution. Accept that some highly-parameterized generic utilities may need to be split into simpler overloaded forms to satisfy `isolatedDeclarations`.

---

**G67-4** — `prefer-nullish-coalescing` autofix incorrectly replaces `||` in assignment expressions where the left operand is a mutable variable that may be reassigned to a falsy non-null value
Teams applying the `@typescript-eslint/prefer-nullish-coalescing` autofix to existing codebases encounter incorrect semantic transformations when `||` is used in assignment expressions where the variable on the left is typed as a non-nullable type but is later reassigned to a falsy value. The pattern `this.count = this.count || 0` where `count` is typed as `number` is autofixed to `this.count = this.count ?? 0` — which changes behavior when `this.count` is subsequently set to `0` and then the assignment runs again: `0 || 0` returns `0` (correct), but `0 ?? 0` also returns `0` (same result in this case). However, in patterns like `options.timeout = options.timeout || DEFAULT_TIMEOUT` where `options.timeout` may be intentionally set to `0` by callers, the autofix from `||` to `??` changes the behavior so that `0` is preserved rather than replaced by `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT` — which is a semantic change that may break existing behavior even though it is the "correct" nullish behavior the rule is enforcing.
Why this matters: The autofix is safe when the intent is to preserve falsy non-null values (the rule's goal), but it is a breaking change when the original `||` behavior was intentional — the developer wanted `0` and `""` to fall through to the default. The rule cannot determine developer intent from the AST alone, so it applies the autofix uniformly, and teams that run the autofix with `--fix` across a large codebase may silently change the semantics of configuration defaults, numeric counters, and string templates that deliberately treat falsy values as missing.
Fix: Run the autofix on a per-file basis with manual review rather than globally, and prioritize fixing `||` on optional properties (`field?: string`) where the falsy-non-null bug is most likely to be a genuine defect. Retain `||` (with an `// eslint-disable-next-line` comment) for assignment patterns where falsy values are intentionally collapsed to a default — add an explanatory comment: `// intentional: 0 and "" treated as absent for this configuration field`. Add an integration test that sets the field to `0` and asserts the default is NOT applied to document the intended behavior.

---

**G67-5** — `@typescript-eslint/no-array-delete` fires in generated code from GraphQL codegen and OpenAPI generators that use `delete` to remove optional fields before serialization
Teams enabling `@typescript-eslint/no-array-delete` encounter unexpected lint failures in auto-generated client code from GraphQL codegen (`graphql-code-generator`) and OpenAPI generators (`openapi-typescript-codegen`, `orval`) that emit `delete obj[key]` patterns to strip `undefined`-valued optional fields before JSON serialization. Although these generators are deleting object properties (not array elements), the generated code sometimes uses computed dynamic property deletion — `delete (requestBody as any)[key]` — which the lint rule flags because `(requestBody as any)` has an index signature and the rule treats index-signature deletion as potential array-element deletion. The false positive is triggered by the `as any` cast that the generator uses to bypass TypeScript's strict optional field constraints.
Why this matters: Autogenerated code is typically excluded from linting via `.eslintignore`, but many teams lint generated client code to catch issues in the generation pipeline itself. When `no-array-delete` fires on generated code, teams either add the generated directory to `.eslintignore` (losing the pipeline validation benefit) or add blanket `eslint-disable` comments to the generated file templates (which requires forking the generator's output templates and maintaining the fork across generator upgrades). Neither resolution is clean, and the root cause — `as any` casts in generated serialization code — is a generator code quality issue that the lint rule surfaces but cannot fix.
Fix: File upstream issues with the code generator to replace `delete (obj as any)[key]` patterns with a typed alternative: `const { [key]: _removed, ...rest } = obj; return rest;` — this eliminates the `as any` cast and the `delete` operator simultaneously, producing a serialization-safe output that satisfies both `no-array-delete` and `no-unsafe-assignment`. As an interim measure, add the generated directory to a targeted `.eslintignore` entry scoped only to the `no-array-delete` rule using `overrides` in the ESLint config rather than a blanket ignore, so other rules continue to apply to generated code.
