## Cycle 65 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 390** — `isolatedDeclarations` enforces explicit return-type annotations on exported functions for parallel declaration emit
```typescript
// tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "isolatedDeclarations": true
  }
}

// ❌ Error: exported function must have explicit return type annotation
// under isolatedDeclarations — tsc cannot infer across files in parallel
export function buildQueryString(params: Record<string, string>) {
  return Object.entries(params)
    .map(([k, v]) => `${encodeURIComponent(k)}=${encodeURIComponent(v)}`)
    .join("&");
}

// ✅ Explicit return type allows .d.ts generation without full type-check pass
export function buildQueryString(params: Record<string, string>): string {
  return Object.entries(params)
    .map(([k, v]) => `${encodeURIComponent(k)}=${encodeURIComponent(v)}`)
    .join("&");
}
```
Tradeoff: `isolatedDeclarations` unlocks parallel `.d.ts` generation in monorepos (eliminating the serial type-check bottleneck that dominates large-monorepo build times), but it mandates explicit return-type annotations on every exported function and class member — a non-trivial annotation burden in codebases that have relied on inference for public APIs, and the migration surfaces every place where inferred return types were intentionally imprecise or where `any` leaks that were previously invisible at declaration sites are now compiler errors.

---

**Pattern 391** — TypeScript 5.5 inferred type predicates eliminate manual `is` annotations on `.filter()` callbacks
```typescript
// TypeScript < 5.5: .filter() callback inferred as (x: T | undefined) => boolean
// — result type is still (T | undefined)[], requiring manual type assertion
const rawItems: (string | undefined)[] = ["alpha", undefined, "beta", undefined];

// ❌ Pre-5.5: filter narrows to boolean but does not narrow the array element type
const oldFiltered = rawItems.filter((x) => x !== undefined);
// type: (string | undefined)[] — the undefined is NOT removed

// ✅ TypeScript 5.5: filter callback infers x is string predicate automatically
const filtered = rawItems.filter((x) => x !== undefined);
// type: string[] — TypeScript now infers the predicate and narrows the array

// Also works on Map lookups — eliminates the common non-null assertion pattern
const countryBirds = new Map<string, string>([["AU", "Emu"], ["NZ", "Kiwi"]]);
const countries = ["AU", "NZ", "US"];
const knownBirds = countries
  .map((c) => countryBirds.get(c))
  .filter((b) => b !== undefined); // type: string[] — no `as string[]` needed
```
Tradeoff: Automatically inferred type predicates in TypeScript 5.5 eliminate the brittle `as T[]` cast or manual `(x): x is T` annotation that was required after every `.filter()` on nullable arrays — reducing noise and the risk of an incorrect manual predicate — but the inference only applies when the filter callback has a single `return` statement, no implicit returns, and does not mutate its parameter, meaning callbacks with early returns or side effects continue to require manual `is` annotations, and developers who are unaware of the "if and only if" predicate semantics may trust inferred predicates that exclude falsy-but-non-undefined values like `0` and `""`.

---

**Pattern 392** — TypeScript 5.5 regex syntax checking catches backreference and grouping errors at compile time
```typescript
// TypeScript 5.5 validates regex literals for syntax errors at compile time

// ❌ Unbalanced parenthesis — caught at compile time, not at test runtime
const badGrouping = /(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})/; // valid
const unbalanced = /(\d+))/; // Error: Unexpected ')'. Did you mean to escape it?

// ❌ Invalid backreference — group 3 does not exist in this pattern
const badBackref = /(\w+)\s(\w+)\s\3/;
// Error: This backreference refers to a group that does not exist.

// ❌ Invalid Unicode property escape
const badUnicode = /\p{InvalidProperty}/u;
// Error: Unknown Unicode property name or value.

// ✅ All groups and backreferences are valid
const isoDate = /^(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})$/;
const repeated = /(\w+)\s\1/; // backreference to group 1 — valid

// ✅ Named capture groups with valid backreference
const namedDate = /(?<year>\d{4})-(?<month>\d{2})-(?<day>\d{2})/;
```
Tradeoff: TypeScript 5.5's compile-time regex syntax checking surfaces malformed patterns (unbalanced groups, invalid backreferences, bad Unicode property escapes) at the IDE error-squiggle level without requiring a test run — shifting a class of parse-time errors left into the editor — but it only validates syntax, not semantics: a regex that is syntactically valid but logically wrong (incorrect character class, greedy vs. lazy mismatch, anchoring error) still passes without error, and developers may develop false confidence that a squiggle-free regex is also a semantically correct one.

---

**Pattern 393** — `const` type parameters preserve tuple and literal types through generic inference without `as const`
```typescript
// TypeScript 5.0: const type parameter modifier on generic functions

// ❌ Without const modifier: string[] inferred — literals are widened
function firstOf<T>(arr: T[]): T {
  return arr[0]!;
}
const v1 = firstOf(["read", "write", "admin"]); // type: string — widened

// ✅ With const modifier: readonly ["read", "write", "admin"] preserved
function firstOf2<const T>(arr: readonly T[]): T {
  return arr[0]!;
}
const v2 = firstOf2(["read", "write", "admin"]); // type: "read" | "write" | "admin"

// Practical use: route definition builder preserves method literals
type Route<T extends { method: string; path: string }> = T;
function defineRoute<const T extends { method: string; path: string }>(r: T): Route<T> {
  return r;
}
const route = defineRoute({ method: "GET", path: "/users/:id" });
// type: { method: "GET"; path: "/users/:id" } — both literals preserved
// Enables exhaustive type checking on method + path combinations at call sites
```
Tradeoff: The `const` type parameter modifier enables literal-type preservation through generic functions without requiring callers to annotate `as const` at every call site — improving ergonomics for route builders, event-name registries, and fluent API chaining — but it prevents the generic function from accepting pre-widened variables (a `string` variable cannot satisfy `const T extends string` when the function expects a literal), which breaks existing call sites that pass computed or mutable strings and requires overloads or conditional widening to support both literal and widened inputs.

---

**Pattern 394** — `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` distinguishes absent properties from `undefined`-valued properties in object types
```typescript
// tsconfig.json: "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true

interface UserPreferences {
  theme?: "light" | "dark";       // optional: may be absent
  language?: string;               // optional: may be absent
  notifications?: boolean;         // optional: may be absent
}

// ❌ With exactOptionalPropertyTypes: assigning undefined to optional property is an error
// because undefined means "explicitly set to undefined", not "property absent"
const prefs: UserPreferences = {
  theme: undefined,   // Error: Type 'undefined' is not assignable to type '"light" | "dark"'
};

// ✅ Omit the property to represent absence
const prefs2: UserPreferences = {
  language: "en",
  // theme is absent — not undefined, just not present
};

// ✅ When you need to explicitly clear a value, use a union type
interface MutablePreferences {
  theme?: "light" | "dark" | undefined;   // explicitly allows undefined assignment
}

// Practical impact: Object.assign patch pattern must use Partial carefully
type Patch<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] };  // no | undefined added — compatible
function patch<T>(target: T, updates: Patch<T>): T {
  return Object.assign({}, target, updates);
}
```
Tradeoff: `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` makes absent properties and `undefined`-valued properties structurally distinct — preventing the subtle bug where `obj.theme = undefined` appears to clear a preference but actually serializes differently from property absence in JSON and REST API payloads — but it breaks every use of `Partial<T>` in update and patch functions because `Partial<T>` adds `| undefined` to all property types, making `Partial<UserPreferences>` incompatible with `UserPreferences` under this flag, requiring a custom `Patch<T>` utility type and a migration of all existing patch/update patterns.

---

**Pattern 395** — `noImplicitOverride` enforces `override` keyword on subclass methods to prevent silent base-class breakage
```typescript
// tsconfig.json: "noImplicitOverride": true

class BaseRepository<T> {
  async findById(id: string): Promise<T | null> {
    return this.db.findOne({ id });
  }

  async save(entity: T): Promise<void> {
    await this.db.save(entity);
  }
}

// ❌ Without override keyword: if base class method is renamed to findByPrimaryKey,
// this silently becomes a NEW method — noImplicitOverride flags the missing override
class UserRepository extends BaseRepository<User> {
  async findById(id: string): Promise<User | null> {  // Error: missing 'override'
    const user = await super.findById(id);
    return user ? this.hydrate(user) : null;
  }
  private hydrate(raw: User): User { return { ...raw, createdAt: new Date(raw.createdAt) }; }
}

// ✅ override keyword makes intent explicit and causes a compile error
// if the base class method is renamed or removed
class UserRepository2 extends BaseRepository<User> {
  override async findById(id: string): Promise<User | null> {
    const user = await super.findById(id);
    return user ? this.hydrate(user) : null;
  }
  private hydrate(raw: User): User { return { ...raw, createdAt: new Date(raw.createdAt) }; }
}
```
Tradeoff: `noImplicitOverride` ensures that subclass methods which shadow base-class methods explicitly declare `override`, causing a compile error when the base class method is renamed or deleted — preventing the class of bugs where a subclass continues to exist with an orphaned override that is now a new method rather than an override — but it generates noisy migration effort in large class hierarchies that accumulated implicit overrides before the flag was enabled, and it does not prevent the complementary problem of overriding a method with an incompatible signature, which `strictFunctionTypes` must address separately.

---

**Pattern 396** — `@typescript-eslint/no-misused-promises` prevents passing async callbacks to synchronous event emitters and array methods
```typescript
// ❌ forEach does not await its callback — unhandled promise, errors are swallowed
const userIds = ["u1", "u2", "u3"];
userIds.forEach(async (id) => {
  const user = await fetchUser(id);  // forEach ignores the returned Promise
  await sendWelcomeEmail(user);       // thrown errors are unhandled
});

// ✅ Use for...of to await each iteration in sequence
for (const id of userIds) {
  const user = await fetchUser(id);
  await sendWelcomeEmail(user);
}

// ✅ Or Promise.all for concurrent execution with proper error propagation
await Promise.all(userIds.map(async (id) => {
  const user = await fetchUser(id);
  await sendWelcomeEmail(user);
}));

// ❌ addEventListener callback is synchronous — async version silently drops the promise
document.addEventListener("click", async (e) => {
  await logClick(e);  // promise is ignored by the event system
});

// ✅ Wrap in a handler that explicitly propagates errors
document.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
  logClick(e).catch(console.error);
});
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-misused-promises` catches the common bug where an `async` callback is passed to `forEach`, `sort`, event emitters, or other APIs that ignore the returned `Promise` — surfacing unhandled promise chains that silently swallow errors in production — but it generates false positives on intentional fire-and-forget patterns (background cache warming, non-critical analytics logging) where the developer has made a deliberate choice to not await, requiring `eslint-disable` comments that reduce the rule's signal-to-noise ratio in codebases that genuinely mix awaited and fire-and-forget async patterns.

---

**Pattern 397** — `@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises` requires every Promise to be awaited, `.catch()`-handled, or explicitly voided
```typescript
// ❌ Promise return value discarded — errors are unhandled
function initializeCache(): Promise<void> {
  return cacheClient.connect();
}

initializeCache(); // no await, no .catch, no void — floating promise, flagged

// ✅ await in an async context
async function startup(): Promise<void> {
  await initializeCache();
}

// ✅ .then/.catch chain for non-async contexts
initializeCache().catch((err) => logger.error("Cache init failed", err));

// ✅ void operator for intentional fire-and-forget (makes intent explicit)
void initializeCache();

// Practical pattern: application startup sequence with sequential error boundaries
async function main(): Promise<void> {
  await initializeCache();
  await connectDatabase();
  await startHttpServer();
}
main().catch((err) => { console.error(err); process.exit(1); });

// Configuration: "checkThenables: true" also catches floating .then() chains
// "@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises": ["error", { "checkThenables": true }]
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises` ensures every `Promise` in the codebase has an error handler or an explicit `void` acknowledgment — preventing the silent failure mode where an uncaught rejection in a floating promise crashes a Node.js process or disappears without logging — but in React and browser event-handler contexts, adding `await` is not always possible (React event handlers are synchronous), requiring either `.catch()` chaining or `void` annotations on every async invocation inside event handlers, which adds syntactic weight to UI event handling code that many teams find disproportionate to the benefit.

---

**Pattern 398** — `@typescript-eslint/prefer-readonly` flags class properties that are never reassigned after construction for immutability enforcement
```typescript
class OrderProcessor {
  // ❌ These properties are assigned in the constructor and never mutated
  // but are not marked readonly — @typescript-eslint/prefer-readonly flags them
  private orderRepository: OrderRepository;
  private emailService: EmailService;
  private logger: Logger;

  constructor(repo: OrderRepository, email: EmailService, log: Logger) {
    this.orderRepository = repo;
    this.emailService = email;
    this.logger = log;
  }

  async process(orderId: string): Promise<void> {
    const order = await this.orderRepository.findById(orderId);
    if (!order) throw new Error(`Order ${orderId} not found`);
    await this.emailService.sendConfirmation(order);
    this.logger.info(`Processed order ${orderId}`);
  }
}

// ✅ Marking as readonly prevents accidental reassignment and
// signals to readers that these are immutable dependencies
class OrderProcessor2 {
  private readonly orderRepository: OrderRepository;
  private readonly emailService: EmailService;
  private readonly logger: Logger;

  constructor(repo: OrderRepository, email: EmailService, log: Logger) {
    this.orderRepository = repo;
    this.emailService = email;
    this.logger = log;
  }

  async process(orderId: string): Promise<void> {
    const order = await this.orderRepository.findById(orderId);
    if (!order) throw new Error(`Order ${orderId} not found`);
    await this.emailService.sendConfirmation(order);
    this.logger.info(`Processed order ${orderId}`);
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/prefer-readonly` catches class properties that could be `readonly` but are not — enforcing structural immutability for injected dependencies, cached lookups, and derived constants — but it only analyzes properties that are never reassigned within the class body, not across the entire call graph, meaning a property passed to a function that mutates it through a reference is still flagged as `readonly`-eligible when it is actually shared mutable state, and marking it `readonly` does not prevent the mutation — it only prevents direct reassignment on `this`, providing weaker safety guarantees than developers may expect from the `readonly` keyword.

---

**Pattern 399** — `@typescript-eslint/explicit-module-boundary-types` requires return-type annotations on all exported functions
```typescript
// ❌ Without explicit-module-boundary-types: return type inferred as any complex union
// — API consumers see whatever TypeScript infers, which may change across refactors
export function parseConfig(raw: unknown) {
  if (typeof raw !== "object" || raw === null) return null;
  return raw as AppConfig;  // inferred return: AppConfig | null — may drift
}

// ✅ With explicit return type: contract is declared and stable across refactors
export function parseConfig(raw: unknown): AppConfig | null {
  if (typeof raw !== "object" || raw === null) return null;
  return raw as AppConfig;
}

// ❌ Async function return type inferred as Promise<{ id: string; name: string }>
// — adding a new field to the return object silently widens the public API
export async function fetchUser(id: string) {
  const row = await db.query("SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE id = $1", [id]);
  return row[0];
}

// ✅ Explicit return type pins the contract — adding fields requires intentional update
export async function fetchUser(id: string): Promise<User | null> {
  const row = await db.query<User>("SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE id = $1", [id]);
  return row[0] ?? null;
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/explicit-module-boundary-types` anchors exported function contracts to explicit type annotations — preventing the class of breaking change where an internal refactor silently widens or narrows an inferred return type that consumers depended on — but it imposes annotation overhead on every exported function including trivial accessors and delegation wrappers, and in codebases that rely on `isolatedDeclarations` (which also requires explicit return types on exports), the rule becomes redundant, applying the same enforcement twice from two different tools with slightly different scope, creating configuration overhead without incremental safety benefit.

---

**Pattern 400** — `@typescript-eslint/switch-exhaustiveness-check` enforces exhaustive `switch` statements on union and enum types
```typescript
type PaymentMethod =
  | { kind: "card"; last4: string; brand: string }
  | { kind: "bank_transfer"; accountNumber: string; routingNumber: string }
  | { kind: "crypto"; walletAddress: string; currency: string };

// ❌ Adding a new union member to PaymentMethod causes a silent runtime gap:
// the switch falls through to the default and the new case is never handled
function formatPaymentSummary(method: PaymentMethod): string {
  switch (method.kind) {
    case "card":          return `Card ending in ${method.last4}`;
    case "bank_transfer": return `Bank transfer from ${method.accountNumber}`;
    // ❌ "crypto" added to union but missing from switch — no compile error without the rule
    default:              return "Unknown payment method";
  }
}

// ✅ @typescript-eslint/switch-exhaustiveness-check flags the missing "crypto" case
// Remove the default to make the switch exhaustive — the rule errors on the gap:
function formatPaymentSummary2(method: PaymentMethod): string {
  switch (method.kind) {
    case "card":          return `Card ending in ${method.last4}`;
    case "bank_transfer": return `Bank transfer from ${method.accountNumber}`;
    case "crypto":        return `Crypto to ${method.walletAddress} (${method.currency})`;
    // No default needed — exhaustiveness check ensures all branches are covered
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/switch-exhaustiveness-check` turns union-member additions into compile errors on every switch that handles the union — preventing the production bug where new variant types are silently handled by a generic `default` branch rather than purposeful logic — but it requires removing or moving `default` branches on exhaustive switches, which conflicts with linting rules that require `default` in `switch` statements (such as `default-case` in ESLint core), creating a rule conflict that teams must resolve by either disabling `default-case` for TypeScript files or using the `allowDefaultCaseForExhaustiveSwitch` option.

---

**Pattern 401** — `@typescript-eslint/no-unnecessary-condition` removes always-true and always-false type guards that indicate stale logic
```typescript
// @typescript-eslint/no-unnecessary-condition flags conditions that TypeScript
// can determine are always true or always false based on static types

// ❌ After a refactor, user.name was made non-optional — the null check is stale
function getUserDisplayName(user: User): string {
  // user.name is typed as string (non-optional) — this check is always truthy
  if (user.name !== null) {   // Warning: This condition is always true
    return user.name;
  }
  return "Anonymous";
}

// ❌ Array literal is always truthy — the length check is the correct guard
function processItems(items: string[]): void {
  if (items) {    // Warning: This condition is always true — arrays are always truthy
    items.forEach(process);
  }
}

// ✅ Remove the stale guard — the type already guarantees non-null
function getUserDisplayName2(user: User): string {
  return user.name;
}

// ✅ Use the correct guard for array emptiness
function processItems2(items: string[]): void {
  if (items.length > 0) {
    items.forEach(process);
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-unnecessary-condition` catches stale type guards left behind after type refinements — conditions that were correct when `user.name` was `string | null` but became tautological after the field was made non-optional — acting as a refactoring hygiene rule that surfaces dead code branches — but it requires type information from the full type checker (making it a slower, type-aware lint rule) and produces false positives in defensive-programming patterns where teams intentionally check conditions that the type system cannot guarantee at runtime (e.g., data from untyped API responses cast with `as`), requiring rule suppression at exactly the call sites where defensive programming is most valuable.

---

**Pattern 402** — `@typescript-eslint/no-base-to-string` prevents `Object.prototype.toString()` coercion from producing `[object Object]` in string contexts
```typescript
interface ApiError {
  code: string;
  message: string;
  details?: Record<string, unknown>;
}

// ❌ Template literal coerces ApiError via toString() — logs "[object Object]"
function logError(err: ApiError): void {
  console.error(`API error occurred: ${err}`);      // "[object Object]" — useless
  const msg = "Error: " + err;                       // same problem with concatenation
}

// ✅ Destructure the fields you want to log
function logError2(err: ApiError): void {
  console.error(`API error: [${err.code}] ${err.message}`);
}

// ✅ Use JSON.stringify for structured logging of the full object
function logError3(err: ApiError): void {
  console.error("API error occurred:", JSON.stringify(err));
}

// ✅ Implement a toString() method if string coercion is intentional and frequent
class AppError extends Error {
  readonly code: string;
  constructor(code: string, message: string) {
    super(message);
    this.code = code;
  }
  override toString(): string { return `[${this.code}] ${this.message}`; }
}

// Now template literal coercion is safe and meaningful:
const err = new AppError("NOT_FOUND", "User not found");
console.error(`Request failed: ${err}`); // "[NOT_FOUND] User not found"
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-base-to-string` prevents the silent data-loss bug where a structured object is string-coerced to `[object Object]` in log messages, error strings, and template literals — a bug that is invisible at the call site but produces undebuggable logs in production — but it fires on every object type that lacks a `toString()` override, including types from third-party libraries where adding a `toString()` is not feasible, requiring broad `eslint-disable` or allowlist configuration for common library types such as `Date`, `Error` subclasses, and ORM entities.

---

**Pattern 403** — `@typescript-eslint/no-confusing-void-expression` prevents `void`-returning expressions from appearing in value positions
```typescript
// ❌ Arrow function that returns a void expression looks like it returns the value
// — the short-arrow form obscures that the return type is void, not string
const logMessage = (s: string): string =>
  console.log(s);  // Error: console.log returns void — this arrow returns void, not string

// ❌ Conditional expression with void branch — one arm is void, the other is a value
function maybeLog(condition: boolean, msg: string): string {
  return condition ? console.log(msg) : msg;
  // void | string — the void from console.log infects the ternary return type
}

// ✅ Use a statement body when the expression is void-returning
const logMessage2 = (s: string): string => {
  console.log(s);
  return s;
};

// ✅ Separate the side effect from the return value
function maybeLog2(condition: boolean, msg: string): string {
  if (condition) console.log(msg);
  return msg;
}

// ✅ Concise callbacks whose body IS intentionally void are fine
["a", "b", "c"].forEach((x) => console.log(x));  // void callback — allowed
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-confusing-void-expression` prevents concise arrow functions from silently returning `void` when developers intended to return the expression value — catching the specific bug where `=> sideEffect()` looks syntactically identical to `=> computeValue()` but produces `undefined` rather than a value — but it conflicts with the common pattern of wrapping `void`-returning functions in concise arrow callbacks (e.g., `arr.forEach(item => logger.log(item))`), requiring a block body for every callback whose body is a `void` expression, adding syntactic noise to the most common logging and side-effect callback patterns in event-driven code.

---

**Pattern 404** — `@typescript-eslint/consistent-generic-constructors` enforces uniform placement of generic type arguments on constructor vs. variable declaration
```typescript
// Two syntactically valid ways to annotate a generic constructor in TypeScript:

// Style A: type annotation on the variable (left-hand side)
const mapA: Map<string, number> = new Map();
const setA: Set<string> = new Set();
const promiseA: Promise<User> = new Promise((resolve) => resolve(fetchUser("u1")));

// Style B: type argument on the constructor call (right-hand side)
const mapB = new Map<string, number>();
const setB = new Set<string>();
const promiseB = new Promise<User>((resolve) => resolve(fetchUser("u1")));

// ❌ Mixed styles in the same codebase — inconsistent, increases cognitive load
const cache: Map<string, CacheEntry> = new Map();   // left-side annotation
const queue = new Queue<Task>();                      // right-side type argument

// ✅ "constructor" mode: enforce right-hand form throughout
const cache2 = new Map<string, CacheEntry>();
const queue2 = new Queue<Task>();
const registry2 = new WeakMap<object, Metadata>();

// ✅ "type-annotation" mode: enforce left-hand form
// (useful when constructors are factory functions that cannot take type arguments)
const cache3: Map<string, CacheEntry> = new Map();
const queue3: Queue<Task> = createQueue();  // factory — only left-hand form possible
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/consistent-generic-constructors` eliminates the style inconsistency where some constructors annotate generics on the left (`const m: Map<K,V> = new Map()`) and others on the right (`const m = new Map<K,V>()`), reducing the visual scanning cost of identifying generic types in constructor calls — but the "constructor" style (right-hand) breaks down when the constructor is a factory function or when the variable declaration needs a type annotation for reasons unrelated to the generic (e.g., widening for a `let` that will be reassigned), requiring a mixed style override that partially undermines the consistency the rule was intended to enforce.

---

### Community Gotchas

**G65-1** — TypeScript 5.5 inferred type predicates silently fail for truthiness-based filters — `0`, `""`, and `false` are not narrowed out
Teams upgrading to TypeScript 5.5 and removing manual `(x): x is NonNullable<typeof x>` annotations from `.filter()` callbacks discover that the automatic predicate inference only applies when the filter condition is a strict equality check (`!== undefined`, `!== null`) — not a truthiness check (`!!x`, `Boolean(x)`, or just `x`). A filter like `.filter(x => !!x)` does not infer `x is T` because the "if and only if" predicate semantics require that when the function returns `false`, the value is definitively NOT of type `T` — but for a truthiness check, `!!x === false` is true for `0`, `""`, and `false`, which are valid members of many non-nullable types. Teams that replace `(x): x is string` with `(x) => Boolean(x)` expecting the same narrowing are surprised to find the array type widens back to `(string | undefined)[]`.
Why this matters: The upgrade path from TypeScript 5.4 to 5.5 creates a false sense of safety — developers see that `filter(x => x !== undefined)` now works without a manual predicate and generalize that all filter callbacks benefit from the same improvement. The truthiness edge case is invisible in code review because `!!x` and `x !== undefined` look equivalent in intent, but their predicate semantics differ in the presence of falsy-but-non-undefined values. The bug surfaces only at runtime when a `0` or `""` value passes a truthiness filter that the developer expected to exclude it.
Fix: Use explicit strict-equality checks in filter callbacks rather than truthiness: replace `filter(x => !!x)` with `filter((x): x is NonNullable<typeof x> => x != null)` and `filter(x => Boolean(x))` with `filter(x => x !== undefined && x !== null)`. For filtering out all falsy values including `0` and `""`, write an explicit manual predicate: `(x): x is T => x !== undefined && x !== null && x !== false && x !== 0 && x !== ""`.

---

**G65-2** — `isolatedDeclarations` rejects inferred return types even when the inference is trivially unambiguous — numeric literals, boolean constants, and array literals all require annotations
Teams enabling `isolatedDeclarations` to speed up monorepo declaration emit discover that the flag rejects inferred return types far more aggressively than expected — not just complex union types and conditional types, but also functions that return a numeric literal, a boolean, or an array of a known type. A function `export function maxRetries() { return 3; }` is rejected even though the return type `3` (or `number`) is unambiguously inferable without a full type-check pass. The TypeScript team's design decision is that `isolatedDeclarations` requires annotations whenever a tool (other than the TypeScript compiler itself) could not infer the type using only the file's own declarations — and since most external tools cannot reliably infer even simple expressions, the flag errs toward requiring annotations for all non-trivially-typed exports.
Why this matters: Teams expect `isolatedDeclarations` to require annotations only for complex or ambiguous types — the ones that would require cross-file inference. In practice, the flag requires annotations on hundreds of exported functions that return simple primitives, driving a migration effort that is far larger than anticipated. The annotation burden is especially high in test utility files and internal helper modules that were never intended to form a stable public API but are technically exported.
Fix: Run `tsc --declaration --emitDeclarationOnly` once with `isolatedDeclarations` enabled and use `@typescript-eslint/explicit-module-boundary-types` to surface all exports that lack return-type annotations. Apply the annotations mechanically using an IDE bulk-fix action (VS Code "Add all missing return types") rather than manually. For internal-only exports that are not part of the package's public API, consider moving them to non-exported files or behind an internal barrel that is excluded from the `isolatedDeclarations` scope.

---

**G65-3** — `@typescript-eslint/no-unnecessary-condition` fires on defensive runtime checks against `as`-cast data, masking the exact locations where type assertions create runtime-type gaps
Teams enabling `no-unnecessary-condition` in a codebase that uses `as` casts to handle untyped API responses find that the rule flags defensive null checks immediately after `as AppConfig` casts — producing errors like "This condition is always true — remove it" on exactly the checks that are most important to keep. The problem is that `as T` tells TypeScript to treat an `unknown` or `any` value as `T`, making the type system believe the value is non-null, and any subsequent check against `null` or `undefined` is flagged as an unnecessary condition. This creates a perverse outcome: the rule suppresses defensive programming at precisely the points in the codebase where the type system's guarantees are least reliable — at the boundary between typed and untyped data.
Why this matters: The `no-unnecessary-condition` rule is designed to catch stale type guards left over from refactoring, but it cannot distinguish between a guard that became unnecessary because the type was genuinely made non-nullable and a guard that appears unnecessary because an upstream `as` cast is lying about the type. The rule fires in both cases, and the developer must suppress it with an `eslint-disable` comment, which reduces the rule's value as a refactoring signal in codebases that have both legitimate stale guards and legitimate defensive guards.
Fix: Replace `as T` casts at API boundaries with runtime validation functions that narrow the type through a type predicate — `isAppConfig(raw): raw is AppConfig` — so that the check happens once at the boundary and TypeScript tracks the narrowed type accurately downstream, eliminating both the `as` cast and the need for subsequent defensive guards. Libraries like `zod`, `valibot`, and `arktype` automate this pattern with schema-derived type guards.

---

**G65-4** — `const` type parameters cause "argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'never'" errors when callers pass widened variables instead of literals
Teams adopting `const` type parameters (TypeScript 5.0) to preserve literal types through generic functions discover that existing call sites that pass variable references (rather than inline literals) produce confusing "not assignable to never" errors. When a `const` generic is constrained as `const T extends string`, passing a `string`-typed variable causes TypeScript to attempt to infer `T` as the minimal literal subtype or — in some inference paths — as `never`, rather than widening `T` to `string`. The error message ("not assignable to never") obscures the actual issue — that the caller needs to either pass a string literal directly or use a non-`const` overload.
Why this matters: The `const` type parameter modifier changes the inference mode for the parameter from widening to non-widening, which is the correct behavior for call sites that pass literals but is incorrect for call sites that pass computed or mutable strings. Since both call patterns are valid TypeScript, adding `const` to a type parameter is a breaking change for any existing call site that passes a widened variable. Library authors who add `const` to existing type parameters to improve literal inference for new use cases silently break existing callers in ways that produce confusing error messages.
Fix: Provide two overloads — one with `const T` for literal call sites and one with `T` for variable call sites — or use a conditional approach where the function accepts both `T` and `readonly T[]` without `const`, and use `as const` at call sites where literal preservation is needed. Alternatively, document that the function requires literal arguments and add a lint rule or type utility to enforce it: `type MustBeLiteral<T extends string> = string extends T ? never : T`.

---

**G65-5** — `@typescript-eslint/switch-exhaustiveness-check` conflicts with the ESLint core `default-case` rule — teams must disable one or configure both to avoid contradictory requirements
Teams enabling both `@typescript-eslint/switch-exhaustiveness-check` and the ESLint core `default-case` rule discover that the two rules enforce contradictory requirements for exhaustive switch statements on union types. `switch-exhaustiveness-check` is satisfied when every union member has an explicit case arm and there is no `default` — the absence of a default is what makes the switch exhaustive, because a `default` clause would absorb any future union members silently. But `default-case` requires every `switch` statement to have a `default` clause, and it has no way to distinguish between a `switch` on a union type (where `default` undermines exhaustiveness) and a `switch` on a raw `string` or `number` (where `default` is a safety net). With both rules active, all exhaustive union switches must either have a `default` (violating `switch-exhaustiveness-check`) or lack a `default` (violating `default-case`).
Why this matters: The conflict surfaces after teams enable `switch-exhaustiveness-check` as part of a TypeScript-specific ESLint configuration upgrade without realizing that their existing ESLint config (often inherited from a shared corporate baseline) already has `default-case` enabled. The contradiction is only revealed when developers write their first exhaustive union switch, receiving two contradictory lint errors. Teams that resolve the conflict by adding an empty `default: break;` or `default: throw new Error("unreachable")` partially defeat the exhaustiveness check's ability to catch missing union members at compile time.
Fix: Disable the ESLint core `default-case` rule for TypeScript files by adding `"default-case": "off"` to the TypeScript-specific section of your ESLint configuration. Replace its safety-net function with `switch-exhaustiveness-check` for typed union switches and an `@typescript-eslint/no-switch-fallthrough` variant for raw-value switches. If a `default` clause is intentionally retained in an exhaustive switch for runtime resilience (e.g., to handle values arriving from an untyped API), add `allowDefaultCaseForExhaustiveSwitch: true` to the `switch-exhaustiveness-check` configuration.

## Cycle 66 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 405** — Vitest `vi.importActual` partial-mock for shift-left module boundary tests
```typescript
// ❌ Mocking the entire module hides the real contract of the module under test:
vi.mock("../api/user-service");
// All exports are auto-mocked — a breaking change in user-service goes undetected
// because the mock never reflects the real function signature

// ✅ Use vi.importActual to keep real behaviour and mock only the I/O boundary:
import { vi, describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import type { UserService } from "../api/user-service";

vi.mock("../api/user-service", async (importActual) => {
  const real = await importActual<typeof UserService>();
  return {
    ...real,
    // only mock the network call, keep all type-safe helpers real
    fetchUser: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ id: "u1", name: "Alice" }),
  };
});

describe("UserProfile", () => {
  it("renders display name from fetched user", async () => {
    const { fetchUser } = await import("../api/user-service");
    expect(vi.isMockFunction(fetchUser)).toBe(true);
    // real validation helpers still run — type coercions are tested
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.importActual` partial mocking keeps real helper functions and type coercions in the execution path — catching type-contract regressions between module versions — but it requires every async-import mock factory to `await importActual`, which adds boilerplate and causes the test module graph to be larger than a pure auto-mock, increasing cold-start time in test suites with dozens of module boundaries.

**Pattern 406** — Vitest `coverage.thresholds` with `autoUpdate` to ratchet coverage upward monotonically
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: "v8",
      // Thresholds gate the CI run — a PR that drops coverage fails the check:
      thresholds: {
        lines: 85,
        functions: 80,
        branches: 75,
        statements: 85,
        // autoUpdate: true tells Vitest to write the new (higher) threshold
        // back into vitest.config.ts after a green run — thresholds only move up
        autoUpdate: true,
      },
      // Exclude generated and declaration files from coverage accounting:
      exclude: ["**/*.d.ts", "**/*.gen.ts", "**/index.ts"],
    },
  },
});

// In CI — fail the pipeline if coverage drops:
// npx vitest run --coverage
// exit code is non-zero when any threshold is not met
```
Tradeoff: `autoUpdate: true` creates a ratchet that prevents coverage regression by committing the updated threshold values back to `vitest.config.ts` after each green run — making coverage monotonically non-decreasing — but it requires write access to source files during CI execution, which conflicts with read-only artifact caching strategies and produces noisy git diffs on every CI run that raises a threshold, requiring teams to configure CI to commit or push the updated config file automatically.

**Pattern 407** — Pact consumer-driven contract test for a TypeScript HTTP client against a REST provider
```typescript
// consumer.pact.test.ts
import { PactV3, MatchersV3 } from "@pact-foundation/pact";
import { fetchUser } from "../api/user-client";
import path from "node:path";

const { like, string } = MatchersV3;

const provider = new PactV3({
  consumer: "UserWebApp",
  provider: "UserAPI",
  dir: path.resolve(__dirname, "../pacts"),
  logLevel: "warn",
});

describe("UserAPI contract", () => {
  it("returns a user object with id and name when user exists", async () => {
    await provider
      .given("user u1 exists")
      .uponReceiving("a GET request for user u1")
      .withRequest({ method: "GET", path: "/users/u1" })
      .willRespondWith({
        status: 200,
        headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
        body: like({ id: string("u1"), name: string("Alice") }),
      })
      .executeTest(async (mockServer) => {
        const user = await fetchUser(mockServer.url, "u1");
        expect(user.id).toBe("u1");
        expect(user.name).toBe("Alice");
      });
  });
});
// Run provider verification in provider repo:
// new Verifier({ providerBaseUrl, pactUrls: ["./pacts/UserWebApp-UserAPI.json"] }).verifyProvider()
```
Tradeoff: Pact consumer-driven contracts catch provider breaking changes before integration environments are involved — reducing the round-trip from a broken deploy to a failing test from hours to seconds — but the pact file must be shared between consumer and provider repos, requiring a Pact Broker or a shared artifact store, and the contract only covers the subset of interactions the consumer test authors think to specify, leaving edge cases (error responses, pagination boundaries) uncontracted and invisible to the provider's verification suite.

**Pattern 408** — Property-based testing with `fast-check` to find edge cases in domain validation functions
```typescript
// email-validator.property.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import fc from "fast-check";
import { normalizeEmail } from "../domain/email";

describe("normalizeEmail — property tests", () => {
  it("output is always lowercase", () => {
    fc.assert(
      fc.property(fc.emailAddress(), (email) => {
        const result = normalizeEmail(email);
        expect(result).toBe(result.toLowerCase());
      })
    );
  });

  it("output contains exactly one @ sign", () => {
    fc.assert(
      fc.property(fc.emailAddress(), (email) => {
        const result = normalizeEmail(email);
        expect(result.split("@").length).toBe(2);
      })
    );
  });

  it("roundtrip: normalizing an already-normalized address is idempotent", () => {
    fc.assert(
      fc.property(fc.emailAddress(), (email) => {
        const once = normalizeEmail(email);
        const twice = normalizeEmail(once);
        expect(once).toBe(twice);
      })
    );
  });
});
// fast-check generates hundreds of random inputs per run, finding shrunk
// counterexamples automatically — no manual edge-case enumeration required
```
Tradeoff: Property-based testing with `fast-check` exercises hundreds of generated inputs per property per run, surfacing edge cases (zero-length local parts, unicode domain labels, case-mixed addresses) that example-based tests never encode — but each test run is non-deterministic in the inputs sampled, requiring a fixed seed for CI reproducibility (`fc.assert(..., { seed: 42 })`), and the time to run 100–500 examples per property multiplies across a large property test suite, making property tests slower than equivalent example-based tests by 5–20x for the same logical assertions.

---

**Pattern 409** — TDD red-green-refactor enforced by a Vitest `--bail` pre-commit hook scoped to staged files
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# .husky/pre-commit
# Run only tests touching files in the current staged set, bail on first failure.
set -euo pipefail

STAGED=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM | grep -E '\.(ts|tsx)$' || true)
if [ -z "$STAGED" ]; then
  exit 0  # No TypeScript files staged — skip
fi

# Run vitest in related mode: only test files related to staged source files
# --bail 1 stops after the first failing test, returning non-zero exit code
npx vitest run --bail 1 --related $STAGED 2>&1
```
```typescript
// Example: write the test first (red), then implement (green), then refactor
// Step 1 — red: test written before implementation exists
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import { parseAmount } from "../domain/amount"; // does not exist yet — test fails

describe("parseAmount", () => {
  it("parses '£1,234.56' as 1234.56 GBP", () => {
    expect(parseAmount("£1,234.56")).toEqual({ value: 1234.56, currency: "GBP" });
  });
});
// Step 2 — green: implement parseAmount to pass the test
// Step 3 — refactor: extract currency-symbol map, re-run hook to confirm green
```
Tradeoff: A `--related --bail 1` pre-commit hook provides fast TDD feedback by running only tests linked to staged files and stopping at the first failure — enforcing the red-green-refactor discipline without running the full suite — but Vitest's `--related` mode resolves the relationship graph using static import analysis at test-start time, which misses tests that import the changed module through a dynamic `import()` call or through a re-export barrel that is not statically resolvable, causing some test regressions to slip through the pre-commit gate.

**Pattern 410** — Playwright component test for an isolated React component with `mount` and accessibility assertions
```typescript
// button.component.test.ts (Playwright CT)
import { test, expect } from "@playwright/experimental-ct-react";
import { SubmitButton } from "./SubmitButton";

test.use({ viewport: { width: 500, height: 200 } });

test("SubmitButton renders accessible label and fires onClick", async ({ mount }) => {
  let clicked = false;
  const component = await mount(
    <SubmitButton label="Send Payment" onClick={() => { clicked = true; }} />
  );

  // Accessibility assertion: button must have a role and visible text
  await expect(component).toBeVisible();
  await expect(component.getByRole("button", { name: "Send Payment" })).toBeEnabled();

  // Interaction assertion
  await component.getByRole("button", { name: "Send Payment" }).click();
  expect(clicked).toBe(true);

  // Snapshot for visual regression (reviewed on every PR diff)
  await expect(component).toHaveScreenshot("submit-button-default.png");
});

test("SubmitButton is disabled and aria-disabled when loading=true", async ({ mount }) => {
  const component = await mount(<SubmitButton label="Send Payment" loading />);
  const btn = component.getByRole("button", { name: "Send Payment" });
  await expect(btn).toBeDisabled();
  await expect(btn).toHaveAttribute("aria-disabled", "true");
});
```
Tradeoff: Playwright component tests render the component in a real browser using Vite's dev server — catching browser-specific rendering differences that JSDOM misses — but the `@playwright/experimental-ct-react` package is explicitly experimental, meaning its API surface changes across minor Playwright versions, and the Vite bundling step adds 2–4 seconds of startup overhead per test worker that makes component test suites significantly slower than equivalent JSDOM-based tests when run with a single worker.

**Pattern 411** — Inline snapshot testing with `toMatchInlineSnapshot` to make regression assertions reviewable in-file
```typescript
// order-formatter.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import { formatOrder } from "../domain/order-formatter";

describe("formatOrder", () => {
  it("formats a completed order for display", () => {
    const order = {
      id: "ord-001",
      total: 99.99,
      currency: "USD",
      status: "completed",
      items: [{ name: "Widget", qty: 2 }],
    };

    // Inline snapshot: the expected value lives beside the test — no external .snap file
    // Reviewers see the before/after directly in the PR diff without opening a separate file
    expect(formatOrder(order)).toMatchInlineSnapshot(`
      "Order #ord-001
       Items: Widget x2
       Total: $99.99 USD
       Status: COMPLETED"
    `);
  });

  it("formats a pending order with missing totals gracefully", () => {
    const order = { id: "ord-002", total: 0, currency: "EUR", status: "pending", items: [] };
    expect(formatOrder(order)).toMatchInlineSnapshot(`
      "Order #ord-002
       Items: (none)
       Total: €0.00 EUR
       Status: PENDING"
    `);
  });
});
// Update: npx vitest run --update — rewrites the inline string in-place
```
Tradeoff: `toMatchInlineSnapshot` keeps expected output co-located with the test assertion — making snapshot diffs visible in the same file during code review rather than requiring reviewers to open a separate `__snapshots__` directory — but the inline string is rewritten by the test runner on `--update`, which changes the whitespace and escaping of the snapshot string in a way that differs between Vitest versions, producing noisy diff hunks in upgrade PRs that contain only whitespace normalization changes with no semantic content.

**Pattern 412** — Stryker mutation testing gated in CI to enforce test suite effectiveness above a mutation score threshold
```json
{
  "mutate": ["src/**/*.ts", "!src/**/*.test.ts", "!src/**/*.d.ts"],
  "testRunner": "vitest",
  "reporters": ["html", "clear-text", "progress"],
  "thresholds": { "high": 80, "low": 60, "break": 60 },
  "timeoutMS": 10000,
  "concurrency": 4
}
```
```typescript
// stryker.config.mjs uses the JSON configuration above.
// Example: a test with 100% line coverage but 0% mutation score
export function isAdult(age: number): boolean {
  return age >= 18; // Stryker mutates >= to > — test must catch the boundary
}

// ❌ Weak test (passes line coverage, killed by mutation of >= to >):
it("returns true for age 20", () => { expect(isAdult(20)).toBe(true); });

// ✅ Boundary test (kills the >= → > mutant):
it("returns true for age 18 (boundary)", () => { expect(isAdult(18)).toBe(true); });
it("returns false for age 17 (below boundary)", () => { expect(isAdult(17)).toBe(false); });
// Stryker mutation score: 100% — all arithmetic operator mutants killed
```
Tradeoff: Stryker mutation testing with `thresholds.break` at 60% blocks merges when the test suite fails to kill more than 40% of code mutants — identifying tests that cover lines without asserting behaviour — but a full mutation test run executes the test suite once per mutant, typically producing 10–100x more test runs than a standard coverage run, making it impractical as a pre-commit gate and forcing teams to run it on a nightly schedule where the feedback loop is too slow to catch the mutation deficit in the same PR that introduced the weak tests.

**Pattern 413** — `jest-axe` accessibility assertions integrated into component tests as shift-left a11y gates
```typescript
// checkout-form.a11y.test.ts
import { render } from "@testing-library/react";
import { axe, toHaveNoViolations } from "jest-axe";
import { CheckoutForm } from "./CheckoutForm";

expect.extend(toHaveNoViolations);

describe("CheckoutForm accessibility", () => {
  it("has no detectable WCAG 2.1 AA violations in default state", async () => {
    const { container } = render(
      <CheckoutForm onSubmit={jest.fn()} initialValues={{ email: "", card: "" }} />
    );
    // axe runs the full axe-core rule set against the rendered DOM
    const results = await axe(container, {
      rules: {
        "color-contrast": { enabled: true },
        "label": { enabled: true },
        "button-name": { enabled: true },
      },
    });
    expect(results).toHaveNoViolations();
  });

  it("error state passes a11y — error messages linked to inputs via aria-describedby", async () => {
    const { container } = render(
      <CheckoutForm onSubmit={jest.fn()} errors={{ email: "Invalid email address" }} />
    );
    const results = await axe(container);
    expect(results).toHaveNoViolations();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `jest-axe` runs axe-core's automated accessibility rule set inside unit tests — catching WCAG violations (missing labels, invalid ARIA roles, contrast ratio failures) at the component level before a QA engineer ever interacts with the UI — but axe-core's automated checks cover only approximately 30–40% of WCAG 2.1 success criteria, with the remaining criteria (logical reading order, focus management in complex interactions, content meaning in context) requiring manual testing, creating a false sense of full accessibility coverage when the axe gate passes green.

**Pattern 414** — `@testing-library/user-event` v14 `setup()` API replacing `fireEvent` for realistic user-interaction simulation
```typescript
// login-form.test.tsx
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
import userEvent from "@testing-library/user-event";
import { LoginForm } from "./LoginForm";

describe("LoginForm — user interactions", () => {
  it("submits with typed credentials after clicking the button", async () => {
    // userEvent.setup() creates an instance with pointer/keyboard state tracking
    // This is required for v14 — do NOT use the legacy userEvent.type()
    const user = userEvent.setup();
    const onSubmit = jest.fn();
    render(<LoginForm onSubmit={onSubmit} />);

    // Realistic simulation: focus, type (with key events), blur
    await user.click(screen.getByLabelText("Email address"));
    await user.keyboard("alice@example.com");
    await user.click(screen.getByLabelText("Password"));
    await user.keyboard("s3cr3t!");

    // Submit via keyboard — tests that Enter-key submission is wired correctly
    await user.keyboard("{Enter}");

    expect(onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalledWith({
      email: "alice@example.com",
      password: "s3cr3t!",
    });
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `@testing-library/user-event` v14's `setup()` API simulates the full sequence of pointer and keyboard events (pointerdown, mousedown, focus, mouseup, pointerup, click) that a real browser fires — catching handlers that listen to specific low-level events that `fireEvent.click` never triggers — but each `await user.click()` call is 5–10x slower than `fireEvent.click` because it resolves multiple microtasks per event, which compounds across test suites with hundreds of interaction assertions and increases total test time by 30–60 seconds in large component test suites.

**Pattern 415** — `eslint-plugin-testing-library` rule set enforcing accessible query priority and preventing implementation-coupled test queries
```javascript
// .eslintrc.cjs
module.exports = {
  overrides: [
    {
      files: ["**/*.test.{ts,tsx}", "**/*.spec.{ts,tsx}"],
      plugins: ["testing-library"],
      extends: ["plugin:testing-library/react"],
      rules: {
        // Enforces query priority: getByRole > getByLabelText > getByPlaceholderText
        // > getByText > getByDisplayValue > getByAltText > getByTitle > getByTestId
        "testing-library/prefer-by-role": "error",
        // Bans getByTestId — data-testid queries couple tests to implementation details
        "testing-library/no-testid-queries": "warn",
        // Prevents findBy* queries from being awaited inside waitFor — double-async pattern
        "testing-library/no-await-sync-query": "error",
        // Prevents redundant act() wrapping around already-awaited queries
        "testing-library/no-unnecessary-act": "error",
        // Enforces screen queries over destructured render queries for consistency
        "testing-library/prefer-screen-queries": "error",
      },
    },
  ],
};
// Example of what the rules catch:
// ❌ const { getByTestId } = render(<Foo />); getByTestId("submit-btn")
// ✅ screen.getByRole("button", { name: "Submit" })
```
Tradeoff: `eslint-plugin-testing-library` enforces accessible-first query usage (role, label, placeholder before testid) which makes tests resistant to DOM structure refactors and aligns with how assistive technologies access the DOM — but the `prefer-by-role` rule requires developers to understand ARIA roles for every interactive element they query, and in component libraries that use non-semantic container elements or custom ARIA role assignments, the rule fires on legitimate `getByText` queries because the element genuinely has no accessible role, requiring per-file eslint-disable comments that create maintenance debt.

**Pattern 416** — MSW (Mock Service Worker) request handler in Vitest integration tests to intercept API calls without a running backend
```typescript
// test/server.ts (shared MSW setup)
import { setupServer } from "msw/node";
import { http, HttpResponse } from "msw";

export const server = setupServer(
  http.get("/api/users/:id", ({ params }) => {
    if (params.id === "u1") {
      return HttpResponse.json({ id: "u1", name: "Alice", role: "admin" });
    }
    return new HttpResponse(null, { status: 404 });
  }),
  http.post("/api/orders", async ({ request }) => {
    const body = await request.json();
    return HttpResponse.json({ orderId: "ord-001", ...body }, { status: 201 });
  })
);

// vitest.setup.ts
beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: "error" }));
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());
afterAll(() => server.close());

// user-profile.integration.test.ts
it("loads and displays admin badge for admin users", async () => {
  render(<UserProfile userId="u1" />);
  await screen.findByText("Alice");         // waits for async fetch
  expect(screen.getByText("Admin")).toBeInTheDocument();
});
```
Tradeoff: MSW intercepts `fetch` and `XMLHttpRequest` calls at the network layer using Node's `http` interception — providing realistic API integration tests without a running backend and matching the exact request/response cycle the browser uses — but `onUnhandledRequest: "error"` causes any unhandled request to fail the test immediately, which breaks tests when a component makes a background telemetry or analytics call that the test author did not anticipate, requiring every non-essential outbound call to be explicitly handled or silenced with `onUnhandledRequest: "warn"`.

**Pattern 417** — Test data builder pattern with TypeScript fluent API to eliminate brittle fixture literals in unit tests
```typescript
// builders/order.builder.ts
import type { Order, OrderItem } from "../domain/types";

export class OrderBuilder {
  private data: Order = {
    id: "ord-default",
    status: "pending",
    total: 0,
    currency: "USD",
    items: [],
    createdAt: new Date("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"),
  };

  withId(id: string): this { this.data = { ...this.data, id }; return this; }
  withStatus(s: Order["status"]): this { this.data = { ...this.data, status: s }; return this; }
  withTotal(total: number, currency = "USD"): this { this.data = { ...this.data, total, currency }; return this; }
  withItem(item: Partial<OrderItem>): this {
    this.data = { ...this.data, items: [...this.data.items, { name: "Item", qty: 1, ...item }] };
    return this;
  }
  build(): Order { return { ...this.data }; }
}

// Usage in tests — reads like a specification, not a JSON blob:
const order = new OrderBuilder()
  .withStatus("completed")
  .withTotal(199.99, "GBP")
  .withItem({ name: "Keyboard", qty: 1 })
  .build();

expect(formatOrder(order)).toContain("£199.99 GBP");
```
Tradeoff: The builder pattern produces readable test data that communicates intent — `withStatus("completed").withTotal(199.99)` is self-documenting in a way that a raw object literal with six required fields is not — but the builder class must be maintained in parallel with the domain type it wraps, and when a field is added to the `Order` type as required, the builder's default object becomes a TypeScript compile error that must be resolved before any test that uses the builder will pass, temporarily breaking the entire test suite rather than just tests for the new field.

---

**Pattern 418** — `tsd` type-level unit tests to verify that TypeScript generic utility types behave as specified
```typescript
// types.test-d.ts (run with: npx tsd)
import { expectType, expectError, expectAssignable } from "tsd";
import type { DeepReadonly, NonEmptyArray, StrictOmit } from "../types/utils";

// DeepReadonly makes all nested properties readonly:
expectType<DeepReadonly<{ user: { name: string } }>>(
  {} as { readonly user: { readonly name: string } }
);

// NonEmptyArray<T> must reject empty arrays:
expectError<NonEmptyArray<string>>([] as never[]);

// Awaited<Promise<T>> unwraps to T (built-in since TS 4.5):
expectType<string>({} as Awaited<Promise<string>>);

// StrictOmit should not permit omitting keys that don't exist on the type:
expectError<StrictOmit<{ id: string; name: string }, "nonExistentKey">>(
  {} as { id: string; name: string }
);

// Assignability test: DeepReadonly must be assignable to the mutable base type:
expectAssignable<{ user: { name: string } }>(
  {} as DeepReadonly<{ user: { name: string } }>
);
```
Tradeoff: `tsd` type-level tests run as part of `tsc --noEmit` and fail at compile time when a utility type violates its specification — catching regressions in generic type utilities without requiring runtime execution — but `tsd`'s `expectType` performs an exact bidirectional assignability check, meaning that `expectType<string | number>(value)` fails if `value` is typed as `string` even though `string` is assignable to `string | number`, requiring developers to use `expectAssignable` instead of `expectType` for supertype assertions, a distinction that is non-obvious to developers unfamiliar with the TypeScript assignability model.

---

**Pattern 419** — Pre-commit `lint-staged` pipeline with type-check, lint, and unit test stages to enforce shift-left quality gates per-file
```json
{
  "lint-staged": {
    "*.{ts,tsx}": [
      "eslint --fix --max-warnings 0",
      "bash -c 'tsc --noEmit --project tsconfig.json'",
      "vitest run --reporter=verbose --bail 1 --related"
    ],
    "*.{js,mjs,cjs}": [
      "eslint --fix --max-warnings 0"
    ],
    "*.{json,yaml,yml}": [
      "prettier --write --log-level warn"
    ]
  },
  "scripts": {
    "prepare": "husky"
  }
}
```
```bash
# .husky/pre-commit
#!/usr/bin/env sh
. "$(dirname -- "$0")/_/husky.sh"
npx lint-staged
# lint-staged runs ESLint fix, tsc --noEmit, and vitest --related in sequence.
# Any non-zero exit aborts the commit and surfaces the failure inline.
# Developers see the blocking error without switching to a terminal tab.
```
Tradeoff: A `lint-staged` pipeline that chains ESLint auto-fix, `tsc --noEmit`, and `vitest --related` runs per-file quality gates on every commit without scanning the entire project — keeping pre-commit latency under 5 seconds on most feature branches — but the `tsc --noEmit` step always type-checks the entire project (not just staged files) because TypeScript's project-level type resolution requires the full dependency graph to be loaded, meaning that a staged change to a single file triggers a full type-check that can take 10–30 seconds in large monorepos, defeating the per-file scoping intent of `lint-staged`.

### Community Gotchas

**G66-1** — Vitest `--related` flag silently skips tests when the import graph is broken by a barrel re-export
When teams add `--related` to their pre-commit Vitest invocation to scope the test run to only the files affected by staged changes, they discover that tests for staged modules are silently skipped rather than run when the staged module is re-exported through a barrel `index.ts` that itself is not staged. Vitest's `--related` resolver traces static `import` statements from test files to source files — if the test imports from `../domain/index` (the barrel) and the staged change is in `../domain/order.ts`, Vitest does not trace through the barrel to identify the relationship, causing the test file to be excluded from the run. The developer sees a green pre-commit gate, pushes, and the CI full run reveals a regression.
Why this matters: The gap between `--related`'s perceived behaviour ("runs tests for my changes") and its actual behaviour ("runs tests whose import graph resolves directly to the changed file without traversing re-exports") is invisible in normal workflows and only surfaces when a regression slips through the pre-commit gate. Teams that rely on `--related` for shift-left defect detection are operating with a false safety net any time their codebase uses barrel exports, which is the majority of TypeScript projects.
Fix: Replace barrel imports in test files with direct imports from the source module (`import { formatOrder } from "../domain/order"` rather than `import { formatOrder } from "../domain"`) to make the import graph resolvable by Vitest's static analysis. Alternatively, add the barrel `index.ts` to the staged files list in the pre-commit hook whenever a module it re-exports is changed — a mechanical step that can be scripted as a pre-commit hook companion that inspects barrel exports and auto-stages them.

---

**G66-2** — `toMatchInlineSnapshot` whitespace normalization rewrites cause misleading "test updated" diffs during Vitest version upgrades
Teams that use `toMatchInlineSnapshot` as their primary regression-testing technique for text formatters, serializers, and CLI output encounter a class of Vitest upgrade failures where all inline snapshot strings are rewritten by the new version of the snapshot serializer — even though the serialized value has not changed. Vitest delegates serialization to `pretty-format`, and changes to `pretty-format`'s whitespace and escaping rules between versions cause every `toMatchInlineSnapshot` call in the codebase to fail with a diff that looks like a regression but is only a formatting artefact. Developers who see hundreds of failing snapshot tests during a Vitest upgrade mistakenly run `--update` to accept all changes, committing the serializer-normalization diffs as if they were intentional changes.
Why this matters: The `--update` reflex — "snapshot tests are failing, update them all" — is the primary failure mode that snapshot testing best-practice guidance warns against. When a Vitest upgrade causes mass snapshot failures, it trains developers to use `--update` without inspecting each diff, which then allows genuine regressions to be accepted silently in the same batch update. The mass-update event resets the entire snapshot baseline, eliminating the regression-detection value that the snapshots were providing.
Fix: Pin `pretty-format` as a direct `devDependency` at the same major version as the current Vitest to prevent the snapshot serializer from changing independently of Vitest. After a Vitest upgrade, run `vitest run --update` on a branch that contains no source changes — review the diff to confirm it is purely whitespace normalization — then commit the snapshot-only update as a dedicated "chore: update snapshots for vitest vX.Y.Z" commit before merging any feature work, keeping the normalization rewrite separate from functional change commits.

---

**G66-3** — Pact broker `can-i-deploy` check omitted from CD pipeline allows a consumer to deploy against an unverified provider version
Teams that set up Pact consumer and provider verification in their CI pipelines but do not add the `pact-broker can-i-deploy` check to their CD (deployment) pipeline expose themselves to the exact class of integration failures that Pact was adopted to prevent. The `can-i-deploy` command queries the Pact Broker for whether the consumer version being deployed and the provider version currently in the target environment have a verified pact between them — but it is a separate step from the contract generation and provider verification steps, and teams that add Pact in phases often skip `can-i-deploy` because it requires configuring the Pact Broker URL and authentication in the CD pipeline. Without `can-i-deploy`, a consumer that generates a new pact can be deployed to production before the provider team has run verification, introducing an incompatible API interaction into production.
Why this matters: The Pact workflow's safety guarantee is: consumer generates contract, provider verifies contract, `can-i-deploy` confirms the verified pair before deployment. Omitting the third step creates a window where contracts are generated and verified but the deployment gate is missing — the Pact Broker contains the verification result, but no tool queries it before the deploy proceeds. Teams that experience a production integration failure after implementing Pact invariably find that `can-i-deploy` was not wired up in the deployment pipeline.
Fix: Add `npx pact-broker can-i-deploy --pacticipant <consumer> --version <consumer-version> --to-environment production` as a required step immediately before the consumer deployment step in the CD pipeline, using the `PACT_BROKER_BASE_URL` and `PACT_BROKER_TOKEN` environment variables that should already be configured for the broker publish step. Add the equivalent `can-i-deploy` check to the provider's CD pipeline for symmetry — the provider must also confirm that its new version is safe to deploy against all registered consumers before deploying.

---

**G66-4** — MSW `onUnhandledRequest: "error"` breaks tests when a third-party SDK makes undocumented background requests
Teams adopting MSW with `onUnhandledRequest: "error"` in their Vitest integration test suite discover that tests begin failing with "MSW: Cannot find a matching request handler" errors that appear unrelated to the component under test. The culprit is a third-party SDK (analytics, error tracking, feature-flag, or A/B testing library) that makes background HTTP requests during module initialization or during a component's `useEffect` — requests that the test author never anticipated because they are not part of the component's documented API surface. The `onUnhandledRequest: "error"` configuration causes these background requests to throw, propagating as a test failure with a misleading error message that implicates the component rather than the SDK.
Why this matters: The `onUnhandledRequest: "error"` setting is MSW's best-practice recommendation for catching missing request handlers in integration tests — it prevents tests from silently passing when the component makes a real network call that the MSW server did not intercept. But third-party SDK background requests are not missing handlers by accident; they are expected requests from code the team does not own and cannot easily suppress. Distinguishing "legitimate missing handler" errors from "SDK background request" errors requires developers to identify which SDK makes requests to the indicated URL and decide whether to add a no-op handler or change `onUnhandledRequest` — a debugging cycle that consumes significant time.
Fix: Add a passthrough handler for known SDK domains at the top of the MSW server setup: `http.get("https://analytics.example.com/*", () => passthrough())` — this explicitly documents which background requests are known and expected while leaving `onUnhandledRequest: "error"` in place for all other unhandled requests. For SDKs that use dynamic or environment-specific domains, use a regex passthrough pattern. If the SDK cannot be easily identified, enable `onUnhandledRequest: "warn"` during the investigation phase and promote to `"error"` once all background requests are catalogued.

---

**G66-5** — Property-based test `fc.assert` uses a new random seed on every run unless pinned, causing non-reproducible CI failures
Teams that add `fast-check` property tests to their Vitest suite without specifying a seed encounter an intermittent CI failure pattern: a property test fails once on a particular CI run (fast-check found a counterexample with the random seed used in that run), but the test passes on re-run and on the developer's machine because the next run uses a different seed that does not exercise the failing input. The CI failure is reported as a flaky test, the PR is re-run until it passes, and the underlying edge case is never fixed because it is not reproducible. This defeats the purpose of property-based testing — finding and permanently eliminating edge cases.
Why this matters: When fast-check discovers a counterexample it prints the failing seed and the shrunk counterexample to the test output, but developers running in re-run mode do not see this output from the failed run — they only see the green re-run. The counterexample and seed are ephemeral in the CI log artifacts unless the team explicitly saves or inspects the failed run's output. The test framework found a defect, printed it to a log that nobody read, and the test system reported the build as passing on retry, effectively suppressing the defect report.
Fix: Pin the `fast-check` seed in all CI runs using an environment variable: `fc.assert(property, { seed: parseInt(process.env.FC_SEED ?? "42", 10) })` — this makes every CI run deterministic and reproducible from the same seed. In local development, use a random seed by reading `Date.now()` when the env var is absent, so developers continue to explore new inputs. Add the seed as a required CI environment variable and configure the CI pipeline to print the seed value at the start of the test run so that a failing seed can be reproduced locally by setting `FC_SEED=<failing-seed>` and re-running. Alternatively, use fast-check's built-in Vitest reporter integration (available in fast-check v3.15+) which records the seed in the test report automatically.
