## Cycle 68 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 420** — `@typescript-eslint/no-mixed-enums` prevents enums from mixing numeric and string initializers in the same declaration
```typescript
// ❌ Mixed enum — some members are numeric, others are string
// The resulting type is a union of number and string literals,
// making exhaustive switch checks unreliable and comparisons error-prone
enum Status {
  Pending  = 0,
  Active   = "ACTIVE",   // Error: mixed initializer styles
  Closed   = 2,
  Archived = "ARCHIVED",
}

// ✅ Purely numeric enum — all members auto-increment or use explicit values
enum NumericStatus {
  Pending  = 0,
  Active   = 1,
  Closed   = 2,
  Archived = 3,
}

// ✅ Purely string enum — all members have string initializers
enum StringStatus {
  Pending  = "PENDING",
  Active   = "ACTIVE",
  Closed   = "CLOSED",
  Archived = "ARCHIVED",
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-mixed-enums` eliminates the footgun where a mixed numeric/string enum produces a heterogeneous union type that breaks exhaustive switch checking — a `switch` exhaustiveness check on a purely numeric enum knows that unhandled members are numeric values, but on a mixed enum, the type is `number | string` and exhaustiveness inference degrades — but it prevents the practical migration pattern where teams add new string-valued members to an existing numeric enum for backwards-compatible serialization without being able to update all members at once.

---

**Pattern 421** — `@typescript-eslint/prefer-enum-initializers` requires explicit initializers on all enum members to prevent silent renumbering when members are inserted or reordered
```typescript
// ❌ Implicit numeric enum — inserting a member changes all subsequent values
// If persisted enum values are stored in a database or over an API, this is data-corruption
enum Permission {
  Read,    // 0
  Write,   // 1
  Execute, // 2 -- if a new member is inserted before this, it silently becomes 3
}

// After inserting Admin as the second member, Execute renumbers
enum PermissionBroken {
  Read,    // 0
  Admin,   // 1 -- NEW: all members after this are renumbered
  Write,   // 2 -- was 1
  Execute, // 3 -- was 2: any stored "2" now incorrectly maps to Write
}

// ✅ Explicit initializers — insertions never change existing values
enum PermissionSafe {
  Read    = 0,
  Write   = 1,
  Execute = 2,
  Admin   = 3, // new members get the next explicit value; no existing value changes
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/prefer-enum-initializers` prevents the silent data-corruption bug where inserting an enum member renumbers all subsequent auto-incremented members — a critical defect when enum values are persisted to a database or serialized over an API — but it increases enum verbosity and forces developers to manually assign and maintain integer sequences, adding toil in codebases that use enums as transient ordinal flags rather than persisted identifiers where renumbering is harmless.

---

**Pattern 422** — `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-enum-comparison` prevents comparing enum members against values of incompatible types using `===` or `!==`
```typescript
enum Direction { Up = "UP", Down = "DOWN", Left = "LEFT", Right = "RIGHT" }

// ❌ Comparing enum member against a raw string — TypeScript allows it but the
// comparison can only match if the raw string happens to equal the enum's wire value
function moveByRaw(input: string): void {
  if (input === Direction.Up) {  // Error: `string` is not comparable to `Direction`
    console.log("moving up");
  }
}

// ❌ Comparing across unrelated enum types — always false at runtime
enum Color { Red = 0 }
enum Size  { Small = 0 }
const c: Color = Color.Red;
// if (c === Size.Small) — TypeScript nominal types prevent this comparison

// ✅ Compare against typed enum values only — caller must hold a Direction
function moveSafe(dir: Direction): void {
  if (dir === Direction.Up) { console.log("moving up"); }
}

// ✅ Parse and validate at the API boundary before comparing
function parseDirection(raw: string): Direction | undefined {
  const values = Object.values(Direction) as string[];
  return values.includes(raw) ? (raw as Direction) : undefined;
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-enum-comparison` catches comparisons between enum members and incompatible types at the points where raw strings should be validated before entering the typed domain — but it fires on legitimate boundary code where the intent is explicitly to test whether a raw string matches a known enum member, requiring every such check to be wrapped in a type-narrowing function even when the comparison logic is correct.

---

**Pattern 423** — `@typescript-eslint/no-duplicate-enum-values` flags enum declarations where two members share the same initializer value
```typescript
// ❌ Duplicate numeric value — TIMEOUT and GATEWAY_TIMEOUT both map to 504
// Reverse mapping from value to name returns whichever member TypeScript emitted last
enum HttpStatus {
  OK              = 200,
  NOT_FOUND       = 404,
  SERVER_ERROR    = 500,
  TIMEOUT         = 504,
  GATEWAY_TIMEOUT = 504, // Error: duplicate value — reverse lookup is non-deterministic
}

// ❌ Duplicate string value — same serialized string for two logical states
enum EventType {
  CLICK = "click",
  TAP   = "click", // Error: TAP and CLICK have the same wire format
  HOVER = "hover",
}

// ✅ Unique values throughout — use a const alias for intentional synonyms
enum HttpStatus2 {
  OK              = 200,
  NOT_FOUND       = 404,
  SERVER_ERROR    = 500,
  GATEWAY_TIMEOUT = 504,
}
const TIMEOUT = HttpStatus2.GATEWAY_TIMEOUT; // alias outside the enum, not a duplicate member
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-duplicate-enum-values` prevents the subtle non-determinism where reverse mapping (`enum[value]`) returns different member names depending on declaration order — a bug that surfaces only when persisted enum values are read back or logged — but it blocks the intentional-alias pattern where a domain concept has two acceptable names for the same underlying code, forcing teams to use a `const` alias outside the enum rather than a second member inside it.

---

**Pattern 424** — `@typescript-eslint/prefer-literal-enum-member` restricts enum member initializers to literals, preventing computed expressions that obscure the resolved value at the declaration site
```typescript
// ❌ Computed enum member — the actual resolved value requires mental arithmetic
const BASE = 100;
enum ErrorCode {
  NotFound  = BASE + 4, // Error: computed expression, not a literal
  Forbidden = BASE + 3,
  ServerErr = BASE + 0,
}

// ❌ Template literal — looks like a literal but contains a computed expression
enum ApiRoute {
  Home    = "/",
  Profile = `/users/${"profile"}`, // Error: embedded template expression
}

// ❌ Bitwise shift — idiomatic for flag enums but obscures the resolved integer
enum Flags {
  Read    = 1 << 0, // Error: shift expression is not a literal
  Write   = 1 << 1,
  Execute = 1 << 2,
}

// ✅ Literal initializers — values are visible without evaluation
enum ErrorCode2 { NotFound = 104, Forbidden = 103, ServerErr = 100 }

// ✅ For bit flags, use a const object with type alias instead of an enum
const AccessBits = { Read: 1, Write: 2, Execute: 4 } as const;
type AccessBit = typeof AccessBits[keyof typeof AccessBits];
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/prefer-literal-enum-member` prevents computed enum initializers that obscure the actual resolved value — which matters when enum values are persisted or compared across service boundaries — but it blocks the ergonomic `1 << N` pattern for bit-flag enums that is idiomatic in TypeScript codebases inheriting from C-family conventions, requiring a migration to `const` objects with manually computed powers-of-two that are less readable when the flag count is large.

---

**Pattern 425** — `@typescript-eslint/no-import-type-side-effects` prevents inline `type` specifiers inside value imports from accidentally triggering module side effects in non-type-aware transpilers
```typescript
// ❌ Inline type specifier inside a value import from a side-effect module
// esbuild/SWC may retain the module import even if all specifiers are type-only
import { type Config } from "./registers-global-side-effect";
// A non-type-aware transpiler emits: import "./registers-global-side-effect"
// which runs module-level side effects unexpectedly in tests and bundled output

// ❌ Mixed import — only the type specifier is stripped; value specifiers remain
import { type User, fetchUser } from "./user-module";
// Safe here because fetchUser is a value, but the inline type style is inconsistent

// ✅ Top-level `import type` is unconditionally stripped by all transpilers
import type { Config } from "./registers-global-side-effect"; // always stripped
import { fetchUser } from "./user-module";      // value import — retained correctly
import type { User } from "./user-module";      // split out for clarity

// ESLint rule to enforce the top-level form:
// "@typescript-eslint/no-import-type-side-effects": "error"
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-import-type-side-effects` prevents the class of bugs where a type-only import from a side-effect module causes unintended module initialization when transpiled by esbuild or SWC in non-type-aware mode — a bug invisible in `tsc`-compiled projects but present in bundler-only pipelines — but it forces developers to split every import that mixes value and type specifiers into two import statements, doubling the import count in files that import many types from value modules.

---

**Pattern 426** — `@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-exports` enforces a single style for re-exporting types across all barrel files — either top-level `export type` or inline `type` modifier
```typescript
// ❌ Inconsistent barrel file — mixes both re-export styles for types
export type { UserProfile };              // top-level export type
export { type OrderStatus, createOrder }; // inline type modifier mixed with value export

// ❌ Missing `type` keyword on a type-only re-export — breaks consumers that use isolatedModules
// export { UserProfile };  // Error under isolatedModules: UserProfile is a type, not a value

// ✅ "type-exports" mode: all type-only re-exports use top-level `export type`
export type { UserProfile };
export type { OrderStatus };
export { createOrder };           // value export — no `type` keyword needed

// ✅ "inline-type-exports" mode: inline modifier in mixed export groups
export { createOrder, type UserProfile, type OrderStatus };

// .eslintrc:
// "@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-exports": [
//   "error", { "fixMixedExportsWithInlineTypeSpecifier": true }
// ]
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-exports` eliminates the dual-mode type re-export style where some barrel files use `export type { Foo }` and others use `export { type Foo }` — a visual inconsistency that adds scanning overhead in large index files — but the two modes are not always interchangeable: top-level `export type` cannot appear in an `export { ... }` list that also contains value specifiers, while the inline mode requires TypeScript 3.8+, meaning the correct choice depends on the project's minimum TypeScript version and per-file export mix.

---

**Pattern 427** — `@typescript-eslint/no-useless-empty-export` removes `export {}` statements that are redundant when the file already has other exports that make it a module
```typescript
// ❌ Redundant export {} alongside real named exports
export const MAX_RETRIES = 3;
export type RetryConfig = { maxRetries: number; delayMs: number };
export {}; // Error: file is already a module — this adds no information

// ❌ Redundant export {} after an import that already makes the file a module
import "reflect-metadata";
declare module "express" { interface Request { userId: string; } }
export {}; // Error: the import already establishes module scope

// ✅ Valid use: isolated file with no imports or exports that needs module scope
// to enable declaration merging or avoid "cannot redeclare block-scoped variable"
export {}; // Valid when this is the ONLY top-level statement in the file

// ✅ Prefer tsconfig "moduleDetection": "force" to make all files modules implicitly
// { "compilerOptions": { "moduleDetection": "force" } }
// Eliminates the need for defensive export {} entirely
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-useless-empty-export` removes the `export {}` boilerplate that developers add by habit when a file already has real exports — preventing the confusion where readers must verify whether the empty export carries semantic significance — but it creates friction with defensive file templates that always start with `export {}`, requiring developers to remember to remove it once real exports are added and to understand that the `moduleDetection` tsconfig option controls whether the removal is truly safe.

---

**Pattern 428** — `@typescript-eslint/no-extraneous-class` prevents classes that contain only static members or are used solely as namespaces, enforcing the use of plain objects or module-level functions instead
```typescript
// ❌ Namespace-only class — all members are static, no instance is ever constructed
class StringUtils {
  static readonly EMPTY = "";
  static isBlank(s: string): boolean { return s.trim().length === 0; }
  static truncate(s: string, max: number): string {
    return s.length <= max ? s : s.slice(0, max) + "...";
  }
}
// Usage: StringUtils.isBlank(x) — the class adds prototype overhead with no benefit

// ❌ Constructor-only class — used purely as a value object with no methods
class Coordinates {
  constructor(public readonly lat: number, public readonly lng: number) {}
}

// ✅ Plain module-level functions replace the static-only class
export function isBlank(s: string): boolean { return s.trim().length === 0; }
export function truncate(s: string, max: number): string {
  return s.length <= max ? s : s.slice(0, max) + "...";
}

// ✅ Interface + factory function replaces the constructor-only class
interface Coordinates { lat: number; lng: number }
function coords(lat: number, lng: number): Coordinates { return { lat, lng }; }
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-extraneous-class` eliminates the anti-pattern of using classes as namespaces or static-method bags — which adds unnecessary prototype chain overhead, prevents tree-shaking of individual methods, and misleads readers into expecting instantiation — but it conflicts with Angular, NestJS, and decorator-based frameworks where classes with only static members or constructor-injection are idiomatic, requiring broad per-file exemptions in framework-heavy codebases.

---

**Pattern 429** — `@typescript-eslint/parameter-properties` enforces a consistent style for constructor parameter properties — either always using shorthand or always using explicit class-body declarations
```typescript
// ❌ Mixed style — some parameters use shorthand, others require explicit class-body declarations
class OrderService {
  private readonly logger: Logger; // explicit class-body declaration

  constructor(
    public readonly orderId: string,  // shorthand parameter property
    logger: Logger,                   // plain parameter — requires manual assignment
    private readonly db: Database,    // shorthand parameter property
  ) {
    this.logger = logger; // manual assignment needed because the param is not shorthand
  }
}

// ✅ "parameter-properties" mode: shorthand consistently for all constructor-injected deps
class OrderService2 {
  constructor(
    public readonly orderId: string,
    private readonly logger: Logger,
    private readonly db: Database,
  ) {}
}

// ✅ "class-property" mode: explicit class-body declarations for all properties
class OrderService3 {
  public readonly orderId: string;
  private readonly logger: Logger;
  private readonly db: Database;
  constructor(orderId: string, logger: Logger, db: Database) {
    this.orderId = orderId; this.logger = logger; this.db = db;
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/parameter-properties` enforces a consistent constructor style that prevents the mixed pattern where some properties use shorthand (`private readonly x: T` in the parameter list) and others require explicit class-body declarations — reducing the cognitive overhead of determining which parameters become properties — but the two modes conflict with DI framework conventions: Angular requires explicit `@Inject()` decorators on explicit parameters while NestJS and InversifyJS prefer shorthand, meaning a single rule setting cannot accommodate both framework files and plain service files without per-directory overrides.

---

**Pattern 430** — `@typescript-eslint/no-require-imports` bans CommonJS `require()` calls in TypeScript files that use ES module syntax, eliminating `any`-typed implicit returns
```typescript
// ❌ CommonJS require() — TypeScript cannot resolve types through require()
// The return type is `any`, which silently disables type checking for all downstream uses
const config = require("./app-config");   // config: any
const { resolve } = require("path");      // resolve: any

// ❌ Dynamic require() as a lazy-load workaround — also untyped
function loadAdapter(name: string) {
  return require(`./adapters/${name}`);   // Error: dynamic require, return type any
}

// ✅ Static ES module import — TypeScript resolves types, bundler tree-shaking works
import config from "./app-config";
import { resolve } from "path";

// ✅ Dynamic import() for lazy loading — typed, async, and ESM-compatible
async function loadAdapter(name: string) {
  const mod = await import(`./adapters/${name}`);
  return mod.default;
}

// ✅ For CJS modules with no type declarations, add an ambient module declaration
declare module "legacy-util" { export function doLegacyThing(x: string): string; }
import { doLegacyThing } from "legacy-util";
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-require-imports` eliminates `any`-typed CommonJS `require()` calls that bypass TypeScript's module resolution — preventing the class of defects where a `require()` return is used without type checking — but it creates friction in dual-CJS/ESM compatibility shims that use conditional `require()`, in Jest test files that rely on `jest.mock()` with `require()` for re-importing mocked modules, and in Node.js build scripts that use `__dirname`-relative paths without an `import.meta.url` equivalent.

---

**Pattern 431** — `@typescript-eslint/no-restricted-imports` blocks imports from deprecated, insecure, or non-optimal modules at lint time with actionable replacement messages
```typescript
// .eslintrc configuration — ban specific modules or named exports with custom messages:
// "@typescript-eslint/no-restricted-imports": ["error", {
//   "paths": [
//     { "name": "lodash",
//       "message": "Use lodash-es for tree-shaking: import { debounce } from 'lodash-es'" },
//     { "name": "moment",
//       "message": "moment is unmaintained. Use date-fns: import { format } from 'date-fns'" },
//     { "name": "crypto",
//       "importNames": ["createCipher", "createDecipher"],
//       "message": "Deprecated and insecure. Use createCipheriv / createDecipheriv instead." }
//   ],
//   "patterns": [
//     { "group": ["../../../*"],
//       "message": "Avoid deep relative imports. Use path aliases: @/module/path" }
//   ]
// }]

// ❌ Blocked — error message explains the correct alternative at the lint site
import { debounce } from "lodash";                    // Error: use lodash-es
import moment from "moment";                           // Error: use date-fns
import { createCipher } from "crypto";                // Error: deprecated API
import { UserRepo } from "../../../repositories/user"; // Error: use @/repositories/user

// ✅ Replacements specified in the rule's message fields
import { debounce } from "lodash-es";
import { format } from "date-fns";
import { createCipheriv } from "crypto";
import { UserRepo } from "@/repositories/user";
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-restricted-imports` provides a project-specific enforcement layer that surfaces deprecated, insecure, or sub-optimal imports with actionable messages at lint time — preventing the pattern where developers copy an import from a Stack Overflow answer without knowing about the project's preferred alternative — but the ban list requires ongoing maintenance and produces false positives in migration shim files that must legitimately import from the old path, requiring per-file `eslint-disable` comments in exactly the files that own the migration wrapper.

---

**Pattern 432** — `@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-assertions` enforces a single assertion style and controls `as any` double-casts that bypass type-safety at boundaries
```typescript
// ❌ Mixed assertion styles — same codebase uses both forms inconsistently
declare const rawInput: unknown;
const a = <string>rawInput;        // angle-bracket style — breaks inside JSX files
const b = rawInput as string;      // as-style

// ❌ `as any as TargetType` double-cast silences the compiler without providing safety
interface UserPayload { id: string; name: string; email: string }
declare const raw: unknown;
const unsafe = (raw as any) as UserPayload; // double-cast: unknown -> any -> UserPayload

// ❌ Asserting directly on an object literal — missing required fields are not caught
function makeUser(): UserPayload {
  return {} as UserPayload; // missing id, name, email — not caught by the assertion
}

// ✅ Consistent `as`-only style + validate before asserting
const title = (document.getElementById("h1") as HTMLHeadingElement).textContent;

// ✅ Use `satisfies` on object literals for type checking without bypassing structural checks
const stub = { id: "u1", name: "Test", email: "t@example.com" } satisfies UserPayload;

// ✅ When a double-cast is necessary, go through `unknown` explicitly (rule allows this)
const validated = raw as unknown as UserPayload; // explicit intent: raw -> unknown -> typed
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-assertions` eliminates the style inconsistency between `<T>` and `as T` and prevents `as any as T` double-casts that silence the type system at API boundaries — catching the hidden defect where an object literal with missing required fields is cast directly to an interface — but the `objectLiteralTypeAssertions: "never"` option is too strict for test factories where `{} as MyType` is intentional, requiring the milder `"allow-as-parameter"` setting to preserve test ergonomics.

---

**Pattern 433** — `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-assignment` flags assignments of `any`-typed values to typed variables, stopping `any` contamination at the point of assignment
```typescript
// ❌ Assigning `any` to a typed variable silently invalidates the type annotation
interface ServerConfig { host: string; port: number }
declare const raw: string;
const parsed = JSON.parse(raw);                 // parsed: any
const config: ServerConfig = parsed;            // Error: unsafe assignment of `any` to ServerConfig

// ❌ Destructuring from `any` spreads `any` to every binding
declare function getContext(): any;
const { host, port, timeout } = getContext();   // host/port/timeout: all any

// ❌ Array element from any[] carries any into downstream typed code
declare function query(): Promise<any[]>;
interface Row { id: string; value: number }
const rows: any[] = await query();
const first: Row = rows[0];                     // Error: unsafe assignment from any[]

// ✅ Validate at the `any` boundary before assigning to typed variables
import { z } from "zod";
const ServerConfigSchema = z.object({ host: z.string(), port: z.number() });
const config2 = ServerConfigSchema.parse(JSON.parse(raw)); // config2: ServerConfig — safe

// ✅ Type-guard for untyped query results
function isRow(r: unknown): r is Row {
  return typeof r === "object" && r !== null && "id" in r && "value" in r;
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-assignment` prevents the silent contamination where a single `any`-typed source (JSON.parse, untyped DB driver, `process.env`) invalidates type annotations throughout the downstream call graph — catching the entire class of defects where the type annotation gives false assurance — but it produces a high volume of errors in codebases without schema validation infrastructure, requiring significant upfront investment in `zod`/`valibot` schemas before the rule can be enabled project-wide rather than incrementally on new files.

---

**Pattern 434** — `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-member-access` flags property accesses on `any`-typed values, preventing `any` from propagating through member chains into otherwise-typed code
```typescript
// ❌ Property access on `any` — each access also returns `any`, infecting the chain
declare function loadRaw(): any;
const raw = loadRaw();
const host    = raw.server.host;              // Error: unsafe member access on `any`
const retries = raw.config.retries ?? 3;      // Error: unsafe member access on `any`
const hosts   = raw.upstream.hosts.join(","); // chain of `any` — no type checking

// ❌ JSON.parse member access — payload.user.id is `any` because payload is `any`
declare const body: string;
const payload = JSON.parse(body);             // payload: any
const userId  = payload.user.id;              // Error: `user` and `id` both `any`
const perm    = payload.user.roles[0];        // Error: unsafe array index on `any`

// ✅ Validate before member access — all downstream accesses are type-safe
import { z } from "zod";
const BodySchema = z.object({
  user: z.object({ id: z.string(), roles: z.array(z.string()) }),
});
const validated = BodySchema.parse(JSON.parse(body));
const userId2 = validated.user.id;            // string — type-safe
const perm2   = validated.user.roles[0];      // string | undefined (noUncheckedIndexedAccess)

// ✅ Ambient declaration for untyped SDKs instead of `any` member access at every call site
declare module "legacy-sdk" {
  interface Cfg { server: { host: string; port: number }; retries: number }
  export function getCfg(): Cfg;
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-member-access` prevents `any` from propagating through member chains — where a single unvalidated source silently disables type checking for every downstream property read — but it is the highest-noise rule in `@typescript-eslint/recommended-type-checked`, firing on every `process.env.VAR` access, `JSON.parse` member read, and untyped SDK call in a codebase that lacks validation wrappers, making it impractical to enable globally before establishing validated-data infrastructure at every untyped boundary.

---

### Community Gotchas

**G68-1** — `const enum` members are inlined by the TypeScript compiler but emit nothing under `isolatedModules`, causing "Cannot access ambient const enums" errors in esbuild and Vite pipelines
Teams using `const enum` to avoid the runtime enum object discover that enabling `isolatedModules: true` — required by esbuild, SWC, and Babel for single-file transpilation — causes "Cannot access ambient const enums when 'isolatedModules' is enabled." The root cause is that `const enum` inlining requires the compiler to read the enum declaration from another file, a cross-file operation incompatible with file-at-a-time transpilation. Teams that relied on `const enum` in a `tsc`-only build and then migrate to Vite or esbuild encounter compile errors on every file that imports a `const enum`, even though the `tsc --noEmit` type-check pass (which ignores `isolatedModules` for checking purposes) still succeeds.
Why this matters: The `isolatedModules` constraint is invisible until a bundler change exposes it. Teams that run `tsc --noEmit` for type-checking and esbuild for bundling have a split pipeline where `tsc` passes but the esbuild bundle fails, reporting the error at bundle time rather than at type-check time and breaking the shift-left principle that defects should surface at the earliest possible stage.
Fix: Replace `const enum` with regular `enum` combined with `@typescript-eslint/prefer-enum-initializers` to keep values stable, or replace with `as const` object literals: `const Dir = { Up: "UP", Down: "DOWN" } as const; type Dir = typeof Dir[keyof typeof Dir];`. Add `"isolatedModules": true` to `tsconfig.json` so `tsc --noEmit` surfaces the incompatibility at type-check time before the bundler ever runs.

---

**G68-2** — `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` adds `| undefined` to every array index and object index-signature access, producing hundreds of type errors on code that was valid under `strict: true`
Teams enabling `noUncheckedIndexedAccess: true` to improve array safety find that the option adds `| undefined` to every `arr[i]` and `obj[key]` access, immediately producing hundreds of TS2345 and TS2322 errors across data-transformation pipelines, test fixture builders, and utility functions that use `arr[0]`, `arr[arr.length - 1]`, and index-based loops where the developer knows the array is non-empty. The volume of errors is far larger than expected because `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is positioned near the `strict` family of flags in the documentation, leading teams to assume it is as safe to enable as `strictNullChecks`.
Why this matters: Teams that enable it globally either disable it immediately after seeing the error count or suppress errors with non-null assertion operators (`!`), which silences the errors without adding the runtime bounds check that would actually make the code safe. The net result is more `!` operators in the codebase — a worse safety posture than not enabling the flag at all.
Fix: Enable `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` incrementally using TypeScript project references. For known-non-empty arrays, use destructuring with defaults (`const [first = fallback] = arr`) or a bounds-checking helper rather than `!`. For index loops, prefer `for...of` or `.forEach()` which avoid indexed access types, or use `.at(0)` with an explicit undefined check to communicate intent.

---

**G68-3** — `JSON.parse` always returns `any` in TypeScript, and `JSON.stringify`/`JSON.parse` deep-clone round-trips silently drop `undefined` values, `Date` objects, and class instances
Teams using `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))` as a cheap deep-clone utility discover that the round-trip silently drops object keys with `undefined` values, converts `Date` instances to ISO-format strings (not back to `Date` objects on parse), and strips functions, `Symbol` keys, and class prototype methods. TypeScript cannot detect the structural transformation because `JSON.parse` always returns `any`. A clone of `{ createdAt: new Date(), deletedAt: undefined }` produces `{ createdAt: "2026-05-14T00:00:00.000Z" }` — a completely different shape — with no compile-time error.
Why this matters: The `JSON.parse` `any` return type creates pressure to add `as MyType` casts that satisfy `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-assignment` without adding actual validation. The cast pattern is more dangerous than the raw `any` because it converts a visible unsafety marker into an invisible lie about the value's shape, silencing both the lint rule and the developer's awareness that the data is unvalidated.
Fix: Use `JSON.parse(raw) as unknown` followed by a `zod` or `valibot` schema parse rather than `as MyType` casts. For deep cloning, use `structuredClone()` (Node.js 17+, all modern browsers) which handles `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, and `ArrayBuffer` correctly and throws a `DataCloneError` for non-cloneable values rather than silently omitting them.

---

**G68-4** — Enabling `@typescript-eslint/recommended-type-checked` without `parserOptions.project` causes all type-checked rules to silently become no-ops, producing zero lint errors on unsafe code
Teams adding `@typescript-eslint/recommended-type-checked` to ESLint discover that type-checked rules — `no-unsafe-assignment`, `no-unsafe-member-access`, `no-floating-promises`, `no-misused-promises` — report zero errors even on obviously unsafe code. The cause is that type-checked rules require `parserOptions.project` to point to a valid `tsconfig.json` so the ESLint parser can build the TypeScript type program. If `parserOptions.project` is missing or wrong, the parser falls back to a type-information-free mode and all type-checked rules silently disable themselves rather than emitting a configuration error.
Why this matters: The silent no-op behavior leaves no signal that the configuration is broken. A developer who enables `recommended-type-checked` and writes `const x: string = JSON.parse("1")` expects a lint error and sees nothing, concluding either that the rule is not enforced or that the assignment is safe. The problem is especially common in monorepos where `parserOptions.project` must enumerate every package's `tsconfig.json` and a missing entry for a new package silently disables type checking for all files in that package.
Fix: Set `parserOptions.project: true` (ESLint flat config) or `parserOptions.project: ["./tsconfig.json"]` (legacy `.eslintrc`) and smoke-test by intentionally writing a `no-floating-promises` violation to confirm it reports an error. In monorepos, use `parserOptions.project: true` in per-package flat config override blocks so each package automatically resolves its nearest `tsconfig.json`. Add a CI check that runs `eslint --rule '{"@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-assignment":"error"}' --print-config src/index.ts` and fails if the rule appears disabled.

---

**G68-5** — `@typescript-eslint/strict-boolean-expressions` flags every non-boolean truthiness check including `if (str)`, `if (arr.length)`, and `while (queue.length)`, making the noise-to-signal ratio too high for most projects
Teams enabling `@typescript-eslint/strict-boolean-expressions` discover that the rule flags virtually every idiomatic JavaScript guard — `if (value)`, `if (str)`, `if (arr.length)`, `while (items.length)` — because these expressions are not strictly boolean. The rule requires `if (value !== undefined && value !== null)`, `if (str !== "")`, `if (arr.length > 0)` instead, significantly increasing verbosity across patterns that every JavaScript developer recognizes as correct and safe.
Why this matters: The rule's strict mode has no per-type opt-out — every non-boolean expression in a boolean context is flagged regardless of whether the truthiness check is actually dangerous. Teams that enable it expecting to catch `if (userCount)` (where `0` is a valid count that should not be treated as falsy) also get errors on `if (username)` (where `""` is the edge case they actually care about) and on `if (user)` (where `null` is the only falsy case and the check is unambiguously correct). The flood of errors causes most teams to disable the rule entirely rather than configure it precisely.
Fix: Use the `allowNullableBoolean`, `allowNullableString`, `allowNullableNumber`, and `allowNullableObject` options to enable the rule only for the specific type categories where truthiness checks are dangerous. The highest-value settings are `allowNullableString: false` and `allowNullableNumber: false` to catch `""` and `0` edge cases, with `allowNullableObject: true` to allow the idiomatic `if (user)` null check. Alternatively, enable `@typescript-eslint/no-unnecessary-condition` which catches provably-always-true or provably-always-false conditions without flagging legitimate idiomatic truthiness checks.

## Cycle 69 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 435** — `@typescript-eslint/prefer-nullish-coalescing` replaces `||` with `??` to avoid swallowing `0` and `""` as falsy defaults
```typescript
// @typescript-eslint/prefer-nullish-coalescing flags logical-OR (||) default patterns
// where the left operand can be 0, "", false, or NaN — falsy but intentionally valid values

// ❌ || swallows the valid value 0 and returns the fallback instead
function getPageSize(size: number | undefined): number {
  return size || 25;   // returns 25 when size is 0 — silently wrong
}

// ❌ || swallows an empty string — a valid empty-label scenario
function getLabel(label: string | null): string {
  return label || "Untitled";  // returns "Untitled" when label is "" — wrong
}

// ❌ Chained || silently replaces an intentional "" env-var "disable" sentinel
function resolveEndpoint(env: string | undefined, fallback: string): string {
  return env || process.env.API_URL || fallback;
}

// ✅ ?? only falls through on null or undefined — preserves all other values
function getPageSize2(size: number | undefined): number {
  return size ?? 25;   // returns 0 when size is 0 — correct
}

function getLabel2(label: string | null): string {
  return label ?? "Untitled";  // returns "" when label is "" — correct
}

function resolveEndpoint2(env: string | undefined, fallback: string): string {
  return env ?? process.env.API_URL ?? fallback;
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/prefer-nullish-coalescing` eliminates the class of bugs where `0`, `""`, `false`, or `NaN` — all valid domain values — are silently replaced by a `||` fallback because they are falsy, and it requires type information to distinguish `T | null | undefined` (where `??` is appropriate) from plain `T` — but migrating existing `||` chains in a large codebase triggers a cascade of fixes in conditional logic that has accumulated defensive behavior depending on the falsy-swallowing semantics, and callers that intentionally use `||` to treat `0` as "not set" must be reviewed individually rather than auto-fixed in bulk.

---

**Pattern 436** — `@typescript-eslint/use-unknown-in-catch-variables` types `catch` bindings as `unknown` instead of `any` to force explicit narrowing before use
```typescript
// @typescript-eslint/use-unknown-in-catch-variables (also enabled by the tsconfig
// option useUnknownInCatchVariables) types every catch parameter as unknown,
// preventing unsafe any access in error handling paths

// ❌ err is typed as any without the tsconfig flag — all property access is unsafe
async function saveUser(user: User): Promise<void> {
  try {
    await db.users.insert(user);
  } catch (err) {
    // TypeScript allows this — err is any — but it may crash at runtime
    logger.error(`DB error code=${err.code} message=${err.message}`);
    metrics.increment(`db.error.${err.type}`);
  }
}

// ✅ err is unknown — must narrow before any property access
async function saveUser2(user: User): Promise<void> {
  try {
    await db.users.insert(user);
  } catch (err: unknown) {
    if (err instanceof DatabaseError) {
      logger.error(`DB error code=${err.code} message=${err.message}`);
      metrics.increment(`db.error.${err.type}`);
    } else if (err instanceof Error) {
      logger.error(`Unexpected error: ${err.message}`);
    } else {
      logger.error(`Unknown throw: ${String(err)}`);
    }
  }
}

// ✅ Utility that converts any thrown value to a string message
function toErrorMessage(err: unknown): string {
  if (err instanceof Error) return err.message;
  if (typeof err === "string") return err;
  return `Non-error thrown: ${JSON.stringify(err)}`;
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/use-unknown-in-catch-variables` closes the catch-block type-safety gap where `any`-typed bindings bypass all narrowing — especially valuable at I/O boundaries (DB, HTTP, filesystem) where the thrown value's shape is genuinely unknown at compile time — but it converts every catch block into a narrowing exercise and is particularly disruptive in codebases with dozens of catch blocks that were written assuming `err.message` is always accessible, driving a migration that must audit each block individually for correctness.

---

**Pattern 437** — `@typescript-eslint/require-await` flags `async` functions that contain no `await` expression, surfacing accidental async promotions
```typescript
// @typescript-eslint/require-await flags async functions whose bodies
// contain no await expression — adding the async keyword without any
// asynchronous operation wraps the return in an unnecessary Promise microtask

// ❌ async added to match an interface — but the implementation is synchronous
interface MetricsReporter {
  report(event: string, data: Record<string, number>): Promise<void>;
}

class ConsoleReporter implements MetricsReporter {
  async report(event: string, data: Record<string, number>): Promise<void> {
    console.log(`[${event}]`, data);   // no await — synchronous console.log
  }
}

// ❌ async used "for safety" in a configuration builder
async function buildDbConfig(env: NodeJS.ProcessEnv): Promise<DbConfig> {
  return {
    host: env.DB_HOST ?? "localhost",
    port: Number(env.DB_PORT ?? "5432"),
    name: env.DB_NAME ?? "app",
  };  // no await — the object literal is constructed synchronously
}

// ✅ Remove async from the synchronous implementation
class ConsoleReporter2 implements MetricsReporter {
  report(event: string, data: Record<string, number>): Promise<void> {
    console.log(`[${event}]`, data);
    return Promise.resolve();   // explicit synchronous fulfilment
  }
}

// ✅ Remove async and return the config directly
function buildDbConfig2(env: NodeJS.ProcessEnv): DbConfig {
  return {
    host: env.DB_HOST ?? "localhost",
    port: Number(env.DB_PORT ?? "5432"),
    name: env.DB_NAME ?? "app",
  };
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/require-await` catches accidental async promotions that add microtask overhead without enabling asynchronous behavior — preventing the anti-pattern where every method is marked async "just in case" — but it requires synchronous interface implementations to use the verbose `Promise.resolve(value)` pattern instead of simply returning the value, and it conflicts with teams that prefer uniform async signatures across all interface implementations to simplify future refactoring.

---

**Pattern 438** — `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-assignment` blocks `any`-typed values from being assigned to typed variables, containing `any` propagation at the source
```typescript
// @typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-assignment fires when an any-typed expression
// is assigned to a typed variable — preventing any from silently overwriting
// the declared type and creating phantom type safety downstream

// Common scenario: using a library with incomplete or no type definitions
declare function parseConfig(raw: string): any;

// ❌ The declared types for timeout and host are lies — the actual values are any
const settings: AppSettings = parseConfig(process.env.APP_CONFIG!);
const timeout: number = settings.timeout;   // Error: unsafe assignment
const host: string = settings.database.host;  // chained unsafe access

// ❌ JSON.parse always returns any — assignment to typed variable is unsafe
const manifest: PackageManifest = JSON.parse(
  fs.readFileSync("package.json", "utf8")  // any — no validation
);

// ✅ Validate at the parsing boundary with a schema — all downstream access is safe
import { z } from "zod";

const AppSettingsSchema = z.object({
  timeout: z.number().int().min(0),
  database: z.object({ host: z.string().min(1) }),
});

const rawConfig = parseConfig(process.env.APP_CONFIG!);
const settings2: AppSettings = AppSettingsSchema.parse(rawConfig);
// settings2 is genuinely typed — AppSettingsSchema.parse throws on invalid data

const PackageManifestSchema = z.object({ name: z.string(), version: z.string() });
const manifest2 = PackageManifestSchema.parse(
  JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync("package.json", "utf8"))
);
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-assignment` acts as a containment barrier that prevents `any` from spreading from untyped library APIs into typed application code — surfacing every point where the type system's guarantees are silently abandoned — but it produces a high error volume in codebases that interface with untyped or loosely typed libraries, requiring either runtime validation at every call site or per-call-site `eslint-disable` comments that trade correctness visibility for development velocity; enabling it in a legacy codebase typically requires a multi-sprint remediation effort before the rule can run clean.

---

**Pattern 439** — `@typescript-eslint/no-unnecessary-type-parameters` removes generic type parameters that are used only once and add no reusability benefit
```typescript
// @typescript-eslint/no-unnecessary-type-parameters flags type parameters
// that appear exactly once in the signature — they cannot establish any
// relationship between types and are equivalent to `unknown` at that position

// ❌ T is a phantom — it appears only as the return type, not in any parameter
function coerceToType<T>(value: unknown): T {
  return value as T;   // cast satisfies T, but provides no actual safety
}
// Caller: coerceToType<User>(apiResponse) — feels typed but is a disguised any-cast

// ❌ T appears only in one parameter position — just use unknown
function validateWith<T>(value: T, predicate: (v: T) => boolean): boolean {
  return predicate(value);
}
// Caller must pass matching types but the generic provides no cross-parameter constraint
// — the same function with unknown works identically for the caller

// ❌ Genuine counter-example — A and B ARE used in relationship
function transform<A, B>(input: A, fn: (v: A) => B): B {
  return fn(input);  // A used in param + fn param; B used in fn return + function return
  // Removing A or B would lose the input→output relationship — valid generic
}

// ✅ Remove phantom T — acknowledge the cast explicitly at the call site
function coerceToType2(value: unknown): unknown {
  return value;
}
// Caller: const user = value as User; — the cast is visible and reviewable
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-unnecessary-type-parameters` prevents phantom generics that create an illusion of type safety without establishing any actual cross-type relationship — particularly harmful in utility functions like `coerceToType<T>` where the `as T` cast satisfies the return type without any runtime guarantee — but it occasionally fires on generics that are syntactically single-use yet semantically meaningful as documentation constraints, and removing them makes API surfaces less self-describing for callers who rely on the named type parameter to understand the function's intent.

---

**Pattern 440** — `@typescript-eslint/no-redundant-type-constituents` removes union and intersection members that mathematically subsume or annihilate other members
```typescript
// @typescript-eslint/no-redundant-type-constituents flags union/intersection
// members that are absorbed by or cancel other members

// ❌ string already includes all string literals — the literals are redundant
type EventName = string | "click" | "keydown" | "submit";
//               ^^^^^^ — string subsumes the literals; narrowing to them is impossible

// ❌ unknown in a union absorbs everything — all other members are unreachable
type ApiResult = unknown | { data: User } | null | Error;
//               ^^^^^^^ — unknown subsumes all; collapses to just unknown

// ❌ never in a union is the identity element — it adds nothing
type Handler = (() => void) | never | (() => Promise<void>);

// ❌ any in an intersection overrides everything — collapses to any
type TypedConfig = { timeout: number; host: string } & any;

// ✅ Constrained union: use only the string literals for proper type narrowing
type EventName2 = "click" | "keydown" | "submit";

// ✅ Remove the subsuming member to restore narrowing ability
type ApiResult2 = { data: User } | null | Error;

// ✅ Remove never and any to restore structural typing
type Handler2 = (() => void) | (() => Promise<void>);
type TypedConfig2 = { timeout: number; host: string };
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-redundant-type-constituents` catches type algebra mistakes where a broad type silently makes narrow types unreachable — particularly harmful in discriminated union APIs where a developer intends `EventName` to be constrained but accidentally makes it freely assignable — but the rule fires on intentional "escape hatch" union patterns (`string | KnownLiteral`) where authors want arbitrary string values while advertising known literals for IDE autocomplete, a legitimate pattern accommodated by the `string & {}` workaround that preserves autocompletion without triggering the rule.

---

**Pattern 441** — `@typescript-eslint/prefer-promise-reject-errors` enforces that `Promise.reject()` and `reject()` callbacks receive `Error` objects rather than arbitrary values
```typescript
// @typescript-eslint/prefer-promise-reject-errors requires that values passed
// to Promise.reject() and the reject() executor callback are Error instances

// ❌ Rejecting with a string — the catch handler receives a string, not an Error
// — no stack trace, no instanceof Error check possible
function loadModule(path: string): Promise<unknown> {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    if (!path.endsWith(".js") && !path.endsWith(".ts")) {
      reject(`Invalid module path: ${path}`);   // string — useless in catch
    }
    // ... dynamic import logic
  });
}

// ❌ Rejecting with a status object — structured but loses the call stack
async function callApi(endpoint: string): Promise<Response> {
  const res = await fetch(endpoint);
  if (!res.ok) {
    return Promise.reject({ status: res.status, statusText: res.statusText });
  }
  return res;
}

// ✅ Reject with a typed Error subclass — stack trace + structured data
class ModuleLoadError extends Error {
  constructor(readonly path: string, reason: string) {
    super(`Cannot load module "${path}": ${reason}`);
    this.name = "ModuleLoadError";
  }
}

function loadModule2(path: string): Promise<unknown> {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    if (!path.endsWith(".js") && !path.endsWith(".ts")) {
      reject(new ModuleLoadError(path, "unsupported extension"));
    }
    // ... dynamic import logic
  });
}

class ApiError extends Error {
  constructor(readonly status: number, readonly statusText: string) {
    super(`HTTP ${status}: ${statusText}`);
    this.name = "ApiError";
  }
}

async function callApi2(endpoint: string): Promise<Response> {
  const res = await fetch(endpoint);
  if (!res.ok) return Promise.reject(new ApiError(res.status, res.statusText));
  return res;
}
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/prefer-promise-reject-errors` ensures that rejection values carry a stack trace and support `instanceof Error` narrowing in catch blocks — complementing `use-unknown-in-catch-variables` to create a complete type-safe async error pipeline — but it prohibits the widely used REST-API pattern of rejecting with a plain object (`{ status, message }`) that carries structured error data beyond a simple string, requiring teams to subclass `Error` for every domain error variant; the subclassing overhead is significant in codebases with many distinct API error shapes.

---

**Pattern 442** — Vitest `expect.extend` with TypeScript declaration merging creates type-safe domain-specific matchers that encode invariants at the unit layer
```typescript
// Domain-specific matchers shift invariant checks left: violations appear
// at unit test time as a single readable assertion, not as multi-line
// manual assertion blocks scattered across the test suite

import { expect } from "vitest";

// Matcher: verify audit-log entry structure
expect.extend({
  toBeAuditLogEntry(received: unknown) {
    if (typeof received !== "object" || received === null) {
      return { pass: false, message: () => `Expected audit log entry object` };
    }
    const entry = received as Record<string, unknown>;
    const required: Array<[string, string]> = [
      ["eventType", "string"],
      ["userId", "string"],
      ["timestamp", "number"],
      ["correlationId", "string"],
    ];
    for (const [field, type] of required) {
      if (typeof entry[field] !== type) {
        return {
          pass: false,
          message: () =>
            `Audit entry missing or wrong type for "${field}": got ${typeof entry[field]}, want ${type}`,
        };
      }
    }
    return { pass: true, message: () => "Valid audit log entry" };
  },
});

// TypeScript augmentation — typed in all test files that import this setup
interface CustomMatchers<R = unknown> {
  toBeAuditLogEntry(): R;
}
declare module "vitest" {
  interface Assertion<T = unknown> extends CustomMatchers<T> {}
  interface AsymmetricMatchersContaining extends CustomMatchers {}
}

// Usage — the entire structural rule is a single typed assertion
it("emits a valid audit entry on user login", async () => {
  const entry = await auditLog.getLatest();
  expect(entry).toBeAuditLogEntry();
});
```
Tradeoff: Vitest custom matchers centralize domain invariant checks into reusable typed assertions, preventing multi-line assertion boilerplate from being duplicated across dozens of tests and making structural requirements visible in test output rather than buried in multi-assertion blocks — but the `declare module "vitest"` augmentation must be loaded in every test file (via `setupFiles` in vitest config) and is tightly coupled to the vitest version's `Assertion` interface shape, breaking silently on major version upgrades where the interface changes.

**Pattern 443** — `lint-staged` scoped transforms run only on staged files, reducing pre-commit hook time from minutes to seconds for large monorepos
```json
// .lintstagedrc.json — transform only staged files, not the full project
{
  "*.{ts,tsx}": [
    "eslint --fix --max-warnings=0 --no-eslintrc --config eslint.staged.config.mjs",
    "prettier --write"
  ],
  "*.{js,mjs,cjs}": [
    "eslint --fix --max-warnings=0",
    "prettier --write"
  ],
  "*.{json,yaml,yml,md}": ["prettier --write"],
  "package.json": ["sort-package-json"]
}
```
```typescript
// eslint.staged.config.mjs — fast pre-commit config, no type-aware rules
// These rules run in <2s even on 100 staged files:
export default [
  {
    rules: {
      "@typescript-eslint/no-unused-vars": "error",
      "no-var": "error",
      "prefer-const": "error",
      "no-console": "warn",
      "eqeqeq": ["error", "always"],
    },
    // DELIBERATELY OMITTED (require parserOptions.project — 10-30x slower):
    // @typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-assignment
    // @typescript-eslint/no-misused-promises
    // @typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises
  },
];
// Full type-aware lint runs in CI: eslint --config eslint.config.mjs
```
Tradeoff: `lint-staged` with a syntax-only ESLint config reduces pre-commit hook latency from 30-90 seconds (full type-aware lint) to 2-8 seconds on staged files — making the hook fast enough that developers don't bypass it with `--no-verify` — but the fast config must omit type-aware rules (the highest-value ones for catching real bugs), maintaining a "passes pre-commit but fails CI" gap that can only be closed with faster type-checking infrastructure or by accepting that some violations are deferred to CI.

**Pattern 444** — `tsc --noEmit --incremental` with a gitignored `.tsbuildinfo` file enables sub-10-second type-check turnaround during development
```typescript
// tsconfig.json — enable incremental type-check caching
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "noEmit": true,
    "incremental": true,
    "tsBuildInfoFile": ".tsbuildinfo",
    "composite": true,
    "declarationMap": true,
    "strict": true
  },
  "include": ["src/**/*", "tests/**/*"]
}

// tsconfig.build.json — production emit (separate cache file)
{
  "extends": "./tsconfig.json",
  "compilerOptions": {
    "noEmit": false,
    "tsBuildInfoFile": ".tsbuildinfo.build",
    "outDir": "dist",
    "declaration": true
  }
}

// .gitignore — MUST exclude tsbuildinfo files (they encode machine-local paths)
// .tsbuildinfo
// .tsbuildinfo.build

// package.json scripts
// "typecheck":       "tsc --noEmit --incremental"
// "typecheck:watch": "tsc --noEmit --watch --incremental"
// "build":           "tsc --build tsconfig.build.json"
// "typecheck:clean": "rm -f .tsbuildinfo && tsc --noEmit"
```
Tradeoff: `tsc --noEmit --incremental` reduces type-check from 45-120 seconds to 3-15 seconds for unchanged files by caching the compiler's analysis state in `.tsbuildinfo` — making pre-commit type-checking feasible — but the cache file encodes absolute local paths, must be gitignored, becomes invalid after TypeScript version upgrades (silently skipping files under some cache-reuse conditions), and can diverge after branch switches with large type changes; teams must document and practice the `typecheck:clean` recovery path before relying on incremental mode in CI.

**Pattern 445** — Knip detects exported symbols, dead dependencies, and unused files that TypeScript and ESLint cannot surface without whole-project graph analysis
```typescript
// knip.json — configure Knip for a TypeScript monorepo
{
  "entry": ["src/index.ts", "src/cli.ts", "src/workers/*.ts"],
  "project": ["src/**/*.ts"],
  "ignore": [
    "src/**/*.test.ts",
    "src/**/*.spec.ts",
    "src/generated/**"
  ],
  "ignoreDependencies": ["ts-node", "tsx"],
  "ignoreExportsUsedInFile": true,
  "rules": {
    "files": "error",
    "exports": "error",
    "types": "error",
    "nsExports": "error",
    "dependencies": "warn",
    "devDependencies": "warn",
    "unlisted": "error",
    "binaries": "warn"
  }
}

// .github/workflows/ci.yml
// - name: Dead code check
//   run: npx knip --no-progress
//   # Fails the CI run on any exported-but-unreachable symbol, file, or dependency
```
Tradeoff: Knip performs whole-project import-graph analysis to identify exports, types, and files unreachable from entry points — dead code that `noUnusedLocals` misses because it only checks file-local declarations — but Knip requires accurate entry-point configuration (a missing entry causes Knip to report live exports as dead), cannot resolve template-literal dynamic imports (plugin registries and locale loaders generate systematic false positives), and the `unlisted` rule fires on runtime-loaded binaries and devDependency-used scripts, requiring per-dependency ignores during initial adoption.

**Pattern 446** — `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-member-access` blocks property access on `any`-typed values, forcing schema validation before accessing untyped external data
```typescript
// @typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-member-access fires when accessing a named
// property on a value that TypeScript considers to be of type any

// ❌ Express req.body is typed as any — every property access is unsafe
import express, { Request, Response } from "express";

const router = express.Router();
router.post("/orders", (req: Request, res: Response) => {
  const userId = req.body.userId;             // unsafe — body is any
  const items = req.body.lineItems;           // unsafe — chained any
  const total = req.body.payment.amount;      // unsafe — runtime crash if missing
  const currency = req.body.payment.currency; // unsafe
  return processOrder({ userId, items, total, currency });
});

// ✅ Validate the body with a schema before accessing any fields
import { z } from "zod";

const OrderSchema = z.object({
  userId: z.string().uuid(),
  lineItems: z.array(z.object({ sku: z.string(), qty: z.number().int().min(1) })),
  payment: z.object({
    amount: z.number().positive(),
    currency: z.enum(["USD", "EUR", "GBP"]),
  }),
});

router.post("/orders", (req: Request, res: Response) => {
  const result = OrderSchema.safeParse(req.body);
  if (!result.success) {
    return res.status(422).json({ errors: result.error.flatten() });
  }
  const { userId, lineItems, payment } = result.data;  // fully typed, safe
  return processOrder({ userId, items: lineItems, ...payment });
});
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-member-access` forces runtime validation at every `any`-typed API boundary, eliminating the entire class of "cannot read properties of undefined" runtime crashes from mismatched payload shapes — but `@types/express` types `req.body` as `any`, meaning the rule fires on every existing Express route handler in a codebase, producing hundreds of errors; teams cannot enable the rule incrementally without either augmenting Express's types globally or suppressing every existing violation.

---

**Pattern 447** — ESLint `no-restricted-imports` enforces architectural dependency rules by failing lint on forbidden cross-layer imports
```typescript
// eslint.config.mjs — architectural boundary rules as lint errors
// Each rule fires before code review, at the point the import is written

export default [
  {
    // Domain layer: pure business logic, no I/O dependencies allowed
    files: ["src/domain/**/*.ts"],
    rules: {
      "no-restricted-imports": ["error", {
        patterns: [
          {
            group: ["*/infrastructure/*", "*/infrastructure/**"],
            message:
              "Domain must not depend on Infrastructure. Define a port interface in domain/ports/ and inject via constructor.",
          },
          {
            group: ["express", "fastify", "pg", "mysql2", "redis", "mongoose", "axios", "node-fetch"],
            message: "Domain must not import I/O libraries. All I/O is infrastructure's responsibility.",
          },
          {
            group: ["../application/**", "../../application/**"],
            message: "Domain must not depend on Application layer (circular dependency risk).",
          },
        ],
      }],
    },
  },
  {
    // Shared utilities: must not import application or feature code
    files: ["src/shared/**/*.ts"],
    rules: {
      "no-restricted-imports": ["error", {
        patterns: [
          { group: ["../features/**"], message: "Shared utilities must not import feature code." },
          { group: ["../application/**"], message: "Shared utilities must not import application code." },
        ],
      }],
    },
  },
];
```
Tradeoff: `no-restricted-imports` with glob patterns detects layering violations at lint time — catching a `domain/` module importing `pg` directly before it ever reaches code review — with zero overhead (no type-checker required) — but it only matches on import path strings (not resolved module identity), must be maintained manually as directory structure evolves, cannot suggest the correct alternative (e.g., which port interface to use), and the error message is the only documentation of the architectural intent, making it critical that messages are specific and actionable.

---

**Pattern 448** — `@typescript-eslint/no-import-type-side-effects` ensures type-only imports are fully elided and cannot trigger unintended module initialization
```typescript
// @typescript-eslint/no-import-type-side-effects requires that type-only
// imports use the `import type` form — not inline `type` modifiers on
// individual specifiers — to guarantee compiler-level elision

// ❌ Mixed import with inline type modifier — when SomeClass is unused at runtime,
// the import statement survives in the emitted JS as `import {} from "./registry"`
// and module initialization code (class decorators, side-effect registrations) runs
import { SomeClass, type SomeType } from "./registry-with-side-effects";

// ❌ Inline type on a sole specifier — looks safe but bundler behavior varies
// Some bundlers preserve `import {} from "..."` as an explicit side-effect import
import { type LogLevel } from "./logging-setup";   // may still load logging-setup.js

// ✅ Full `import type` — guaranteed elision by TypeScript compiler regardless of bundler
import type { SomeType } from "./registry-with-side-effects";
import type { LogLevel } from "./logging-setup";

// ✅ Explicit value import when the module initialization IS wanted
import { SomeClass } from "./registry-with-side-effects";  // intentional side-effect

// tsconfig.json — enforce at compiler level (TypeScript 5.0+):
// "verbatimModuleSyntax": true
// Forces all type-only usage to use `import type` — compile error otherwise
```
Tradeoff: `@typescript-eslint/no-import-type-side-effects` eliminates the bundler-specific bug where inline `type` modifiers on mixed imports leave empty `import {}` statements that still trigger module initialization (class decorator registration, logger setup, DI container population) — critical in library packages and treeshaken bundles — but enabling `verbatimModuleSyntax` alongside this rule is a pervasive breaking change in codebases that use barrel files, requiring `export type { Foo }` for every type-only re-export.

**Pattern 449** — Oxlint as a pre-commit fast-path runs 50-100 AST rules in under 500ms, reserving type-aware ESLint for CI only
```json
// .oxlintrc.json — configure Oxlint for maximum pre-commit throughput
{
  "$schema": "./node_modules/oxlint/configuration_schema.json",
  "rules": {
    "no-unused-vars": "error",
    "no-console": "warn",
    "eqeqeq": ["error", "always"],
    "no-var": "error",
    "prefer-const": "error",
    "no-duplicate-imports": "error",
    "no-shadow": "error",
    "no-undef": "error",
    "no-debugger": "error",
    "no-empty": "warn"
  },
  "env": { "browser": true, "node": true, "es2022": true },
  "ignorePatterns": ["dist/", "node_modules/", "*.generated.ts", "*.d.ts"]
}
```
```typescript
// Two-tier lint pipeline in package.json:
// "lint:fast": "oxlint src/",
// "lint:full": "eslint --config eslint.config.mjs src/ --max-warnings=0"

// .lintstagedrc.json — oxlint runs pre-commit, ESLint runs in CI
// "*.{ts,tsx,js}": ["oxlint --fix"]

// .github/workflows/ci.yml:
// - name: Type-aware lint
//   run: npm run lint:full
//   # Runs @typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-*, no-misused-promises, etc.

```
Tradeoff: Oxlint's Rust-based parallel AST traversal provides 50-100x faster lint times than ESLint on large TypeScript codebases, making meaningful lint feedback practical on every pre-commit or file-save without developer-visible latency — but Oxlint does not support type-aware rules (requiring `parserOptions.project`) and cannot execute ESLint plugins, so the two-tier architecture is mandatory; type-safety violations (the most impactful class of bugs) bypass pre-commit and are only surfaced in CI, partially defeating the shift-left goal.

---

### Community Gotchas

**G69-1** — `verbatimModuleSyntax` breaks existing `export { Foo }` barrel re-exports when `Foo` is a type, causing hundreds of immediate compile errors on adoption
Teams enabling `verbatimModuleSyntax: true` (TypeScript 5.0) to enforce type-import elision discover that every index barrel file that re-exports types with `export { SomeType }` immediately fails compilation with "Re-exporting a type when the '--isolatedModules' flag is provided requires using 'export type'". In large codebases with dozens of barrel files, this produces 50-200 simultaneous compile errors. The root cause is that `verbatimModuleSyntax` requires the developer to explicitly declare whether each binding is a type or a value at the import and export sites — the compiler no longer infers this — so every `export { X }` where `X` is a type must become `export type { X }`.
Why this matters: Teams treating `verbatimModuleSyntax` as a "drop-in" tsconfig flag are surprised by the migration volume. The flag is especially disruptive in monorepos where public packages use barrel files as their public API surface. Automated codemods (`ts-morph`-based scripts or the VS Code "Add missing import type" bulk action) can handle 80% of cases, but edge cases like namespace re-exports (`export * from`) and conditional re-exports require manual review. Teams that attempt the migration in a feature branch without first quantifying the change surface frequently abandon it or introduce inconsistencies.
Fix: Before enabling `verbatimModuleSyntax`, run `tsc --noEmit` with a temporary config that adds `"isolatedModules": true` (which enforces the same type-export rule without other semantic changes) to preview the required changes. Apply fixes file-by-file starting with leaf packages, working toward root packages. After migration, verify bundle sizes are reduced — smaller outputs confirm the type-import elision is working correctly and justify the migration effort.

---

**G69-2** — Knip incorrectly flags as "unused" all exports consumed only through dynamic `import()` calls whose module path is a template literal or a computed string
Teams adopting Knip for dead-export detection find that entire directories (plugin implementations, locale files, feature modules) are reported as "all exports unused" when those exports are consumed exclusively through dynamic imports with computed module paths. The root cause is that Knip performs static import graph analysis and cannot resolve template-literal module specifiers to specific files. A dynamic import like `await import(\`./plugins/${pluginName}\`)` is opaque to Knip — it sees `./plugins/analytics.ts` exists but has no way to connect the template path to that file.
Why this matters: The false positives are not just noise — they cause teams to add `// @knip:ignore-export` or broad `ignoreExportsUsedInFile` suppressions to every file in the plugin directory, polluting the source and masking genuinely dead exports that accumulate over time. Teams that encounter this limitation early often disable Knip's export analysis entirely rather than managing per-file suppressions, losing the primary value of the tool. The issue is compounded in monorepos where plugin discovery patterns appear in multiple packages.
Fix: Add explicit `entry` patterns in `knip.json` listing plugin directories as entry points (`"entry": ["src/plugins/**/*.ts"]`), telling Knip to treat all exports from those files as reachable without requiring a traced import chain. For higher precision (detecting genuinely dead plugin exports), replace template-literal dynamic imports with a static registry object mapping plugin names to literal `import()` calls — Knip can resolve literal-path dynamic imports statically.

---

**G69-3** — `lint-staged` running `prettier --write` followed by `git add` re-stages formatting changes that were intentionally left unstaged, silently modifying the commit content
Teams using `lint-staged` with a config that runs `prettier --write` discover that when a developer stages only part of a file using `git add -p` (interactive patch staging), `lint-staged` formats the entire file and re-stages all changes — including the hunks the developer intentionally left unstaged. The commit ends up containing the full formatted file rather than only the staged hunks, introducing "ghost changes" that mix formatting noise with the semantically meaningful change.
Why this matters: The `git add -p` workflow is used by developers who practice atomic commits — one logical change per commit for clean, reviewable history. `lint-staged`'s re-staging behavior silently defeats this practice: `prettier --write` writes to the filesystem file (not the staged copy), and `lint-staged`'s automatic `git add` after the transform stages the entire formatted file including the unstaged changes. Because the pre-commit hook succeeds, the developer has no indication that the commit contains more than they intended. This accumulates as formatting-mixed-with-logic commits that are difficult to review and bisect.
Fix: Use `prettier --check` in the `lint-staged` config instead of `prettier --write` — it fails the commit on formatting violations without modifying files, prompting the developer to format manually before re-staging their intended changes. For automatic formatting that respects partial staging, use Biome's `--changed` flag or `@prettier/plugin-git-staged`, both of which operate on the staged file object rather than the filesystem file and avoid re-staging unstaged content.

---

**G69-4** — `tsc --incremental` silently skips re-checking files when the `.tsbuildinfo` cache was generated by a different TypeScript version, producing a stale "all green" result
Teams relying on `tsc --noEmit --incremental` as a pre-commit or CI gate discover that after a TypeScript version upgrade, the `.tsbuildinfo` file from the previous version may be partially reused rather than fully invalidated — particularly in CI systems that cache `node_modules` and in developer environments where the upgrade was applied with `npm install` without wiping `node_modules`. Type-check skips files whose entry in the stale cache appears valid, missing errors that the new TypeScript version would have reported.
Why this matters: TypeScript version upgrades routinely introduce new errors on previously valid code — narrower type inference, new strict checks, changed narrowing semantics. The `.tsbuildinfo` cache was built under the old type-checker's judgement; it cannot be correct under the new version. Teams that do not actively invalidate the cache after upgrading TypeScript can ship code that fails type-check under the CI TypeScript version while appearing clean on developer machines with a stale cache. The gap is only discovered when the next CI run that lacks the cached `.tsbuildinfo` (a new CI runner, a fresh checkout) reports errors that were silently skipped for days.
Fix: Implement a `postinstall` script that compares the installed TypeScript version against a `.typescript-version` sentinel file and deletes all `.tsbuildinfo` files if the version changed. Alternatively, embed the TypeScript version into the `tsBuildInfoFile` name (e.g., `.tsbuildinfo.5.4.5`) so different versions never share a cache file, eliminating the need for a cleanup script.

---

**G69-5** — `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-assignment` flags `useState` initializers in React when the initial value is typed as `any` by inference, even when the state type is explicitly annotated
Teams enabling `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-assignment` in a React + TypeScript codebase find errors on `useState` calls where the initial value comes from an `any`-typed source — a common pattern when state is initialized from URL search parameters, `localStorage.getItem()`, or a prop typed as `any` by a third-party library. The rule fires even when the state type is explicitly annotated as `useState<User | null>(parsedUser)` — the annotation on the hook narrows the stored type but does not change the type of the initializer argument passed at the call site, which is still `any`.
Why this matters: React codebases routinely initialize state from browser APIs and untyped sources. Teams interpret the error as a false positive because they believe the explicit `<User | null>` annotation makes the assignment safe. In practice, the annotation is a lie if `parsedUser` is `any` — `useState<User | null>(null as unknown as any)` also satisfies the annotation. Teams who add `eslint-disable` comments to suppress the error at `useState` initializers are removing the rule's signal at exactly the component boundaries where unvalidated external data enters the React tree, which is where runtime type errors most commonly originate.
Fix: Validate the `any`-typed source before passing it to `useState`. Write dedicated typed accessor functions for browser APIs: `function getStoredUser(): User | null { const raw = localStorage.getItem("user"); if (!raw) return null; const parsed = JSON.parse(raw); return UserSchema.parse(parsed); }`. The function returns a genuinely typed value, `useState` receives a `User | null` (not `any`), and the rule is satisfied without suppression. This also centralizes the validation logic so schema changes propagate automatically.
